## XII.

Constat itaque Paracelsistarum, Weigelianorum, Mysticorum, Quakerorum & cæterorum, qui communi illuminatorum nomine vocari solent, opiniones fanaticas in eo conspirare, quod præter corpus & animam rationalem sit in homine substantialis quædam pars divinitus ipsi, &, ut plerique non dissimulant, ex ipsa divina essentia concessa. Eandem doctrinam de tribus partibus hominis satis prolixe explicat Felgenhawer im *Vorhoff/ im heiligen und Allerheiligsten am Tempel GOttes*: cujus fanatici libelli lectiones singulæ singularum partium rationes & Fanaticorum de iis somnia satis declarant. Conferri etiam meretur Bartholomaei Sclei *anständige allgemeine GOttes Lehre*/ nec non das *Buch des Zeugnisses des verborgenen Ackerschatzes*/ cujus Autor se ipsum vocat HIEL, das *einwesige Leben GOttes*/ ut & des von GOtt hocherleuchteten Matthes Weyer *gründlicher Unterricht*/ & similia a furiis illis conscripta librorum portenta, indigna sane quibus legendis quis bonas ac irrevocabiles horas perdat.

## XIII.

Cæterum hæc de triplici hominis parte doctrina principem in ipsorum Matæologia locum obtinet. Hanc enim non modo Christianismi totius, sed omnis in universum sapientiæ, quæ in cælo & terra est, fundamentum continere ineptissime jactitat Autor des *Vorhoffs* Cap. XII. At vero si quem forte lateat se quinque habere sensus, vel quæ sit visus vel auditus aut reliquorum natura, anne propterea statuendum, quod isti munere suo fungi nequeant? Non equidem puto. Interim Andreas Christophorus Rafelius hoc dogma tantis extollit encomiis ut non vereatur in *Der Neujahrs Posaune* hunc in modum de eo loqui: *Das ist eigentlich der rechte Grund-Fels/ und das gewisse Fundament/ darauff das Hauß unsers Christenthums soll gesetzet/ geleget und fundiret werden/ soll es bestehen: und daraus alles predigen/ lesen/ schreiben/ GOttes Wort hören/ singen/ beten/ gute Wers*

Theologus Sutor Jacobus Böhmius per spiritum intelligit hominem internum spiritualem, substantiam spiritualem, quæ tertiam constituat partem hominis essentialem, omnibus hominibus, fidelibus & infidelibus inexistentem, per primi hominis lapsum debilitatam sed non penitus extinctam. Vid. Myst. magn. C. XX. Quakerorum de tertia hac parte sententiam explicat Barclajus Apolog. Religionis veræ Christianæ Thef. V. & VI. Consentiunt nimirum illi cum reliquis in eo, quod omnes in universum homines, quotquot in mundum veniunt, intra se habeant præter corpus & animam spiritualem substantiam, ab ipso Deo implantatam, ad gubernandum eos in rebus spiritualibus, sicuti ratio ad dirigendum in rebus naturalibus. Hanc spiritualem substantiam dicit Barclajus esse vehiculum Dei, in quo est & immediate habitat æternum verbum, quod erat apud Deum & Deus erat verbum, realem & spiritualem substantiam: & eandem perhibet esse internum substantiate femen in cordibus nostris, & in impiorum quoque cordibus subsistere, tum quando mortaliter peccant. Omnes igitur in eo conspirant, quod præter corpus organicum anima vegetante & sentiente instructum ipsamque animam rationalem fit tertia quædam substantia ab anima rationali realiter distincta, quæ in ordine ad spiritualia fit ejusmodi propemodum intelligendi & appetendi principium, quale est anima rationalis respectu eorum, quæ naturaliter a nobis cognoscuntur.

XI.

Origo substantiæ hujus spiritualis nec a Barclajo nec a complicibus callide eam dissimulantibus explicatur. Weigelianos ac Böhmistas divinum ortum non dissimulare §. IV. vidimus. Quin Abraham a Franckenberg totidem verbis hoc profitetur in Nofce te ipsum p. 110. *Der ewige Mensch ist aus dem ewig-sprechendem Wort Gottes / aus der Licht-Welt / aus Gottes eigenem Wesen / & p. 52. So ich eine andere Materie wäre als aus GOtt selber / wie würde ich denn sein Kind seyn.*

Quod si non de Orthodoxæ, sed Pseudo-Theologiæ suæ dogmatibus intelligunt, non inficiamur, plerasque opinionum fanaticarum ex hac hypothesi veluti limoso fonte profluxisse. Quicquid enim de statu hominis ante lapsum, de imagine Dei, & peccato originis fabulantur, ficuti nihil fanum, nihil cum orthodoxia conspirans complectitur, sic arenoso huic fundamento superstructum est. Ex impura hac scaturigine promanarunt confictæ ab iis distinctiones, inter hominem, verbum Dei, cultumque divinum, internum & externum, quibus a genuinis primitivæ Ecclesiæ Doctoribus probatis scripturæ interpretationibus, ac sensu literali ad mysticum, & immediatas internas revelationes, ab auditu verbi cultuque publico ad sabbathum suum internum credulas mentes sub singularis sanctitatis specie abducunt. Continet hoc dogma famosum illud γνῶθι σεαυτὸν, quod consequendæ salutis fundamentum continere plurimi ipsorum jactitant. Eandem originem agnoscunt Annihilationes, Introversiones, Recollectiones, quæ ficuti a Böhmio, Hoburgio, Antonia Bourignonia, miris extolluntur encomiis, sic orthodoxæ Protestantium doctrinæ e limpidis divinarum scripturarum fontibus haustæ e diametro repugnant. Idem de Christificationibus, Deificationibus & similibus figmentis atque vocabulorum monstris dicendum, quibus fanam de Regeneratione doctrinam veluti obscurissimis nebulis tenebrarum filii involvunt.

<meta>continues from previous page: the author is beginning to discuss what the "Spirit" or spiritual substance is in the view of these thinkers.</meta>

understood by this Spirit or spiritual substance, it is best to hear their own testimony. The <term>Shoemaker-Theologian Jacob Boehme</term> understands by "spirit" the internal spiritual man, a spiritual substance that constitutes the third essential part of man, existing in all people—both the faithful and the unfaithful—which was weakened by the fall of the first man but not completely extinguished. See *The Great Mystery*, chapter 20. <term>Barclay</term> explains the opinion of the Quakers concerning this third part in his *Apology for the True Christian Religion*, theses 5 and 6. They certainly agree with the others in this: that all people everywhere, as many as come into the world, have within themselves, besides a body and a soul, a spiritual substance implanted by God himself to govern them in spiritual matters, just as reason directs them in natural matters. Barclay says this spiritual substance is the <term>vehicle of God</term> <gloss>Latin: vehiculum Dei</gloss>, in which the eternal Word (which was with God and was God) exists and immediately dwells—a real and spiritual substance. He also claims this is the internal <term>substantial seed</term> in our hearts, which subsists even in the hearts of the wicked, even when they sin mortally. All of them, therefore, conspire in the idea that besides the organic body (equipped with a vegetative and sensitive soul) and the rational soul itself, there is a certain third substance really distinct from the rational soul. In relation to spiritual things, this substance is almost the same kind of principle for understanding and desiring as the rational soul is in relation to those things we know naturally.

### XI.

The origin of this spiritual substance is not clearly explained by Barclay or his associates, who craftily disguise it. We saw in section 4 that the Weigelians and Boehmists do not hide its divine origin. Indeed, <term>Abraham von Franckenberg</term> professes this in so many words in *Know Thyself*, page 110: <note>original: "Der ewige Mensch ist aus dem ewig-sprechendem Wort Gottes / aus der Licht-Welt / aus Gottes eigenem Wesen"</note> "The eternal man is from the eternally-speaking Word of God, from the world of light, from God's own essence." And on page 52: "If I were of another matter than from God himself, how then would I be his child?"

<summary>This page defines the "Spirit" as a third substance or "substantial seed" dwelling in all humans, which Quakers call the "vehicle of God" and Boehmists link to God's own essence.</summary>
<keywords>Jacob Boehme, Robert Barclay, vehicle of God, substantial seed, Abraham von Franckenberg, divine essence, internal man</keywords>

### XII.

It is therefore clear that the fanatic opinions of the <term>Paracelsians</term>, <term>Weigelians</term>, <term>Mystics</term>, <term>Quakers</term>, and the rest—who are commonly called by the name "the Illuminated"—conspire in this: that besides the body and the rational soul, there is in man a certain substantial part granted to him by God, and, as most do not hide, granted from the very essence of God. <term>Felgenhauer</term> explains this same doctrine of the three parts of man quite at length in *The Forecourt, the Holy, and the Most Holy Place of the Temple of God*. The individual readings of this fanatic pamphlet sufficiently declare the nature of each part and the dreams of the Fanatics concerning them. It is also worth comparing the *Decent Universal Doctrine of God* by <term>Bartholomaeus Sclei</term>, as well as the *Book of the Witness of the Hidden Treasure in the Field*, whose author calls himself <term>HIEL</term> <gloss>The Uniform Life of God</gloss>. Also, the *Thorough Instruction* of the "highly enlightened by God" <term>Matthes Weyer</term>, and similar monstrous books written by those furies—truly unworthy of anyone wasting good and irrevocable hours in reading them.

### XIII.

Furthermore, this doctrine of the threefold part of man holds the chief place in their <term>Mataeology</term> <gloss>vain or useless discourse</gloss>. For the author of *The Forecourt* foolishly boasts in chapter 12 that this contains the foundation not only of all Christianity, but of all wisdom in general that exists in heaven and on earth. But truly, if someone were perhaps unaware that they have five senses, or what the nature of sight or hearing or the rest might be, should it therefore be concluded that those senses cannot perform their function? I certainly do not think so. Meanwhile, <term>Andreas Christophorus Rafelius</term> extols this dogma with such praises that he does not fear to speak of it in this way in *The New Year's Trumpet*: <note>original: "Das ist eigentlich der rechte Grund-Fels/ und das gewisse Fundament/ darauff das Hauß unsers Christenthums soll gesetzet/ geleget und fundiret werden/ soll es bestehen: und daraus alles predigen/ lesen/ schreiben/ GOttes Wort hören/ singen/ beten/ gute Wercke / sollen und müssen herfliessen."</note> "This is actually the right bedrock and the certain foundation upon which the house of our Christianity shall be set, laid, and founded, if it is to stand: and from it all preaching, reading, writing, hearing God's Word, singing, praying, and good works shall and must flow."

<summary>Wiedeburg dismisses the "threefold man" doctrine as "vain discourse" (Mataeology), despite its proponents—like Felgenhauer and Rafelius—claiming it is the bedrock of all Christian wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Felgenhauer, Bartholomaeus Sclei, Matthes Weyer, Mataeology, bedrock of Christianity, the Illuminated, Hiel</keywords>

# Book Six

<margin>The sea and the hidden rivers</margin>
the sea receives an entrance, as it holds just as much space there; or perhaps even more, since the upper regions had to be shared with so many living creatures. Desolate places, even without an inhabitant, float more freely on the waves. Who would prevent the waters from fluctuating there and being driven by the winds, which every interval of the earth and every space of air creates? Therefore, a storm, having arisen greater than usual, can shake a part of the earth, having been driven more vehemently. For among us, too, many places that had been far from the sea were suddenly struck by its approach, and the waves invaded villas placed within view, which were heard from afar. There, too, the sea can retreat and uncover the lower depths, which does not happen without a movement of the substance. I do not believe you will hesitate for long to believe that there are subterranean rivers and a hidden sea. For whence do these things spring? Whence do they come to us, if not because the origin of moisture is contained within? Come, when you see the <term>Tigris</term> <gloss>a great river in Western Asia</gloss> interrupted, drying up in the middle of its course—and it is not turned away entirely, but diminishes little by little as the waters become invisible, and then is consumed—where do you think it goes, if not into the dark places of the earth? Especially since you see it emerge again, no smaller than the one that had flowed before. What of when you see the <term>Alpheus</term> <gloss>a river in Greece</gloss>, celebrated by the poets in Achaia, submerged, and then pouring forth in Sicily, after having crossed the sea, the most pleasant fountain of <term>Arethusa</term> <gloss>a nymph transformed into a fountain</gloss>? Moreover, you are not unaware that among the opinions held by those who narrate the flooding of the <term>Nilus</term> <gloss>the Nile river</gloss>, one is that it breaks forth and increases from the earth, not from waters above, but from those returned from the depths. Indeed, I myself <note>referring to the historian's own experience or report</note> have seen two centurions whom Nero Caesar, a man who loves truth as much as he loves other virtues, had sent to investigate the source of the Nile.

<summary>Seneca discusses subterranean waters, the connectivity of hidden seas, and the mysterious sources of rivers like the Tigris and the Nile.</summary>

On Natural Questions.

I heard them narrating that they had performed a long journey when, provided with assistance from the King of Ethiopia and armed with letters of recommendation for the kings further on, they had reached the distant parts. "We arrived," they said, "at immense marshes, the exit of which neither the inhabitants knew, nor could anyone hope to find. For it was so entangled by waters and grasses that the waters were not navigable to ships—which the marsh, muddy and covered in vegetation, would not bear unless it were small and capable of carrying only one person." There, he said, we saw two rocks from which a huge force of the river fell. Whether that is the head of the Nile or an addition, or whether it is born there or returns into the earth after having been received from a previous course, do you not believe that whatever it is, it rises from a great lake of the earth? For it must have moisture scattered in many places and collected at the bottom so that it can erupt with such great force. Some judge that earthquakes are caused by fire, while others do not attribute it to the same cause. Primarily <term>Anaxagoras</term> <gloss>a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</gloss>, who believes that the earth is shaken by a cause almost similar to how the air is shaken, when, in the lower part, a spirit forces dense air and clouds together in the same way that clouds are accustomed to break among us. Fire flashes from this collision of clouds as the air is forced out. It rushes to meet this as it seeks an exit, tearing apart what opposes it until it finds a path to the sky through narrow spaces, or makes one through force or damage. Others do not judge that fire is the cause, but rather that it burns in many places it encounters and consumes everything nearest to it. If these places fall down because they have been eaten away, then a movement of those parts follows, which, deprived of the supports beneath them, slip until they collapse, with nothing occurring to intercept the weight. Then, calm is restored, and vast chasms open.

<summary>The author describes an expedition to the Nile's source and details the theories of Anaxagoras regarding the causes of earthquakes, specifically through the action of spirit and fire.</summary>
<keywords>Nile, Ethiopia, Anaxagoras, earthquakes, fire, air, spirit.</keywords>

De lactuca. Ca. XXII.
Lactuca vt dicit Isidorus ex lactei humoris exuberantia est vocata. vel quia nutricientes mulieres lacte implet. hec in viris veneris motum arcet cuius duplex est species. scilicet domestica et agrestis qua feralia vocamus. quod dorsum eius aculeos habet duros ad modum ferre. vt dicit Isidorus libro. xvii. capitulo ultimo. de qua dicit Plinius in dietis. lactuca agrestis domestice in forma est similis. sed longiores habet frondes. subtiliores. asperiores. et minus virides. propter sue humiditatis paruitatem. et ideo multum est amaritudinis et ponticitatis respectu illius que domestica est. quia maioris est caloris et siccitatis. et ideo multi dicunt quod menstrua puocat et humores crudos expellit. vt dicit Dyascorides. lactuca pro domestica frigida est et humida secundum gradum et in neutra qualitate excedit modum. et ideo eius usus grauisui medicine. subtilibus subam et marie qui erit recens. et ideo cito digeritur et stomachi arsuram et morsuram et colera rubea sedat. sanguinis ebullitionem refrigerat. infomnietate placat. capitis dolorem et fumo colerico sanat. lac in mulieribus multiplicat et semen in viris generat augumentar. et accidit propter bonitatem sanguinis que gignit in pfecta quantitate. et in pfecta etate sed quando antiquatur et indurat minuitur eius humiditas et amaricat. et vsu eius sanguis pessimus generatur. virtus visina inde deficit et debilitatur. cuius causa est sensus animalis mortificatio. quod cum sua ponticitate ipsum suffocat naturale. et ideo talis lactuca generare voletib. maxime est nociua. nam materia gelat. coagulat seminale. et precipue semen eius si in cibo aut in potu sepe assumatur. De lappa. Ca. XXIII.
Lappa est herba habens folia lata et spissa circa terram habens in sumitatibus bastularum quedam capitella spinosa et aculeata sed recurua que vestibus transeuntium solent adherere. Vnde dicit Isidorus libro. xvii. lappa est dicta eo quod habeat caulez in gente terram dispositam et grecis philatropos vocatur. quod vestibus hominum adhereat ob asperitatem sui. et nascit iuxta muros. et ob philatropos. i. amans hominem. quia quadam affectione videat homis adherere vestibus. Lappe species duplex acuta et rotunda ad similitudinem pedis caballi disposita. vt a multis vocat vngula caballina. et vtriusque folia huis et horribilis sunt odoris pariter et saporis. vt dicit Dyascorides. Sed Plinius libro. xxvi. lappe multe sunt species et omnes sunt medicinales. Nam ictibus scorpionum medent. nec feriunt homine si inunctus fuerit succo eius. decoctio eius radicis iuuat dentes et etiam cofirmat si tepida in ore teneat. semen eius inetri cabilia vicia stomachi curat. resicientibus sanguine. pdest dissenteriis subuenit. naz radice eius cum vino fistit aluum. sed sola datur adiuuat calculosos. tota herba trita cum atungia valet et strumae. Duculus Pli. fm Plate. lappa siue lappacii est herba calida et sicca habens virtutem dissoluendi. relaxandi. aperiendi et attenuandi. et ideo valet contra scabiem. pruritum. ferpigine et impetigine. et intercutaneum os sumit humores. apostematum dissoluit duricie et tumore. valet contra frigidas ydropisim et splenis opilatoem. succus eius cum ruthe admistus cerebru purgat et reumatica sufluitate si in modica quantitate

# Book XVII

<note>A decorative initial L begins the section.</note> The collector gathers the barks of the lentisk or mastic tree at the end of spring, cuts them, and cleanses the area and places clean cloths underneath so that nothing falls onto the ground. Therefore, that which is clear and clean and white is to be selected; that which admits foreign matter and is dark is to be thrown away. It cleanses and purifies the brain and makes one expectorate mucus. It assists the digestive power and attenuates viscosity. Liquefied on a warm tile, it marvelously solidifies all broken gems, etc. Pliny also says, as does Dioscorides, that the lentisk is a thorny tree with a deep root, divided into many parts, having fruit like the myrtle, but smaller and red. When it is mature, its rough wool inside the skin and its juice heal the flux of women.

<note>A decorative initial D begins the section.</note> On the Lily, Ch. XXI
The lily is a herb of milky flower, whose whiteness shines among the foliage, though a gold color glows within. Regarding the lily, Dioscorides and Platearius say: The lily is hot and moist. And one is wild, another domestic, and one bears a purple flower, and another a white one, which is efficacious, and another a saffron or purple one. Moreover, the lily is a maturative; therefore, it avails against abscesses if it is crushed with lard. Also, it possesses a softening quality; therefore, it avails against the hardness of the spleen if its juice is mixed with old oil and well-incorporated, and the region of the spleen is anointed with it. Also, it possesses a cleansing force; therefore, it avails for beautifying the face if its powder is mixed with rose water and the face is washed with it. Also, it is mitigative; therefore, its leaves, boiled and applied, avail for places that have been burned. The root does the same if crushed with oil and applied. Also, it is extractive and resolutive, and it induces the menstrual purge. Also, it possesses a repressive quality against tumors; therefore, it avails against abscesses and inflammatory redness if the root is crushed with oil and applied. <note>Thus</note> Dioscorides. Regarding the lily, Pliny says: "The roots of the lily are ennobled in many ways by their flower. For, carried with wine, it heals the bite of a serpent and avails against foulness and poison. Boiled in wine and mixed with oil, it dissolves corns and nodes of the feet. It restores hair to burned places. Boiled in wine with honey added, it aids the veins or nerves of fish <note>likely an error for "nerves/tendons of the body"</note>. Boiled leaves in wine heal wounds. The seed applied with sulfur is good for the sacred fire. The flower and leaves assist the needs of ulcers." <note>Thus</note> Pliny, Book XX, Ch. XII. Also in the same book, Ch. V: "The lily rose is the first in nobility, and from the kinship of the flower, a noble ointment or oil is made, which is called oil of lilies. Thus also from roses, rose oil is accustomed to be made." From the root proceeds a stalk sometimes three cubits long; then from its summit the flower hangs down, repairing and dilating itself from a narrow point into breadth in the manner of a little bell, inverted in the circuit of the lips, having within as if a thin thread containing in itself the seed, yellow in the middle. Wherefore the lily lacks nothing of glory, as it is abundant in the effectiveness of the fragrance of color and odor. Its color is threefold: white, red, and purple. <note>Thus</note> Pliny, Book XX, Ch. V. But the lily has a root with many bulbs assisting it, like garlic, as Aristotle says in the book *On Vegetables*. And in each bulb is the seed-germ, and therefore in every place it grows where it is planted. Regarding this, look there and in the same place regarding garlic in the letter A. Aristotle says furthermore to the aforementioned: "The stalk of the lily is knotty and curves into the ground, and it is multiplied and propagated by seed and root, and if you do not find the bulb immediately within a few days, you will find it, and from every node of its stalk it emits a little bulb as if that were of its tunics or of the bulbs, namely bulbs of the root, and this is very marvelous." Also in the same place it follows: "The flowers of the lily are first green, then they become white. And if the stalk is cut off entirely from the root, because all the humor of the stalk is included, the natural heat in the marrow turns itself to the upper part of the stalk and digests the matter of the flower itself, and then the little flower expands and becomes white, the humor having first been digested." And therefore, as poets have compared the lily to the human intellect, it solicits at the end for the eternal. Also in the same place, it is said that the lily has no seed-reason in the seed and root, and it differs and goes further, like garlic, and has a seed-reason in many places. Regarding this, look there and regarding garlic and onions in the letter A and L. The lily, moreover, with the stalk newly cut with the flower, if inserted into clay soil, keeps its flower in freshness for a long time. The lily flower, when it is whole and intact, remains long and smells sweetly. Broken by the hands and rubbed, it stinks much. The flower itself, with the seed, holds it in place of fruit. The whole power which the lily has in the stalk and root, it shows in the head, namely in the flower and in the seed. And the more the flower rises high on the stalk, the more humbly the head inclines. Its flower is, moreover, exterior and flat, sweet to the touch, and round in form, delightful and joyful to the sight. Internally, it is sprinkled with golden grains in its cavity, which tincture like saffron. And seven little stalks sustain these tincture grains. Wherefore, it is composed of very white leaves simultaneously touching each other, and from seven grains, it places its seed in the place of fruit with marvelous beauty, and by the benefit of the flower, it is protected by the tenderness of the seed from the harm of cold air.

<summary>This page details the medicinal and botanical properties of the lily, referencing its uses in treatments for abscesses, wounds, and snakebites, while also exploring its symbolic and physical structure.</summary>

### On Lettuce, Ch. XXII
Lettuce, as Isidore says, is so named from the exuberance of its milky humor, or because it fills nursing women with milk. This herb restrains the motion of lust in men. Its species is twofold: domestic and wild, which we call <term>feralia</term> <gloss>wild/brutish</gloss>, because its back has hard prickles in the manner of a wild beast, as Isidore says in Book XVII, in the last chapter. Regarding it, Pliny says in his *Diets*: "Wild lettuce is similar in form to domestic, but it has longer leaves, thinner, rougher, and less green because of the paucity of its humidity, and therefore there is much bitterness and astringency compared to that which is domestic, because it is of greater heat and dryness." And therefore many say that it provokes menses and expels raw humors, as Dioscorides says. Lettuce, as the domestic, is cold and moist according to the degree and in neither quality exceeds the mean. And therefore its use is of great medicine for subtle stomachs, and especially when it is fresh, and therefore it is quickly digested and calms the burning and biting of the stomach and red bile. It cools the boiling of the blood. It calms sleeplessness. It heals headache and choleric smoke. It multiplies milk in women and generates and increases seed in men, and this happens because of the goodness of the blood which it generates in perfect quantity and in perfect age. But when it becomes old and hard, its humidity is diminished and it becomes bitter, and by its use the worst blood is generated. The visine <note>likely visional</note> power fails and is weakened, the cause of which is the mortification of the animal sense, because with its astringency it suffocates the natural [spirit]. And therefore such lettuce is most harmful to those wishing to generate, for it gels and coagulates the seminal matter, and especially its seed if it is often assumed in food or drink. <note>Thus</note> Isaac in his *Diets*. Pliny, however, in Book XX, Ch. VIII, says about lettuce: "There is a species of lettuce born spontaneously which they call 'caprina' <note>goat-lettuce</note>, which, when protected in the sea, kills fish, and they are in the vicinity. Its stalk and leaves, crushed with salt, heal incised nerves. Another species of lettuce is that which is born in fields, whose leaves crushed with polenta heal ulcers, and this the Greeks call 'isopon' <note>good-hyssop</note>. The third species is that which grows in woods, which they call 'steraton,' whose leaves crushed with pus heal wounds. With the root and leaves, they mitigate the sacred fire <note>St. Anthony's fire/erysipelas</note>. There is also another species of this lettuce, round and short, which many call 'beratia,' whose juice hawks take by scratching the herb...

<column-break/>
...and there, dyeing their eyes, they dispel obscurity and dimness when they grow old. The juice of this herb heals the eyes and especially when mother's milk is mixed with it. It treats the bites of serpents and the stings of scorpions if its juice is drunk with wine and the crushed leaves are applied to the wound as a plaster. It also dispels and calms every inflation. The seed of lettuce, as much wild as domestic, calms the imaginations of lust in dreams and does not allow the body to be polluted if it is frequently assumed in food. However, its frequent and excessive use causes obscurity of the eyes." Pliny attributes many other praises to it in the same chapter, but let these suffice.

### On Burdock, Ch. XXIII
Burdock <note>or Lappa</note> is a herb having broad and thick leaves around the ground, having on the tips of the stalks certain thorny and prickly little heads, but recurved, which are accustomed to adhere to the clothes of passersby. Whence Isidore says in Book XVII: "Burdock is so called because it has a stalk disposed toward the earth, and it is called 'philanthropos' <note>lover of man</note> by the Greeks, because it adheres to the clothes of men on account of its roughness." And it is born near walls, and because of "philanthropos," i.e., "loving man," because it seems with a certain affection to adhere to the clothes of men. The species of burdock is twofold: sharp and round, disposed in the likeness of a horse's foot, wherefore it is called by many 'horse hoof.' The leaves of both are of horrible odor and taste alike, as Dioscorides says. But Pliny in Book XXVI says: "There are many species of burdock, and all are medicinal. For they treat the stings of scorpions, and they do not strike a man if he has been anointed with its juice. The decoction of its root aids the teeth and also firms them if held warm in the mouth. Its seed taken inside cures stomach ailments. To those vomiting blood, it assists in dysenteries. For its root with wine stops the flux of the belly, but given alone, it aids those with stones. The whole herb crushed with lard avails against scrofula." <note>Thus</note> Pliny. According to Platearius: Burdock or <term>lappacium</term> <gloss>dock/burdock</gloss> is a herb hot and dry, having the power of dissolving, relaxing, opening, and attenuating. And therefore it avails against scabies, itching, herpes, and impetigo, and it takes humors from under the skin. It dissolves the hardness and tumor of abscesses. It avails against cold dropsy and obstruction of the spleen. Its juice mixed with rue cleanses the brain and rheumatic superfluity if in a small quantity...

<summary>This page explores the medicinal uses and classical classifications of lettuce and burdock, detailing their efficacy in treating various bodily ailments including ulcers, eye afflictions, and digestive issues.</summary>

...but they can also assist in the great matters of national governance. Their benefits are infinite; students should recognize this for themselves.

Universal use is shared by all nations.

In a civilized nation, there is no place where tools are not used, and this is firmly established. Yet, in remote and desolate regions, such as the people of the Green-Headed Country located seventy degrees north of the equator—which can be called the most remote and wild of countries—they still know how to use leather boats to gather fish and bows and arrows to hunt birds and beasts. Thus, the public utility of tools is the same throughout the great earth. How vast it is!

Creation and transmission remain the same through the ages.

What if he is only a man, if he is only a King, and if his work is only the gathering of Israel and the return to Palestine? What wrung sighs from David, or even from Solomon? Solomon himself saw the temple magnificently raised from its foundations, made august by the cloud of Divine Glory, and consecrated with a thousand sacrifices. And if he primarily looked for glory and riches, behold! the Lord promised Solomon: (1) *I will give you riches and substance and glory so that no king before or after you shall be like you.* He also had all Kings as his tributaries, if any faith is to be given to the Rabbis. What then (let them say) what was lacking to him from these things which they attribute to their Messiah? For what reason did they yearned to see a man in no way different from Solomon himself? Indeed, according to the promise of God, they desired to see one who could not even be compared to a mere man.

# Rubea autem metalla in colore admixtione diuersa sunt a dictis: sicut satis ostendimus cum de coloribus metallorum ageret. 

Habet autem ferrum secundum se specialem determinationem extra alia elementa. Dicamus igitur eris compositionem supponentes que iam dudum probata sunt omne metallum ex sulphure componi & argento viuo. Ponamus igitur argentum viuum esse bonum non feculentum siue lutulentum, no[n] tamen ab humore extraneo omnino purgatum: substantiam sulphuris esse feculentam & adurentem & in parte accensam: sicut argento viuo per substantiam & qualitates commisceri. nunc enim absque dubio conuertit ipsum in ruborem & non poterit eidem propter utriusque non plenam subtiliationem bene misceri / tunc efficiet es quod non est omnino bone mixtionis. propter quod multa fer inde resoluitur / & multum euaporat in igne quia cum sulphur in parte incensum est. ideo quedam partes argenti viui amplius quam alie purificatur & consumit in eis superfluum humidum & in illis partibus videbitur habere venas auri. In alijs autem ubi minus digestum est erit scalosum & ignobile & terrestre propter adustionem / & hanc diuersitatem in cupro quod inuenitur in theutonicis partibus in loco qui <margin>Goslaria</margin> goslaria vocatur expresse inuenimus. & ideo etiam hoc cuprum melius omnibus alijs estimatur tanquam venas auri habens immixtas / & non est improbabile quin sulphur illi eris sit mictu cum arsenico rubeo in aliqua quantitate. & ideo sit magis adurens sulphur illius metalli quam alterius.

<margin>Cupru[m] i[n] auricalcu[m] vertit[ur]</margin>
Nunc igitur scimus materiam eris / quoniam est metallum ex argento viuo plusquam oportet aliquantulum habens per commixtionem adurentis sulphuris ad formam ruboris deducti / ex qua autem natura sulphur sit adurens in precedentibus satis determinatum est. Arsenicum autem calcinatum sit quidem nigrum ex rubeo / sed postea & sublimatum in alutel quod est vas opertum cum collo alto vt sepius diximus reuertitur album ad instar niuis / & si sepius iterentur talis calcinatio & sublimatio tunc efficitur multum album & acutissimum / & ex acumine eri coniunctum liquando penetrat in ipsum & conuertit in candorem. si tamen diu stet in igne es expirabit arsenicum & tunc redit pristinus color cupri sicut de facili probatur in alchimicis. Hi autem qui in cupro multum operantur in nostris partibus parisius videlicet & colonie & in alijs locis in quibus fui & vidi experiri uertunt cuprum in auricalcum per puluerem lapidis qui calamina vocatur. & cum euaporat lapis adhuc remanet splendor obscurus declinans aliquantulum ad auri speciem. Vt autem albius efficiatur & ita citrinitati auri magis sit simile immiscet aliquantulum de stagno. propter que etiam auricalcum multum de ductibilitate cupri amittit. Et illi qui decipere volunt & splendorem similem auro inducere ligant lapidem: ita quod diutius remanet in ere in igne no[n] euaporans cito ab ere. 

Ligatur autem per oleum vitri tostatur enim fragmenta vitri & conuertuntur in puluerem & spargitur in testam super es postquam immissa est calamina / & tunc vitrum piectum enatat super es & non sinit euaporare lapidem & lapidis virtutem: sed reflectit vaporem lapidis in es. & sic dumque fortiter purgat es & adurunt in eo materie feculente. Tandem tamen euaporat etiam oleum vitri. & tunc euaporat virtus lapidis / sed auricalcum efficitur multo splendidius quam esset sine illo. Qui aut[em] adhuc amplius assimilare auro intendit. has purgationes per opesum & vitri oleum sepius iterat / & loco Auricalci stagni ponit argentum & immiscet auricalco. Et hoc efficit ita rutilum cum colore citrinum quod multi credunt ipsum esse aurum cum in veritate adhuc remaneat sit in specie eris. 

<margin>Hermes</margin>
Hermes autem dicit quod si eri liquefacto tuchia puluerizata siue sit tuchia alba siue rubea quod ipsum in colorem auri conuertit. Quid autem sit tuchia in sequenti libro ubi de medijs aget dicetur. sed hic sufficiat est quod tuchie adustione assumitur terrestreitas & purgat ab ere superfluum humidum ipsius. & ideo tunc erit pulchrius. tamen & virtus tuchie euaporat per ignem si diu steterit in igne. & ideo nisi aliud medicamen fuerit euaporabit tuchia. & tunc erit pristinus color cupri. Dicit etiam Hermes cum quo concordant experta. quod si es tale aspersum super acetum vel vrinam pueri masculi virginis locet penetrabit virtus urine siue aceti substantiam eris & conuertet ipsum in virorem. Si autem iterum per se solum es locetur super racemos expressos solo vapore vini conuertetur in optimum colorem viridem plucentez. Si autem huic colori auripigmentum siue arsenicum approximatur & precipue adustum condemnando destruit virorem & inducit colorem fuscum terrestrem ad opacitatem declinantem. Huius causa autem ex dictis facile manifestatur. est enim sal aperitiuum / & ideo aperit cupri substantiam seque si in tenues laminas deductum sit / & tunc vapor acetus aceti vel urine incendit ipsum: quod tamen est a sulphure nimis accenso. propter quod humidum terrestre adiunctum leue quod est ignitum in ipso virore accipit sicut colera calidissima & pessima que est sicut erugo eris vt dicunt medici. Quoniam autem primo vapor non est adeo acutus sicut vapor vini coniuncti / tunc non ita intensam inducit rubedinem. & ideo manet auri color placidus. Auripigmentum autem est excellen[ter] adurens & ideo cum hoc approximat substantie sic colorate comburet modicum humidum quod est in ipso. & tunc manet quod est terrestre opacum. per eundem modum quo etiam colera adusta relinquit cinerem melancolicum accidentalem calidissime melancolie secundum experta medicine. Tanta igitur de eris natura & effectibus dicta sunt.

<meta>The previous page concluded the discussion on the nature of silver, focusing on its purity and its relationship to quicksilver. This page transitions into the "red metals," specifically iron and copper, explaining their composition and the alchemical processes used to alter their appearance to resemble gold or produce pigments like verdigris.</meta>

<sig>n ij</sig>

# Red metals, however, are different in their color and mixture from those already mentioned: as we have sufficiently shown when we dealt with the colors of metals.

Iron has a specific nature of its own beyond the other elements. Let us therefore speak of the composition of **copper** <note>original: "eris"; here referring to copper or its alloys</note>, assuming what has long been proven: that every metal is composed of **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>. Let us suppose that the quicksilver is good and not dreggy or muddy, yet not entirely purged of external moisture. Let the substance of the sulfur be dreggy, burning, and partially ignited, just as it is mixed with the quicksilver in substance and quality. For now, without doubt, it turns the quicksilver red; because both are not fully refined, they cannot mix well. Then it creates copper, which is not of an entirely good mixture. Because of this, much of it is consumed and much evaporates in the fire, since the sulfur is partially burnt. Therefore, some parts of the quicksilver are purified more than others, and the superfluous moisture in them is consumed; in those parts, it will seem to have **veins of gold**. In other parts, however, where it is less "digested" <term>digestio; the natural "cooking" or ripening of minerals in the earth</term>, it will be scaly, base, and earthy due to the burning. We have clearly found this diversity in the copper found in the German regions, in the place called <margin>Goslar</margin> **Goslar**. Therefore, this copper is esteemed better than all others, as if having veins of gold mixed in. It is not improbable that the sulfur of that copper is mixed with red **arsenic** in some quantity, and therefore the sulfur of that metal is more "burning" than that of others.

<margin>Copper is turned into brass</margin>
Now we know the material of copper: it is a metal made from quicksilver, having a bit more than is proper through the mixture of burning sulfur, which leads it to a red form. The nature by which sulfur is "burning" has been sufficiently determined in what preceded. **Arsenic**, when calcined <note>heated to a high temperature to remove volatile substances</note>, turns black from red; but afterward, when **sublimated** <note>turned into vapor and then solidified</note> in an **alutel** <note>original: "alutel"; a pear-shaped vessel used in alchemy for sublimation</note>, which is a covered vessel with a high neck as we have often said, it returns white like snow. If such calcination and sublimation are repeated often, it becomes very white and very sharp. Because of this sharpness, when joined to copper by melting, it penetrates it and turns it white. However, if it stays in the fire a long time, the copper will "breathe out" the arsenic, and then the original color of the copper returns, as is easily proven in alchemical works. Those who work much with copper in our regions—namely in Paris, Cologne, and other places where I have been and seen experiments—turn copper into **brass** <note>original: "auricalcum"; orichalcum</note> by using the powder of a stone called **calamine** <note>zinc ore</note>. When the stone evaporates, a dim splendor still remains, inclining somewhat toward the appearance of gold. To make it whiter and thus more similar to the yellow of gold, they mix in a little **tin**. Because of this, the brass loses much of the ductility <note>the ability to be hammered thin or drawn into wire</note> of the copper. Those who wish to deceive and induce a splendor similar to gold "bind" the stone so that it remains longer in the copper in the fire and does not evaporate quickly.

It is "bound" by **glass oil**: fragments of glass are toasted and turned into powder, which is sprinkled into the crucible over the copper after the calamine has been put in. Then the melted glass floats over the copper and does not allow the stone or its virtue to evaporate; instead, it reflects the vapor of the stone back into the copper. Thus, for a while, it strongly purges the copper and burns away the dreggy materials in it. Eventually, however, even the glass oil evaporates, and then the virtue of the stone evaporates; but the brass is made much more splendid than it would be without it. He who intends to make it resemble gold even more repeats these purgings with the glass oil often, and in place of tin, he takes **silver** and mixes it with the brass. This makes it so ruddy and yellow in color that many believe it to be gold, though in truth it remains in the species of copper.

<margin>Hermes</margin>
**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says that if powdered **tutty** <note>original: "tuchia"; zinc oxide collected from smelting furnaces</note>, whether white or red, is added to melted copper, it converts it to the color of gold. What tutty is will be discussed in the following book where we deal with intermediate substances. But let it suffice here that by the "burning" of the tutty, the earthiness is removed and it purges the copper of its superfluous moisture; therefore, it will then be more beautiful. However, the virtue of the tutty also evaporates through fire if it stands in the fire for a long time. Unless another "medicine" <note>an additive or reagent</note> is used, the tutty will evaporate, and then the original color of the copper returns. Hermes also says, and experience agrees, that if such copper is sprinkled with vinegar or the urine of a virgin male child, the virtue of the urine or vinegar will penetrate the substance of the copper and turn it green. If, however, the copper is placed by itself over pressed grape skins, it will be converted into an excellent, shining green color by the vapor of the wine alone. But if **orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic ore</note> or arsenic is brought near this color, especially if it is burnt, it destroys the green and induces a dark, earthy color inclining toward opacity. The cause of this is easily shown from what has been said. For salt is opening, and therefore it opens the substance of the copper, especially if it has been hammered into thin plates; then the sharp vapor of the vinegar or urine ignites it, which comes from the overly-ignited sulfur. Because of this, the light earthy moisture joined to it, which is ignited, takes on that greenness, much like the hottest and worst bile which physicians call the "rust of copper." Since at first the vapor is not as sharp as the vapor of joined wine, it does not induce such an intense redness, and so the gold color remains pleasant. Orpiment, however, is excellently "burning," and so when it approaches a substance colored this way, it burns the small amount of moisture in it; then what remains is the earthy opacity. This is the same way that burnt bile leaves behind a "melancholic ash," according to medical experience. Thus, so much has been said concerning the nature and effects of copper.

### Chapter Eight: On the nature and admixture of gold.

<summary>This page explains the chemical nature of copper as a mix of sulfur and mercury, detailing how medieval craftsmen in cities like Paris and Cologne used calamine, arsenic, and tutty to create brass or gold-like imitations. It also describes the production of verdigris (green pigment) through the reaction of copper with acidic vapors like vinegar or wine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of metallurgy, moving from the "red metals" (copper) discussed on the previous page to the nature, properties, and purification of gold. The text cites authorities like Hermes Trismegistus, Plato, and Empedocles to explain why gold is the "most perfect" metal.</meta>

<sig>a iij</sig>

# **B**ut it must be objected by those concerning the nature of gold that, according to **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origins of alchemy.</note>, it is the only metal in which no "sickness" <note>imperfection or impurity</note> appears. For neither part of its matter is infected or out of balance. Since, like other metals, it is composed of **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>, its sulfur is most lucid and pure, brought to a state of purity through the strongest washings so that it has no combustible oiliness at all, nor any phlegmatic, watery moisture that might evaporate. Perhaps in hollow places where the solid surface is frequently sublimated and "digested" <term>digestio; a natural ripening process similar to slow cooking within the earth</term> by a temperate heat, a process called **pepansis** <note>original: "pepansis"; a Greek term for the ripening of fruit or the "cooking" of humors/minerals</note> occurs. Its earthy substance, which is incorporated into the sulfur, is pure, extremely subtle, and suspended like a vapor throughout the entire substance of the sulfur's radical moisture. For this reason, it remains that the heat of that sulfur is balanced in its temperament, receding from nothing; and this acts as the **masculine power** in the composition of gold.

Similarly, its quicksilver has two substances purified to the extreme. For a third quality within its own heat is refined—not merely divided materially, but most subtle in a vaporous way—frequently sublimated in the cavities of the earth by the life-giving heat of the sun and stars. Likewise, the watery part is refined in the same way through repeated purification; and since it contains "glass-like" qualities <note>clarity or transparency</note>, it is refined most delicately. It is established that when these are mixed together by heat and the disposition of a place that stifles and reflects the vapor back into itself, they are bound together by the strongest bond of mixing. 

<margin>Why gold is heavy.</margin>
<margin>Why gold is not burnt.</margin>

Sulfur, however, does not enter into the composition of gold merely through its quality, but through its substance; and since it is of a subtle substance, it penetrates everywhere through the quicksilver and colors it by coagulating it. Since both are brought by sublimation to the form of the "superior elements" <note>the celestial or pure elements</note>—which agree in their transparent nature with the "perpetual body" <note>referring to the incorruptibility of the heavens</note>—both will possess a great deal of transparency. And when many parts of the matter are thickened together, they will stand firm. For this is a property of a subtle substance: that when it stands firm through coagulation, it will contain many parts in a very small space. Therefore, contracted transparency produces a **yellow color**, and its subtlety produces the greatest solidity. The constancy of many parts together in a small space and position produces **weight**, as is proven by those things reasonably demonstrated in the book *On the Heavens and the World* <note>referring to Aristotle's "De Caelo et Mundo"</note>. 

It also follows from its solidity and temperament together that gold evaporates little or not at all; therefore, it has almost no smell. For although a smell is not essentially a smoky evaporation, a strong smell often accompanies smoky evaporation. Because of this, it further follows that gold is more incorruptible than any other metal and withstands fire better due to the extremely strong mixing in its composition. For smoky evaporation indicates a certain corruption of bodies, which is less in silver and greater in copper. From these facts, we find the reason why things that do not burn gold, such as sulfur, arsenic, and certain others, do burn silver. For the cause of this—

---

—kind of mixture is that all of its earthy part is defended from burning by its moisture, and all of its moisture is held back by the earthy part so that it does not fly away through evaporation. This connection **Plato** calls a "covenant," and **Empedocles** calls the "glue of siblings" <note>original: "collam germanorum"; a metaphor for the strong chemical/alchemical bond between related elements</note>. 

<margin>The virtues of gold.</margin>

Because of the balanced temperament of gold, it is considered "hot and moist." It is beneficial for **trembling of the heart** <note>palpitations</note> and for **melancholy** which makes a person sad; and because of this, it helps those whose condition makes them talk to themselves. Gold provides relief against these passions whether it is rubbed on the body in its specific form or even taken internally when ground up. 

<margin>Why gold does not stain.</margin>

Due to its solidity, it does not easily affect the bodies it touches. Therefore, it is worn in rings and other ornaments. Silver, however, stains a little, and other metals stain a lot because they "touch" what they contain <note>they rub off on the skin</note>. This is because their oily moisture is entirely separated from them, mixed with burnt earthy matter, and this stains like the soot of an oily body. 

<margin>Grains.</margin>

The great purity of gold's matter means it is very rarely found mixed with other bodies, but almost always pure; for when it is mixed with others, it cannot retain such purity and thus degenerates into copper. Conversely, it is very rarely found unless it is incorporated into stones. Furthermore, it is often found as grains of sand, because such great purity must exist in small amounts, elevated from and almost expelled by that matter, and thus distinct. However, a grain is sometimes found together with **marcasite** <note>iron pyrites, often called "fool's gold"</note>.

From these facts, it is clear why these two metals—namely gold and silver—were chosen by the wise men of old as the material for **coinage**. For they have this special benefit of aiding and comforting the human temperament, and they are more durable and noble than the rest. 

<margin>The purification of gold.</margin>

The things that purify gold are sharp and very dry, such as salts (especially sea salts), the soot of oily but dry bodies, and crushed brick. When gold is to be purified, a clay vessel is made in the shape of a **cucurbit** <note>a gourd-shaped alchemical flask</note> or a small dish. Over this vessel, another similar one is placed and sealed at the joints with a tenacious clay which alchemists call the **Lute of Wisdom** <note>original: "lutum sapientie"; a specialized sealant used to make vessels airtight</note>. In the upper part, there are many small holes through which vapor and smoke may escape. The gold is then thinned into short, thin plates and arranged in the vessel so that every layer of plates has a powder of mixed soot, salt, and flour-like brick above and below it. It is cooked in a strong fire until it is most pure and the ignoble substances within it are consumed. 

The "Lute of Wisdom" from which these vessels are made is itself created from crushed pottery shards, mixed again and fired. For this vessel, when placed in the fire, is not diminished by the sensible consumption of the fire. However, the Lute of Wisdom is prepared in another way in alchemical works, but let that which the goldsmiths use suffice here. Thus is gold purified, and nothing in it is burnt away except the ignoble substance. Because of this, Hermes elegantly says in his alchemical works: 

> "Sulfur itself, by a certain subtle affinity of sulfur to which all metals are related, burns through and incinerates all their bodies—but gold it does not. For its pores are tight and indissoluble." 

However, gold which is found more abundantly in our times...

<summary>This page explains the alchemical composition and unique properties of gold, highlighting its incorruptibility, medicinal benefits for the heart and mind, and the specific methods used by goldsmiths and alchemists to purify it using the "Lute of Wisdom."</summary>
<keywords>gold, quicksilver, sulfur, Hermes Trismegistus, alchemy, Lutum sapientie, purification, melancholy, metallurgy, Empedocles, Plato</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the speaker’s formal introduction. He shifts from discussing the skepticism of the audience to explaining the specific administrative circumstances that led to him standing in the speaker's chair today: the primary official, Johannes Cornerus, is incapacitated by illness.</meta>

<header>Dissertation on loathing & hatred</header>

For, against my will—I do not lie—and **beyond expectation and hope** <note>Greek original: καὶ παρὰ δόξαν καὶ ἐλπίδα</note>, contrary to hope and opinion, I am drawn forward, I who by no means deemed myself worthy of such **HONOR**. For I know, and know well, nor do I deny, that those who now preside over this University and its Colleges, who exercise the public and professorial tongue with praise, and who have offered their services to this present proceeding, could have brought more reason and authority to persuasion, more weight and efficacy to moving the heart, and more elegance and beauty to delighting the ear. I do not deny it, I say; I praise this judgment willingly and **with both thumbs** <note>original: "utroque pollice," a Roman idiom meaning to give full and enthusiastic approval, derived from the amphitheater where spectators used their thumbs to signal a gladiator’s fate</note>; indeed, I do not blush to add my own opinion to this; I do not refuse it.

But since the Reverend, Most Distinguished, and Eminent Man, Lord **JOHANNES CORNERUS** <note>Johannes Cornerus (1597–1680) was a prominent theologian and official at the University of Jena</note>, Doctor of Sacred Theology, Dean and Canon of the same Faculty and of the Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Keeper of the Seal and primary Executor for the Most Reverend Archbishop of Mainz and Prince-Elector, our most merciful Lord, and Ordinary Vice-Chancellor of this our University—who, due to adverse health, is now attending to a **serious illness** <note>original: "morbum sonticum," a specific legal and medical term for an illness so severe it legally excuses a person from fulfilling their duties or appearing in court</note>, and for that reason is unable to perform himself what would otherwise be his duty—has seen fit that something be granted to me also in this proceeding; and since the Philosophical College—whose leaders I once felt to be my own teachers, and whom I still cherish with a mindful and grateful spirit—has commanded me to grant the **PETITION**, and has ordered that I should make the Candidates (whom I love for their singular gifts of mind) masters of their **WISH**; the Will of this man has now been a law to me. His Authority has stood for my reason. Both of these so stirred me in my idleness and pushed me in my hesitation that, although I am conscious of my own insignificance and well know how **scanty is my furniture** <note>original: "curta supellex," a metaphor from the Roman satirist Persius referring to a lack of mental resources or learning; literally "a short supply of household goods"</note>, I nevertheless did not hesitate to ascend this chair and carry out the duty entrusted to me. And indeed, this

<meta>This page follows the speaker’s humble apology for his own inadequacy, where he explained that he is standing in for the high-ranking official Johannes Cornerus. He now transitions into his defense against critics and introduces the specific topic of the dissertation: the strange phenomenon of physical antipathies toward food.</meta>

<header>Lipsius’s singular dissertation on food & drink.</header>
<sig>A 3</sig>

The single judgment of our **CORNERUS** <note>Johannes Cornerus, the official mentioned on the previous page who was unable to attend due to illness.</note> concerning me will easily protect me—just as the shield of **AJAX** protected **TEUCER** <note>original: "Teucrum clypeus Ajacis." In the *Iliad*, the archer Teucer often stood behind the massive shield of his half-brother Ajax for protection while shooting. The speaker implies Cornerus’s endorsement acts as his protective shield against critics.</note>—so that I am not attacked as an innocent man by idle people (of whom the earth and sea are full) either by the bites of envy or the barks of slander. Furthermore, this will win me favor and a hearing among you, **LISTENERS**, so that you will receive the reason for which I have come onto this stage with both mind and ears, in accordance with your singular kindness. And so here I fix my foot; I am content with this one thing: that if I say nothing more, you should know that there are many other things favoring this action of mine. I consider the whole cause of my speech to be told, and it would be nothing if anyone anxiously but fruitlessly searched for another.

Nor indeed in this philosophical assembly will I prepare a long speech about **PHILOSOPHY** in general, which is truly a gift of **GOD** and the sweetest food for the soul; nor have I decided to speak specifically about its parts and aids; nor am I here to pursue its benefits and praises, lest I be judged to be **doing what has already been done** <note>original: "actum agere," a Latin legal and theatrical idiom for repeating a finished task needlessly</note> and writing an **Iliad after Homer** <note>original: "post Homerum... Iliada scribere," a proverb meaning to undertake a task that has already been perfected by a master</note>, the source of geniuses.

Concerning **ANTIPATHY** or loathing, nausea, abstinence, and the miraculous hatred of food and drink in certain people, I shall say something for the sake of an introduction, and so that I may not be entirely **without a contribution** <note>Greek original: ἀσύμβολος (*asymbolos*). In ancient Greek social gatherings, a "symbolon" was a contribution to a communal meal; to be "asymbolos" meant to enjoy the feast without bringing anything to the table.</note>.

For we see that not a few sitting at the table with us abstain entirely from **Meat** or **Fish**. We see that they do not taste **Wine**, **Beer**, **Milk**, or **Honey**, and do not touch **Cheese**, **Butter**, or **Apples**. And there are those who cannot digest **Strawberries**, **Garlic**, or **Eggs**, nor endure the scent of a **ROSE** or an **APPLE**. We see, I say, **Listeners**, we see all these things. But those who can explain the cause here—I mean an **adequate, necessary, and sufficient cause** <note>These are technical terms from Scholastic logic used to define a complete scientific explanation</note>—are rare; and if I were to say there are almost none, I would certainly say nothing wrong nor against the truth.

<summary>The speaker defends his right to speak based on the endorsement of Cornerus and introduces his topic: the mysterious medical and philosophical causes behind "antipathies," or intense physical revulsions to common foods and scents.</summary>
<keywords>antipathy, food loathing, Cornerus, Ajax and Teucer, philosophy, nausea, medical causes, strawberries, roses</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the biography of the physician and alchemist Nicolas Barnaud. It follows a discussion of the satires and theological accusations leveled against him, specifically regarding the authorship of controversial works during his time in Geneva.</meta>

### 5. Nicholas Barnaud,

which was published under the title *The Genevan Ape* <note>original: *Le Magot Génévois*</note> in 1613. However, since this work—as Marchand proves—is a satire on the Synod of Montpellier and the Reformed <note>Protestant</note> church in general, it deserves no credit. Meanwhile, it is certain that Barnaud was in close contact with Faustus Socinus <note>a prominent Italian theologian and founder of Socinianism, which rejected the Trinity</note>, who also dedicated his *Defense of his Disputation on the passage in the seventh chapter of Romans* <note>original Latin: *Defensionem Disputationis suae de loco VII. Cap. ad Rom.*</note> from the year 1595 to him. At that time, Barnaud had already translated Socinus's work *On the Authority of Holy Scripture* <note>original Latin: *de auctoritate scripturae sacrae*</note> into French and published his translation in 1592.

He resided in Geneva between 1575 and 1599, but moved to Leiden in the latter year, and in 1601 to Gouda, where he presumably died. This is everything known about him, and his name would likely have been forgotten by posterity—neither remembered as a physician nor as a friend of Socinus—had he not kept his memory alive among the lovers of the **Great Art** <term>Great Art; a traditional name for Alchemy, specifically the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone</term> through various alchemical writings, which he seems to have written especially in the final years of his life. These, along with his other writings, are as follows:

*Wake-up Call for the French and their Neighbors* <note>original French: *Reveil Matin des François et de leurs Voisins*</note> by Eusebius Philadelphus, Cosmopolitan, in the form of a dialogue. Edinburgh, (Geneva,) 1574, octavo. Likewise translated into Latin under the title: *Dialogues by Eusebius Philadelphus, Cosmopolitan, for the [benefit] of the Gallic and other nations* <note>original Latin: *Dialogi ab Eusebio Philadelpho, Cosmopolita, in Gallorum et caeterarum nationum...*</note>

Similarly, lead is turned into tin by granulating the lead, washing the granules often with false water <note>original: "aqua falsa"</note>, and cementing it with a moderate fire <note>original: "igni modico"</note>, and finally reducing it. Paracelsus, in book 7 of his work on the transmutation of things, teaches how to do this through the cementation of plates of <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> and <term>Oil</term> <gloss>alchemical symbol for oil</gloss>. Conversely, tin turns into lead by calcining the tin often and administering a strong fire to it so that it may separate more quickly and the dross may be removed. In the same way, it is not very difficult to change LEAD into COPPER by way of cementation with vitriol; our friend performed an experiment of this matter not long ago and gifted us with a portion of this artificial copper.

Finally, and in conclusion of this chapter, we wish to append the words of an anonymous author, which are found in Chapter 14 of the <term>Magia Naturalis</term> <gloss>Natural Magic</gloss> by Wolffgang Hildebrandus, New Edition, page 764, under the title: "A non-entity in the transformation of metals / is the reversal of imperfect metals into other imperfect ones / such as iron into copper et cetera," since they are diametrically opposed to the other authors contained in this chapter; the same words are as follows:

> Since the patrons of alchemy—Gaston Claveus in his Apology for Gerhard, Johann Vossius in his book on Philosophy, chapter 15, and others—use the transmutation of iron into copper as a foundation, so to speak, and put it forward as a certainty, we must first extricate ourselves from this.

There is a strong inclination and close affinity of iron with and into copper. The poets depict this when they have their thoughts on the unseemly intercourse of both. With this very thing, they give one to understand how gladly Mars marries Venus, or iron marries copper, and how the courageous magnanimity of Mars yields to the beauty of Venus, in that the caressing of Venus far surpasses the sternness of Mars. Hence, some <term>chemists</term> <gloss>alchemists</gloss>, imagining an equal friendship between copper and iron, hold that they embrace one another with a natural inclination, and that iron, by means of <term>vitriol</term> <gloss>sulfate mineral</gloss>, is with little effort combined and layered together into ore, bound with an indissoluble band of love and affinity, and cannot be brought apart again by any discord.

The bravest authors prove this. Agricola, in his books on the nature of those things that flow from the earth, and in the 9th book on the nature of fossils or mines, calls it "Sinolniz." Georgius Wernerus, Royal Councilor and Administrator at the Czar, writes of the wonderful waters in Hungary. Joh. Baptista Porta, <term>book</term> 5, <term>magic</term> <term>chapter</term> 4. Wann das auch geschehen, so thue diesen Spiritum Vini in einen Glaß-Kolben, mit samt der Extraction, thue darzu ein wenig der Tincturæ Corallorum, und der Quintæ Essentiæ von der Rhebarbar, gieb einem Menschen davon ein drey oder vier Tropffen, giebt gelinde Sedes, und purgirt ohn einiges Reissen, wann du recht damit bist umgangen in der Präparation, macht Leichterung des Gebüts, und ist eine gute Artzney allen denen, so da begehren subtile Stuhl-Gänge.

Es möchte aber wohl einen Artzt verwundern, wie diese Artzney gelinde Sedes geben könte, weil das Antimonium sonsten eine durchdringende reißende Materia ist, und die Rhebarbar ihm zugegeben wird, welche per se auch eine purgirende Kraft hat, der lasse sich nicht wundern, dann das Antimonium wird durch solch Mittel also getödtet,

<header>des Antimonii.</header>

Grind the antimony small and sublime it with half as much <term>salarmoniac</term> <gloss>sal ammoniac</gloss>. Put what has sublimed into a glass retort and drive it over into a receiver for a third time. Separate the <term>feces</term> <gloss>dregs</gloss> from it each time. Finally, sweeten the <term>salarmoniac</term> well away from it and <term>reverberate</term> <gloss>roast/calcine</gloss> the material of the antimony in a well-sealed vessel with a gentle fire, not driven too strongly, until it becomes like cinnabar ore. When that has happened, pour a strong distilled wine-vinegar over it and extract its <term>rubedinem</term> <gloss>redness</gloss>. Draw off the vinegar until a powder remains at the very last. This must happen in a <term>bad unser lieben Frauen</term> <gloss>bain-marie/water bath</gloss>. Then extract it again with <term>spiritu vini</term> <gloss>spirit of wine</gloss> so that the <term>feces</term> come away from it; then you have the extraction clean and clear.

When that has also happened, put this <term>spiritum vini</term> into a glass flask along with the extraction, add a little of the <term>tincturæ corallorum</term> <gloss>tincture of coral</gloss> and the <term>quintæ essentiæ</term> <gloss>fifth essence</gloss> of rhubarb. Give a person three or four drops of it. It provides gentle <term>sedes</term> <gloss>stools/bowel movements</gloss> and purges without any tearing, provided you have handled it rightly in the preparation. It makes for a lightness of the spirit and is a good medicine for all those who desire subtle bowel movements.

However, it might well astonish a physician how this medicine could provide gentle <term>sedes</term>, because antimony is otherwise a penetrating, tearing substance, and rhubarb is added to it, which by itself also has a purging power. Let him not be astonished, then, for the antimony is killed by such means

<summary>The author explains the process of killing the caustic nature of antimony through sublimation and extraction to create a gentle, effective purgative medicine.</summary>
<keywords>Antimony, Sal Ammoniac, Cinnabar, Bain-marie, Extraction, Rhubarb, Purgative</keywords>
auditTranslation:
<header>Triumph-Wagen</header>

because of its poisonous, purging property, so that in this respect it can attack nothing. But as soon as a <term>purgans</term> <gloss>purgative</gloss> from the <term>simplicibus</term> <gloss>simple herbs</gloss> is added to it, the latter has the power and authority, by its nature, to open and expel. But the prepared antimony need not concern itself in the meantime with the stomach for the expulsion; rather, it has and obtains all the better room and good, comfortable opportunity to act and look around in other ways without hindrance—yes, I say, to search, for which it has been ordained, and for which it can then perform its own task all the better without hindrance.

And let every person believe me—since I have received no reason for laziness in writing this of myself—that this prepared elixir goes through the body and cleanses it, just as gold is cleansed of its impurity through antimony. And if all things and all use of virtue were to be written down at length, I would have to approach the dear GOD in heaven and ask Him to grant me a longer life to further boast of, investigate, and share His infinitely high, wondrous deeds after the correct learning, so that others would have the same astonishment to recognize and observe alongside me before their Creator, and would likewise be able to thank Him for it.

In order to now further satisfy my intention, as I was determined to describe the virtue of antimony, as far as I have

<column-break/>

obtained it in my experience: the other things, which are still hidden from me and which I have not yet brought out of the <term>Spieß-Glas</term> <gloss>antimony</gloss>, of these I rightfully remain silent, as it does not befit me to judge of strange things which are outside of my experience. Rather, I leave the same to another judge who has also learned something through his diligence, since it is not well possible for any human to finish learning in antimony, because the time of human life is short and antimony is very round and without end (as I have already given understanding before), and something new is found therein daily and always.

<summary>The text concludes the author's argument on the efficacy of antimony, emphasizing the humility of the alchemist before the infinite complexity of nature and the necessity of continued study.</summary>
<keywords>Antimony, Elixir, Purgative, Alchemy, Virtue, Nature</keywords>

These are the practical social and moral virtues like justice and temperance used in daily life.</note> of which we are capable.

<margin>On the Topic of Virtues</margin>
For him, essence is solely "being," because of the absence of all form and the essence of that which is; but perfection through that which is formed comes from God. For as you are of the First Being, so you are not of the first good of the same. For rather, essences and virtue are from this; but only essence according to the **progression** <note>original: "proodon." In Neoplatonism, this is the process of the One overflowing or "proceeding" into the lower levels of reality.</note> from it, which is present to all from God. But perfection is according to the **return** <note>original: "epistrophen." This is the soul's movement back toward its divine source after its descent into the material world.</note> to it. Nor does he demand to be perfected, for he alone is, unless he is a beginning toward the earthly. Therefore, just like one painting from a model, or otherwise taking the prescribed **archetype** <note>original: "archetypian," a primary pattern or blueprint in the divine mind.</note> for the imitation, if he did not keep it with him to record it, so too he who would sketch and color virtue within himself could not otherwise be assimilated to God through the divine, unless he had used that alone to record it. And because of this, my own self will be accurately fashioned after the prototype through the contemplation of the Reason and the model.

### On Virtues

One who possesses the **theoretical virtues** <note>original: "theoretikas aretas." These are virtues of pure contemplation and intellectual vision.</note> is called "God-fathered" <note>original: "theopator." A technical term for the highest level of Neoplatonic virtue where the soul becomes like the source of the divine.</note>. One who has the **purificatory virtues** <note>original: "kathartikas." Virtues that "cleanse" the soul of material attachments.</note> is called "daemonic" <note>original: "daimonios." This does not mean "evil," but refers to a spiritual or "spirit-like" being that bridges the gap between humans and gods.</note>. One who has the **civic virtues** is called "excellent" <note>original: "spoudaios." A term for the person who performs their human duties and social roles with moral excellence.</note>. He who is beloved of God is called "God-fathered," because the soul's state is toward what is called "divine" through theoretical virtue. It is necessary

<column-break/>

therefore, that which is darkened must be assimilated to God, changing from the "excellent" man into the "daemonic." If it becomes divine—which is again "God-fathered"—the one among us who is only "excellent" might at some point also change into vice. But perhaps the divine man is not [subject to change], namely the theoretical man. He who is beloved of God, the "God-fathered," who is seen to be entirely obedient to the divine, might at some point be transferred to the innate, being the very form of virtue from himself, and having become divine in color.

<margin>On Intellect</margin>
### On Intellect

Every **Intellect** <note>original: "nous." In this context, it refers to the higher, divine Mind that perceives truth directly and intuitively, rather than through step-by-step logic.</note> holds its essence, its power, and its activity as eternal. For its whole essence is present all at once. It neither increases nor decreases; nor was it not present yesterday. Its essence alone is similar to itself; for it thinks the whole and the all as a complete whole together. It neither sees the past nor knows the future as something yet to be, but knows everything as it is in the "now." It is not moved, nor is it embellished, nor does it reason through syllogisms <note>original: "syllogizomenos." The Intellect does not need to argue from point A to point B; it simply "sees" the truth.</note>—which is like an echo where the soul reaches a conclusion by placing perceptions. Instead, all knowing is found in its very being. For being unmoved, it could not be measured by time, neither in its essence, which is in its **indivisibility** <note>original: "amereian." A state of being that cannot be split into parts.</note>, from which its essence is unmoved. But the intermediate and middle of these is like an eternal power that has been allotted its substance.

Everything that is divided is divided either by magnitude or by quantity. But if it is eternal in every respect and I assume a certain body, it is therefore indivisible.
