<meta>This page continues Psellos’s exploration of the Neoplatonic hierarchy of being. Having established the role of virtues and archetypes on the previous page, the text now moves into a technical distinction between the body and the mind, specifically focusing on the "Intellect" (Nous) and the "Soul" (Psyche) and their respective capacities for self-knowledge and divine participation.</meta>

Similarly, regarding the body, it is clear that the soul thinks of itself and **returns to itself** <note>original: "pros heauto epistrephei." In Neoplatonic thought, this "return" or "reversion" is the act of a conscious being looking inward to its own source rather than outward at material things.</note>. For no body thinks of itself. How is this evident? Because its thinking is not divided, whereas everything in a physical place is divisible. For this reason, those who study these matters do not consider them material. Since every individual substance possesses a share of the **immaterial intellects** <note>original: "nois aulois." These are "mind-beings" that exist without physical matter.</note> which are unparticipated. Nor is it fragmented. For those things which subsist for the sake of the world remain **unchanging**; and these are distinct from those things which change. And it was necessary that form not be the same as that which is below it, but rather that it transcend it. The entire order of things there does not descend from its own rank; its unique character merely proceeds forward, while remaining in its own forms and identities. Some things exist according to their nature, others according to their connections.

### + On the Intellect +

Because the **unparticipated intellect** <note>original: "amathekton nous." This refers to a "pure" Mind that exists independently and is not "shared out" or diluted by being joined to a physical body.</note>, and that which is unparticipated in the primary form, holds itself within itself. It possesses the measure of its own essence, both in its primary aspects and in those that transcend it. Hence, even the unparticipated intellect thinks in a "formal" way. For even if it is unparticipated, a certain manifestation is given to those things that come after it from its own existence. And it thinks of the **soul** and the **forms of nature**. It does not think of them merely as they exist in nature, for it does not know lower things in a lower way, nor higher things in a higher way; rather, it knows both "formally" (according to their ideal patterns). It does not change along with the things it thinks about. For it has the power to look toward the better, and it wills to look toward the lesser. Therefore, as its nature is, so it thinks both of itself and of the things after it. It does not possess things as they are in their changing states, but rather as their causes, knowing even the lower things through their higher forms.

<column-break/>

<margin>ai</margin>
...in a sensory formation. 

### + On the Soul +

Every soul is divine. One type is **self-complete** <note>original: "autotelos," meaning it is perfect in itself and doesn't need a body to function.</note>, while another is directed by the Intellect <margin>o</margin> toward a diversity of things that always remain, specifically the divine souls. Every divine soul acts in a "soul-like" manner. Every soul that is formed we hold to be eternally moving. Every change is a movement of the soul. Every soul is, in part, an essence that exists apart from the body, **unchanging and imperishable**. It is a **middle life** <note>original: "zoē mesē." Neoplatonists viewed the Soul as the "horizon" or bridge between the eternal, indivisible divine realm and the temporary, divisible material realm.</note> between the indivisible beings and those beings divided among bodies. Every soul that can be participated in also possesses an eternal activity, making use of what is immediately above it and being made like that which is primary. From all these things, souls exist as the **paradigms** (models) of the essences and the living substances mentioned.

### + On the Soul +

Concerning the "passions" (affections) of the soul: the highest part of the soul is united only with the **intelligible** <note>original: "noētois," the realm of pure thought/forms.</note> and is capable of "seeing" them. The lowest part of the soul communicates with **sensible** (physical) things, known through the senses and through opinions. The middle part is **discursive reason** <term>Dianoia: the type of logic that moves step-by-step, like a mathematician, rather than the instant "seeing" of the higher Intellect.</term>. Up to this point, it is similar; reasons and opinions belong to the "living being" (the human). For this multi-faceted nature of ours consists of divine portions. For **desire** is a "multi-headed beast." **Spirit** (or anger) is a "lion-like crowd." But the **true part** of us is the Intellect and something even more divine within us. The truest part of us is the friend of the **uniform** <note>original: "monoeidous," meaning simple, single, or monadic, as opposed to the complex and messy material world.</note>, which gazes upon sacred things.

<summary>This page defines the hierarchy of Intellect (Nous) and Soul (Psyche), explaining how the Mind remains unchanged while thinking of changing things and how the Soul serves as a bridge between the divine and material worlds. It concludes with the Platonic tripartite division of the soul using the imagery of the beast, the lion, and the divine intellect.</summary>

# 323

## TO ARES.

Hymn 65; while Ares is asked there to pause in his deeds and turn to works of peace, the poet here prays for a peace-inclined heart. The lust for war is called (line 12) "bitter wickedness" <note>original: *kakotēs pikrē*</note> and (line 13) "the soul’s deceptive impulse" <note>original: *psychēs apatēlos hormē*</note>, while the laws of peace, by contrast, are "harmless" <note>original: *apēmones*</note> (line 16). Throughout the entire first half, the hymn is indistinguishable from the Orphic hymns <note>A collection of late-antique hymns attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus, known for their philosophical and mystical tone rather than the narrative style of Homer.</note>.

It is therefore quite remarkable how this hymn could have found its way among the Homeric ones. According to *Baumeister* (p. 103), it was included as Homeric by the compiler of our collection out of ignorance. However, since it is established from the introduction to the hymns that the Alexandrian scholars <note>The librarians and scholars of the Great Library of Alexandria who standardized the Greek literary canon.</note> were already familiar with the smaller Homeric hymns, at the very least a subsequent addition to the collection must be assumed. *Bücheler*, on the other hand (p. 1), and *Guttmann* (in his critical history, p. 43) attribute its inclusion to a scribe’s error. The former believes the hymn entered our collection at the time when the Homeric hymns were combined with the Orphic ones. Yet, since this connection between Homeric and Orphic hymns is not consistent, *Bücheler’s* assumption remains just as uncertain as *Baumeister’s*.

1. **"Exceeding in strength"** <note>original: *hypermeneta*</note>, like **"savior of cities"** <note>original: *polissos* (vs. 2)</note> and **"livelihood"** <note>original: *biotēs* (vs. 10)</note>, are words found only in this hymn. — Ares is also called **"heavy-charioted"** <note>original: *brisarmatos*</note> in Hesiod's *Shield of Heracles* 441; Athena is called **"golden-helmeted"** <note>original: *chryseopēlēx*</note> in Callimachus 5, 43.

3. **"Strong-handed"** <note>original: *karterocheir*</note> appears otherwise only in the very late *Palatine Anthology* 9, 210. — **"Mighty with the spear"** <note>original: *dorysthenēs*</note> was already used by Aeschylus in *The Libation Bearers* 158.

4. When Ares is called the **father of Victory** <note>original: *Nike*</note> and the **ally of Divine Law** <note>original: *Themis*</note> here, it is a purely symbolic expression without any mythological basis. In Hesiod’s *Theogony* 384, Victory is the daughter of Styx and Pallas.

5. **"Sovereign"** <note>original: *tyrannos*</note>. Cf. Aeschylus, *Prometheus Bound* 224: "the sovereign of the gods." Archilochus fragment 25, 3: "I do not desire a great sovereignty." Compare *Bergk*, *Lyric Poets*, Vol II, p. 390. According to the scholarly notes <note>original: *Scholia*</note> on Sophocles' *Oedipus the King*, the word is a later development: "It is clear that the name of 'sovereign' is more recent; for neither Homer nor Hesiod nor any other of the ancients names a 'sovereign' in their poems." A shorter version of this appears in the notes on Aeschylus' *Prometheus Bound* 224. The word is used here in the sense of "absolute ruler" or "lord."

# 324

...brave men. Cf. *Orphic Hymn* 55, 11. — "turning the bright circle" <note>original Greek: *paraugea kyklon elissōn*</note>. According to Preller (*Mythology* I, p. 269), the sun is meant here, though this is hardly correct. According to the usual explanation, which finds strong support in line 10, "beaming down a mild light" <note>original Greek: *prēy katastilbōn selas*</note>, the text refers to the planet Mars, which is famously known to glow with a reddish light. Cf. Bergk, as cited above, p. 752.

7. **"Among the seven-pathed stars of the ether"** <note>original Greek: *aitheros heptaporois eni teiresin*</note> was already explained by Matthiae through Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher from the 5th century AD whose commentaries often touch on celestial mechanics.</note>, *Hymn* IV, 7: "whether you dwell in the ether above the rims of the seven circles" <note>original Greek: *eite kai hepta kyklōn hyper antygas aithera naieis*</note>. Bergk noted that one cannot think of celestial spheres <note>The ancient Greek concept that stars and planets were fixed to rotating crystalline shells.</note> before the time of Anaximander <note>An early Greek philosopher (c. 610–546 BC) credited with the first mechanical model of the world.</note>. However, no one would likely date this hymn as far back as Anaximander's time.

8. **"Above the third arch"** <note>original Greek: *tritatēs hyper antygos*</note> is explained by the passage from Proclus just cited.

9. **"Hear me, beaming down"** <note>original Greek: *klythi katastilbōn*</note> is supported by *Orphic Hymns* 3, 9; 27, 11; and 33, 27. Hemsterhuys and Ilgen wrote "beam down" <note>original Greek: *katastilpson*, the imperative form</note>. — "Courageous" <note>original Greek: *eutharseos*</note> in manuscripts D and M is an obvious improvement over "flourishing" <note>original Greek: *euthaleos*</note> found in manuscript E and some of the Paris class, which usually has a short *a* but occasionally appears with a long *a*. Jacobs already wrote "well-blooming" <note>original Greek: *euthēlē*</note> in *Palatine Anthology* 9, 247.

10. **"Life"** <note>original Greek: *biotēta*</note>—perhaps "youth" <note>original Greek: *neotēta*</note>? "The word *biotēta* points to a very late period," according to Bernhardy, *History of Greek Literature* II, I, p. 417.

16. **Ares as a bringer of peace?** This is based, as A. Matthiae already recognized, on the view that the one who brings the harm can also heal it.

17. Wolf and Ilgen followed Barnes in writing "violent" <note>original Greek: *biaias*, feminine form</note>, but Baumeister correctly defended "violent" <note>original Greek: *biaious*, masculine form</note> by citing Plato's *Republic* 3, 399 A. and *Laws* 10, 885 A.

# CYNEGETICVS

### PRAEFATIO

Cynegetici de aetate et fide post Fischerum et Valckenaerium ambigitur. Equidem hoc tantum sentio, libellum nostrum qualem nunc legimus non ab ipso Xenophonte scriptum esse. Sed, ut statim dicam id quod mihi veritatis aliquam speciem habere videtur, haud scio an *σύγγραμμα* reliquerit in quo regularum seriem in usum venatorum iuniorum, artis venatoriae et laudationem et defensionem contra Aristippum, *κατηγορίαν* sophistarum extemporalem litteris mandasset, compilata Antisthenis sapientia : id autem Diodorus filius, seu quisquis fuerit cuius in manus venerit, scribendi genere in suum morem immutato in lucem edere statuerit manente tamen nomine Xenophontis. ### PREFACE

The age and authenticity of the *Cynegeticus* <note>On Hunting</note> are subjects of debate following the work of Fischer and Valckenaer. For my own part, I believe only this: the little book as we now read it was not written by Xenophon himself. But, to state immediately what seems to me to have some appearance of truth, I suspect he left behind a <term>σύγγραμμα</term> <gloss>treatise</gloss> in which he had committed to writing a series of rules for the use of young hunters, a eulogy and defense of the art of hunting against Aristippus, and an extemporaneous <term>κατηγορίαν</term> <gloss>accusation</gloss> against the sophists, compiled from the wisdom of Antisthenes. This material, however, Diodorus his son—or whoever it was into whose hands it fell—decided to publish, altering the style of writing to his own fashion, yet retaining the name of Xenophon. Although many have detected in our little book many signs of Xenophon's own studies and learning, no one, I think, has even attempted to refute those very weighty arguments of Rademacher, by which he demonstrated that its style is entirely alien to the custom of Xenophon. And as for Herbert Richards, who was inclined to vindicate the authority of the whole book on account of certain words and locutions peculiar to Xenophon, I fear he has not sufficiently weighed how many and how great are the arguments brought to the contrary.

<summary>The preface addresses the scholarly controversy surrounding the authorship of the 'Cynegeticus', suggesting it is a heavily edited compilation rather than an original work by Xenophon.</summary>

<header>PREFACE</header>

Most recently, G. Koertius initiated a study on that part of the *Cynegeticus* <note>On Hunting</note> which is called technical, though he was cut short by death before he could bring it to completion. He first set forth that not only is the arrangement inconvenient, but the instruction itself is so incomplete and obscure that it could hardly be useful to hunters. It must be admitted that he argued this point correctly; yet, it confirms our conjecture regarding the origin of this little book. For the heir of Xenophon, a man certainly not unversed in rhetorical studies but little skilled in writing, preserved the series of events whole, just as he had found them written down in the volume handed to him, and he did not dare to add anything from his own knowledge that might clarify the rules or organize them into a suitable order.

"But," says Koertius, "many precepts in this part of the work are so false that they could in no way have been written by a man truly skilled in the art of hunting." The Fates prevented him from explaining and establishing this opinion with a full number of examples. But I would say that some things, at least, which he criticized or was about to criticize, are controversial rather than false. For the writer of the *Cynegeticus* advises that when a hare has been caught by the dogs, the hunter should hand it over to them to be torn apart. Koertius criticizes this advice as entirely absurd. Yet Blanius, a man no less knowledgeable in the art of hunting than Koertius, recommends the very same thing. What of it? In his book *On Horsemanship*, Xenophon praises Simon for teaching that the quality of a horse's feet is revealed by the sound; yet Bourgelat and Berenger declare this to be clearly false. Learned men struggle against one another over these and such matters, and no one could easily judge what is right or true in any given art. Therefore, not for this reason would I deprive Xenophon of the *Cynegeticus* simply because some who are hunters today attack part of its precepts. Nor, even if we grant that the author of the *Cynegeticus* often speaks nonsense, can it be understood why Arrian, especially since he disagrees not infrequently, never leveled such an objection against him.

For the purpose of reviewing the most corrupt text of all, the manuscripts known as Vindobonensis A and Vaticanus B are by far the most useful, regarding which, if you please, see what I have already stated in the preface to the book *On Horsemanship*. # Νικοσθένης — νιφετός

**Nicosithenes** is a proper name.
<margin>a</margin> **Nicostratus** the comic poet. Athenaeus mentions him in the second book of the *Deipnosophistae*, and says that his plays are *Pandrosos*, *Antyllus* (which also seems to be by Philetaerus), *Hierophantes*, *Clene*, as well as *Abra*, *Hesiod*, *Diabolus*, *Anterosa*, *Hecate*, *Mageirus*, *Otis* <note>or perhaps *Patriotae*</note>, *Plutus*, *Syrus*, *Apelaunomenos*, *Pseudosegmatias*, and *Tocistes*. I found these listed in a collection.
<margin>b</margin> **Nicostratus** the Macedonian rhetorician. He was ranked among the ten lesser rhetoricians, a contemporary of Aristeides and Dion Chrysostomus. He lived during the time of the Emperor Marcus Antoninus. He wrote a *Decamythia*, *Icones*, *Polymythia*, *Thalatturgos*, and many other works, as well as eulogies for Marcus and others.

**Nicophon**, son of Theron, an Athenian comic poet, contemporary of Aristophanes the comic poet. Among his plays are these: *Coming Up from Hades*, *Birth of Aphrodite*, *Pandora*, *Encheirogastores* <gloss>Hand-to-mouthers</gloss>, *Sirens*.

**Nicochares**, son of Philonides the comic poet, an Athenian comic poet, contemporary of Aristophanes. Among his plays are *Amymone*, *Pelops*, *Galatea*, *Heracles Marrying*, *Heracles Choragus*, *Cretans*, *Laconians*, *Lemnians*, *Centaurs*, *Cheirogastores* <gloss>Hand-to-mouthers</gloss>.

**Nicuris** is a place name.

**Nikōen** <gloss>may they conquer</gloss> and **nikōē** <gloss>may he conquer</gloss> are optative forms.

**Nicon**. This man, having won victories in boxing, wrestling, the pancratium, the footrace, and other events at Olympia, Nemea, the Isthmus, and other games, received, as they say, fourteen hundred wreaths. After he departed from among men, one of those who had hated him while he was alive approached his statue and whipped it, until the statue fell and struck the offender. The children of the man pursued the statue for murder, and the Thasians cast it into the sea, in accordance with the law of Draco the Athenian, which mandates exile for inanimate objects that kill. When the Thasians were suffering misfortune, the Pythian oracle commanded them to bring it back. While they were at a loss as to how to raise it, fishermen who had cast their nets for fish brought up the statue. The Thasians then set it up where it had originally been. *Pausanias* 6.11, concerning Theagenes.

**nin** <gloss>them/her/him</gloss> <note>original: "νίν"</note>; "If the people here were to speak of them..." (Sophocles, *Oedipus at Colonus* 43). "You are the one who..."

<column-break/>

"...speaks of them, not I: for you are the one performing the deed, and deeds find their own arguments" (Sophocles, *Electra* 624).

**Nineveh**, a city, and **Ninevite**, one from that same city.

**Niobe** is a proper name.

**Nireus**, the handsome and well-formed.

**Nisa**, a city. And **Nisaea**, a city.

**Nisaea**, a harbor of the Megarid.

**Nisaeum**, a place in Persia where the swiftest horses are produced, called Nisaean. Others (Herodotus 7.40) say it is a large plain in Media, named Nisaeum. This plain, therefore, bears the large horses. **Nisaeus** is a proper name, and refers both to the citizen and the horse.

**Nisibis**, genitive *Nisibeōs*, is the name of a city. **Nisibenian** is the citizen.

**Nisus** is a proper name. "And to Nisus fell the Megarid."

**nissomenos** (Homer, *Iliad* 13.186), returning, and **nissonto** (13.119), they were returning.

**nitarion** and **bitarion**, diminutives used toward women. *Nitarion* is like "little nestling," that is, a young girl. Symmachus says, "Nitarus" is often used as a reproach for softness, and "Batos." They also called small, female vessels *batylai*, and there is a play by Theopompus titled *Batyle*. Others say these are types of plants; he wishes to say, therefore, that he held me like flowers. Aristophanes (*Plutus* 1012): "And by Zeus, if she noticed me feeling sad, she would use the pet names *nitarion* and *bitarion*."

**Nitarius** is a proper name.

**Nitereion**, a promontory.

**Nitria**, a place.

**Nitron** <gloss>natron/soda</gloss>.

**Nitocris** is a proper name.

**Niphades** <gloss>snow-flakes</gloss>; "And words like snowflakes" (Homer, *Iliad* 3.222).

**niphei**, it is snowing, and **niphomena**, being snowed upon.

**Niphetos**, snow falling in fine particles. There are four types of freezing of the watery moisture in the air: above the earth, to a lesser degree, is snow, and to a greater degree, hail; on the earth below, to a lesser degree, is frost, and to a greater degree, ice. *Niphetos* is not a freezing, but rather this quality concerns a different coloring. "As the land of the Scythians is often sprinkled with snow, and it is impossible for them to live without a cold climate."

<header>νιφοσιβεῖς — νομοθέται a</header>

**niphosibeis** <gloss>snow-lashed</gloss>, stormy; (Sophocles, *Ajax* 669) "For even terrible and most powerful things yield to honors. Snow-lashed winters give way to a fruit-bearing summer."

**noēma** <gloss>thought/idea/invention</gloss>; (Aristophanes, *Knights* 1203) "The thought was the goddess's, but the theft was mine." For this is how the demagogues used to play tricks, attributing their own schemes to the goddess, saying that the goddess suggested it, but I snatched it up.

**Noēmonos** <gloss>a proper name</gloss>.

**noēta** <gloss>intelligible things</gloss>, the non-sensible, the invisible.

**notheia** <gloss>illegitimacy</gloss>, secret birth, prostitution.

**notheia** <gloss>illegitimate share</gloss>. That which is given to illegitimate children from their paternal inheritance is called this, and it was up to one thousand drachmas. Thus Lysias, Isaeus, Aristophanes (*Birds* 1643), Hyperides, and Demosthenes in the speech against Aristocrates (213). Harpocration.

**notheuei** <gloss>adulterates/falsifies</gloss>, he deceives, he alienates.

**nothos** <gloss>bastard</gloss>, the stranger.

**noidiōn** <gloss>thoughts/notions</gloss>. He derived *noidion* as a diminutive from the plural *hoi noi* <gloss>the minds</gloss>. Others say it comes from reproaches and abuse, from *oinē* <gloss>wine</gloss> and drunkenness. Aristophanes (*Knights* 100): "I will sprinkle everything with little plans, little maxims, little notions."

**nomades** <gloss>nomads</gloss>, grazing herds. And Scythian tribes; "For among the nomadic Scythians wanders Straton" (Aristophanes, *Birds* 942). Used of those who disturb and persist, since the Scythians, because of the unbearable cold of winter, pack their belongings onto wagons and depart to another land. He who does not have a wagon there is judged dishonored among them.

**nomaditēs** <gloss>nomadic life</gloss>, the private life.

**nomadōn** <gloss>of nomads</gloss>, of wild, barbaric people, those called wagon-carriers or wagon-dwellers.

**nomai** <gloss>divisions/distributions</gloss>.

**nomaia** <gloss>from the pasture</gloss>; in epigrams (AP 6.157): "And the blood of the pasture-fed kid shall flow over you."

**nomarchai** <gloss>provincial governors</gloss>, the rulers of the districts of the land among the Egyptians; they were in power under Ptolemy, the one after Alexander son of Philip.

**Nomas** is a proper name, the lawgiver of the Romans.

**nomeus** <gloss>herdsman</gloss>, shepherd.

**nomē** <gloss>impulse/spread of fire</gloss>; "The spread of the fire happened to be active and effective" (Polybius 1.48).

<column-break/>

**nomizomena** <gloss>customary things</gloss>, customs, or things supposed; Aristophanes (*Plutus* 1186): "Do you not receive your customary portions from these?" Since it was the custom for the priest to receive what was left over from the sacrifice: hides and thighs. Cf. the entry *kolakretēs* <gloss>collector of public funds</gloss>.

**nomizousin** <gloss>they use</gloss>, instead of "they use as currency." And *nomizousin* instead of "they consider"; "Which they consider the greatest honor from the king for private citizens."

**nomion** <gloss>just/lawful</gloss>. And a *nomion* melody is that which is sung in the pasture.

**nomisma** <gloss>coin/custom</gloss> signifies two things: the lawful custom, as Aristophanes in *Clouds* (249), "We have no currency <note>original: "νόμισμα"</note>," and the stamping of minted bronze. The Byzantines used a small coin.

**nomizomenōn** <gloss>lawfully managed</gloss>; "He threw in stamped gold coins, and in some, tetradrachms of those clearly accepted as currency." And again: "Four thousand talents of the bronze accepted as currency in Alexandria."

**Nomitor** is a proper name.

**nomographoi** <gloss>law-writers/decemvirs</gloss>. Among the Romans, in the three hundred and first year after the foundation of the city, the office of the consuls having been abolished, ten law-writers were entrusted with the protection of public affairs. For a certain time, as they interpreted the law for the profit and pleasure of the citizens, they seemed moderate and most suitable of all to rule. For these men, having written the ten tables in both local and Greek laws, set them up on the so-called *kyrbeis* <gloss>three-sided tablets</gloss>. But in the second year of their leadership, having incurred the charge of tyrannical weight, they were dissolved, after Appius especially stirred the multitude to hatred of the decemvirate, for he intended to ruin the virgin daughter of a certain man—who was not obscure in military affairs—being gripped by a hot desire for the girl. The father killed her with his own hand, fearing the tyranny of Appius, as he was rushing to ravish the girl by force. At this, the entire military was moved, stripped the ten of their authority, and forced them to pay penalties for the crimes committed during their rule.

**nomothesia** <gloss>legislation</gloss>, the setting of a law.

**nomothetai** <gloss>lawgivers</gloss>. In olden times Moses, and afterwards Christ Jesus.

<summary>This page defines terms related to the letters N and the early Greek alphabet, specifically focusing on comic poets, historical figures (Nicostratus, Nicon), and the development of legal terminology (nomisma, nomothetai).</summary>

<margin>12</margin> <note>This continues the technical analysis of the legal "definition."</note> Definition by inclusion. It is called this when, the defendant giving a different name to the act, the prosecutor says he is liable to both names, so that it is a double charge, since it contains two accusations. An example is the general who forced himself upon the girl placed in his care by the ambassador, and being judged for public wrongs, he answers that he has not wronged the public but only committed a forced act, while the ambassador claims he is liable for both. The introduction is from the opponent, but the speech is carried forward through one form, the judicial. For the end of this is justice and the preparation is through justice.

***

The licentiousness, O men of the jury, and the <term>hybris</term> <gloss>outrage</gloss> which Meidias always uses against everyone, I think not one of you nor of the other citizens is ignorant. I, doing exactly what each of you if outraged would have chosen to do, did this myself and brought a preliminary charge of wrongdoing against this man regarding the festival, not only having received blows from him at the <term>Dionysia</term>, but also having suffered many other <margin>2</margin> violent things throughout the entire <term>choregia</term> <gloss>period of sponsoring the chorus</gloss>. When the entire people, acting well and doing what is right, were so angry and provoked and showed such great zeal for the wrongs they knew I suffered, so that even though this man and some others on his behalf did everything they could, they were not persuaded, nor did they look at the wealth of these men nor their promises, but with one mind voted against him, many people coming to me, O men of the jury, both of you who are now in the court and other citizens, thought it right and urged me to prosecute and deliver this man to you. As it seems to me, O men of Athens,

<header>AGAINST MEIDIAS.</header>

by the gods, it was for two reasons: they both thought that I had suffered terrible things and they wished at the same time to take vengeance for what they had seen him do to others, as he is bold and disgusting and <margin>3</margin> no longer even controllable. Since things are this way, all things that it was proper for me to guard have been justly kept for you, and I am here to accuse as you see since someone is bringing the case in. I have refused much money, O men of Athens, which I might have taken on the condition that I would not accuse him, and I have <margin>4</margin> endured many petitions and favors and, by Zeus, threats. But for what remains among you after this, the more this man has troubled and sent around messages (for I saw him just now before the courts doing such things), the more I hope to have justice. For I would not think so poorly of any of you, neither that you will neglect those things about which you yourselves were zealous toward me, nor that, so that Meidias might outrage others without fear in the future, any of you will vote, having sworn an oath, anything <margin>5</margin> other than what he thinks is just. If, therefore, O men of Athens, I were going to accuse him of illegalities or of a corrupt embassy or some other such charge, I would not think it right to ask anything of you, thinking that it belongs to the accuser regarding such things only to prove them, and to the defendant to ask for mercy. But since he corrupted the judges, and because of this the tribe was unjustly <margin>6</margin> deprived of the tripod, and I myself received blows and was outraged in such a way as I do not know if any other <term>choregos</term> was ever outraged, and I come into court following the vote of condemnation which the people made because they were indignant and shared in my anger over these things, I will not hesitate to also make a request. For if it is possible to say this, I am now the one on trial, if indeed for an outraged man to meet with no justice is a kind of calamity. Ἐν πρέσβεσι ἡ παρ’ ἡμῶν ἡ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἀποστέλλονται. καὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἀποστέλλονται χρὴ φιλοτίμως τε καὶ δεξιῶς τούτους ὑποδέχεσθαι. καὶ γὰρ τιμῶσι αὐτοὺς τοὺς δὲ ἐπιμελῶς ὑπὸ αὐτοῦ δὲ ἀσφαλῶς ἔχειν εἰς σιωπὴν διδάσκειν ἐπερωτώμενοι αὐτὸν κἂν γε τῶν λίαν ἀπρεπῶν πρέσβεων ὦσιν ὠφελεῖσθαι ἐκείνων τε καὶ ἡμῶν εἶναι ἵνα τῶν ἐθνῶν ἐμφανίζῃ αὐτοῖς τὴν ἡμετέραν σπουδὴν ἀσφαλῶς ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ οἱ πλησιόχωροι ἡμῶν καθιστάμενοι. ἔνθεν δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν ἔχουσι δύναμιν. εἰ δὲ μάλα πολὺ ἡμῶν διεστηκόσιν ὧδε πλῆθος στρατὸς εἴη ἀνδρεῖος. χρὴ γῆλε πᾶντον ὑπ’ ἐς γυναῖκαν καλλῇ ἐμφανίζειν αὐτοῖς πλῆθος δὲ ἀνδρῶν καὶ ὅπλων εὐσχημίαν καὶ τύχην ὑψηλά. οἱ δὲ παρ’ ἡμῶν πρέσβεις ἀποστέλλονται χρὴ τούτους πρῶτον μὲν ἐπ’ εὐσεβείᾳ γνωρίζεσθαι καὶ μὴ ἐπ’ ἐκκλησίᾳ κατηγορηθέντες ποτὲ δημοσίᾳ κατακρίνωνται. εἶναι φρονίμους τὴν φύσιν, εὐνοοῦντα κοινὰ ὧδε καὶ πρὸς ἀρνοῦντες ὅθεν σωτηρίων κάθ’ ἕρ ἡ γουλίο. καὶ τὴν ἀποστολὴν προθύμους ἀλλὰ βεβαιώσεως καθάπερ οἱ ἀγωνίαις ἰατροί. ὁ μὲν παρὰ παρχηδονίοις δεβυοῦται καὶ πρὸς ρωμαίους περὶ εἰρήνης πρέσβευον ἀπεσταλμένος ὁμοῦσιν ἐπανελθεῖν προϋπέθετο. τῶν ρωμαίων τὴν εἰρήνην οὐκ ἀπεδέξαντο. ὁ δὲ πρὸς ρωμαίους ἀφίκετο ἀπαγορεύειν τὸν ρωμαίων ῥήτορα ἀσύμφορον αὐτῶν οὐδὲν πειθὼ δ’ αὐτοὺς ἐπανελθεῖν πρὸς παρχηδονίους τὸν ὁρῶν φιλόμενος. ὅτε μὲν ἐς βαβυλῶνα τῆς αἰγύπτου τὸν πέρσην ἀνηγέας τὰ αἰγυπτίων διέλουσιν χρὴ δὲ τοὺς πρέσβεῖς παραχωρεῖν, πρὸς οὓς ἀποστέλλονται φαίνονται ἐπιχαρῆσε. μεγάλο φύγωσι ἄμφω δὲ οἱ οἰκεῖα τάδε τῶν πολεμίων ἐκείνῳ ποιοῦντες ἀλλαγῇ.

...and the bright [part] inside the four-sided leather screen <note>original: "δέρρις"</note>. It should be arranged and wrapped in the center, and of the sides, the three should be of black leather, but where the light shines through, it is clear to those walking well. It is also good for them to wear a small shield, covering the whole of the body while dressed and divided, [for] those hunting <note>original: "σευποκυνηγῶν"</note> and the soles of the feet. One must wear leather [shoes] on the soles because of the caltrops <note>original: "τριβόλους"</note> and the brambles. When this is perceived by them—this, on one hand, for the eagerness of those in front, and this, on the other, for fear so that they do not become lazy while fleeing. In addition to these, one must bring that soldiers be chosen for the preparation of the camp, likewise, as many as are carrying while walking and having struck down an enemy, so that it seems to the enemies that a large multitude is coming upon them; and those who use the capture of the opponents should recognize some among them, and calling out to themselves while pretending to be fleeing, so that the opponents follow the commanders and obey them because of the camp being clearly and foolishly occupied [by them], and these follow. The other part, from where the enemies came upon us, and which leads toward the enemy [side], [one must] destroy, so that the enemies might have a place of flight, or [else] it compels them to stand their own ground, having flowed back from the attack.

<margin>I know this myself, but nevertheless</margin>
Regarding defectors

It is necessary to receive those who are defecting, and to benefit them in this way; but one must guard against the good [ones] in case they are taken by us, and are worshiped, but rather they should be bound by the laws of the fountains <note>original: "πηγῶν νομιμοῖς"</note>; but for the more noble among them, [one should] treat [them] in the enemy [camp] if we wish, provided they have goodwill, and especially those who come together according to the city. One gathers the war thus if these have defected to us; and the less valuable of them [one should] bring with [the] army, where the signals are, and when struck it becomes [clear] as to the signs, as one must trust those many of their own; it is necessary not only to serve us, [but to] send gifts to the enemies, so that in the end [we may] enslave three hundred of them in the march, having sent them gifts, [and] through them, take the city.
Regarding scouts
[The methods] invented for the scouts <note>original: "καταλίκων"</note>, so that by them, while being straightened, [we may see] the affairs of the opponents, it is clear to us to know [how] to choose...

<summary>The page concludes with specific logistical details for night gear, the handling of defectors to infiltrate enemy lines, and the tactical use of scouts for intelligence.</summary>
<keywords>night gear, defectors, psychological warfare, infiltration, scouts, intelligence gathering</keywords>

The nature of a good thing arises from external sources. Nor should these things be prepared against the enemy, or, when acting with other neighbors, failing in the agreement of the neighbors. Therefore, when it is reported that the enemy is preparing against us, it is necessary first to set [our position] in safety, such as the previously mentioned cities and lands. Then, one must aim to reach a state of desperation while observing the rest, and clearing out one's own places through which they intend to pass, so that the agreement back to us may be a clear trap for the enemy and profitable to us. As for what we give, whether we eat—for example, if we are campaigning with others and it is reported that the enemies are with us—it brings profit to us to be annoyed at those warring, and likewise if others are campaigning against them. Whether it is a civil war or [a war] of neighbors, one remains quiet, for the one warring often makes peace with himself while watching the foreigners, but one must be a neighbor. Those who have descended should each give back to those who are aware of the initiation <note>original: "μυσάγωγία"</note> what is proper. Both neighbors must have acted safely, as it is necessary for all of them to deliberate, and in what manner, and within what place—only the marketplace, through which many of our people and foreigners come up, while looking toward the trade. For in this, they will be more able to take the enemies. Hence, as the day progresses, again the same things of others [are returned] to them, and [one is] returning wars and showing us what is said among our own—the enemies and how their things are hostile. It is necessary for all those who command not to be of the same race as the opponents, nor to have suffered any great evil <margin>others kill</margin> from us, such as wives, children, parents, or brothers being there because of us, the longing for whom might make them wish for the enemies to be allowed into any place, not otherwise plotting against their own. It is necessary for them to be wise by nature, and those who are said to be warring well, <margin>fifth plaque</margin> having chosen those who are prepared. Furthermore, they must be experienced in the places through which they will pass. They must also be personally arriving.

<summary>This page discusses strategic caution when dealing with neighbors and foreign allies, emphasizing the necessity of securing one's own territory, managing trade and intelligence, and vetting military commanders to ensure loyalty.</summary>
<keywords>military strategy, diplomacy, intelligence, borders, betrayal, loyalty</keywords>

for those things that are necessary for existence, so that he might enjoy the future state of his own youth <note>original: "νότητος", likely referring to spiritual renewal or vigor</note>, he did not make a judgment. He says what kind of end follows after the neglect. For these people, the tyranny arises from the very things that are more useful and leads toward this sacred servitude. For the sinners, there will be food that remains wretched; but for the righteous, there is an abundance apart from accusations. For them, the suffering is in no way able to represent the manner of life in a tragic way. For through the working of the secret things of Christ <note>original: "χριστοῦ"</note>, Christ is found in my own affairs. Some things, having his body <note>original: "σῶμα"</note> and an end that has a hard appearance, he provided from his own flesh and blood. In this way, he might offer grace <note>original: "χάριν"</note> to them. But the garments of grace he hews with iron and they are cut into small pieces. He leads the way, rather, by dividing the stones with naked ash. He himself will point out the paths to those who work the mines. The entire work is divided by the cutting of atoms <note>original: "ἀτόμων", referring to indivisible particles or small fragments</note> and according to this manner. For they themselves and they alone, by the grace that sparkles in their own words, do not cut from the stones, but from themselves; and they cut through the breeze. They undermine a multitude, not immediately, but the body of Christ which is from him alone and of stone. But the body of the choir; and again from them a portion on the left hand, in which there also, in a similar way, they define a broken and similar portion to those of the wicked. These alone, with stones bound to those who act afterward, competing with stone-cutters, as if seating the stone like a bark or shell; and having transformed the foundations of the body in many ways. And the fragments, rather, fall to the ground, not according to their own appearance and power, but toward the eye upon the sun's rebuke, with no one permitting it. But the men and

But from the place where this excavated material is carried away in equal portions, they also collect the rubble according to the laws established previously in those places. This material they consider among the worthless things, having handed it over. The elders, who are most observant of the laws, transport the stone. These men are considered great by those called overseers <term>epopousin</term> <gloss>those who watch over or inspect</gloss>. For those within thirty years of age bear witness to the others. Likewise, having received it with courage, they strike it with iron tools upon silver-like surfaces. And they perform the greatest grinding in a similar manner, at the same hour, using thick pieces in part. In this way, the law honors the women who have been trained together after the watches. To the men and the leaders, there are a multitude of mills in a row. Upon these, they perform the treading of the stone just like the others, and all the women from the market are present. In this way, they describe the process. My breath <note>or perhaps "the scent"</note> exists as a captive of the body. They grind, and they continue grinding until the whole measure is reduced to dust, which is the portion handed over. All these people are those who have come to the number of captivity, facing death, even this very death. But for those who are entreating, the refinement <term>katargasmon</term> <gloss>working down or processing of ore</gloss> succeeds. Those called the "hares" <note>likely a technical term for a specific class of laborer or a specific tool</note> say all these things, having undertaken the royal service for the whole task. The labor is of such a kind: they cover the strength of the marble with woolly coverings. Upon flat boards, there is a spreading and an inspection as if we were burying someone. It is not upright. The exhausted land has flashed forth the name of gold. While carrying water, they rub it with their hands; at first lightly, then more vigorously. I am purified <note>original: "agnooumai", likely a scribal error for "agnizomai"</note>. For that which is exhausted flows away together with the influx of the boarding.

<summary>This page describes the labor-intensive process of gold mining and refining, involving the transport of ore, the use of mills by men and women, and the final washing of the crushed material on boards.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the transition from Proclus’s mathematical discourse on the World Soul toward the physical application of these principles. Having established that the universe is bound by geometric and harmonic proportions, he now examines how these "powers" manifest in material bodies and the human form, using the analogy of a physician to explain how Nature maintains the "health" or balance of the cosmos.</meta>

# Commentary on Plato’s Timaeus

<page-num>288</page-num>

...common in **power** <note>original: "dynamei" (δυνάμει). In this context, it refers to an inherent faculty or potentiality that allows a body to act or be acted upon.</note>. Bodies also have certain causes; some kinds are manifest to us, while others are the causes themselves. For among these, some are understood to have an intellectual power, while others have different sorts. This is the case with our own bodies: while some things are visible, it is not always clear why all bodies are subject to the forces that compel them. For within the body, the passage of time is seen in the changes of their composite parts. Since a middle-ground mastery exists over all the **elements** <note>original: "stoicheia" (στοιχεία). The fundamental building blocks—fire, air, water, and earth—which Proclus views as being governed by higher spiritual principles.</note>, the underlying essence uses them, though they are clearly part of Nature itself. It performs its work according to this principle. And therefore, it is composed of presences, the phases of which are counted in number. For while some are able to act through numbers, natural things follow after. The whole universe is seen by those who look, but regarding the elements, these things are not the same. We possess the powers of bodies, both those that synthesize and those that are functional; for bodies were given to us, yet the state of their powers is not judged solely by the senses, nor are they all the same, so that all things are even now part of the same bodies. It is composed of power even in its parts.

For you might say that something in the senses is infinite compared to other bodies, as it has become the means for diagnosis, and is the cause of all these same things. Or perhaps this power has been put forward as either a theoretical science or a medicinal one, like the nature of health. For if bodies do not all become a certain thing by nature, it happens through the causes of **physicians** <note>original: "iatron" (ἰατρῶν). Proclus frequently uses the doctor as an analogy for the Demiurge or Nature, both of whom "prescribe" order to chaotic matter.</note>; for they provided the active causes and some power, or perhaps the entire synthesis of the body is brought toward this. Or if they are made through the ways of the **flesh** <note>original: "sarka" (σάρκα).</note>, it is not possible to define them as indivisible. Just as one might wish for all powers to be authoritative, they each arise specifically in their own way. We speak of the advantage and the division of the beginning of bodies; they would surely incline toward where a certain body of the generations is compared. It is necessary to say that they are as wretched and pitiable as we can imagine.

Natural philosophy teaches the truth. And it is simply this: we see some of their powers as desirable, while another power was composed of all the parts that fulfill such a thing. According to the appearance of communion and the **symmetry of bulk** <note>original: "onkou symmetrias" (ὄγκου συμμετρίας). The mathematical balance of physical volume or mass.</note>. And as far as the sensory perceptions are concerned, these things are common to all; to be ignorant of them is to lose them. There is a method for these things to relate the part to the whole of the subject matter. For instance, things known by us would not have this order of theirs through this method, even if the first orders are from the **connatural** <note>original: "symphyton" (συμφύτων). Things that are grown together or share an innate nature.</note> bodies. Such a world is for us a governing principle. Because we have known whether it exists and what its particularity is, and the seasons themselves; but one must not be so bold as to treat them as a desert. Even if a certain opinion from them was mistaken until the end. Since there are certain—

<column-break/>

<page-num>289</page-num>

—on the other hand, acting as an opponent to everything through the **harmonies** <note>original: "harmonion" (ἁρμονιών). Referring to the musical and mathematical ratios that Proclus believes hold the physical universe together.</note>. From this, the cause or the path arose and continued. These are the distinguishing marks of how things come to be; for they were innate to the universals, and exist through the world, both in the parts and the whole. It appeared as though the things within the ruins were moving into the world. The cause is most similar toward the external. And so all things, if one understands that all these things are fitted together, are positioned as the seat of the **Eternal** <note>original: "aidiou" (αϊδίου). The timeless, unchanging realm of the divine.</note> itself. Therefore, all things have been joined together through its own nature and remain undivided, just as the scripture stands. There is also something indivisible, and the **demiurgic reason** <note>original: "demiourgikon logon" (δημιουργικὸν λόγον). The creative blueprint or "word" of the Creator that organizes the cosmos.</note> itself is handed down as that which is without disposition, even within natural things. Such is the nature of the intentions within the creator. I say these things exist through the bond of these elements. And indeed, such things are unsubstantial due to their nature, yet they are synthetic; for this is the nature of the whole world, that it be extended, and the one seat of all things leads out from the messengers.

The nature of the gods is in those things in which both being and the divine exist. Insofar as the sovereignty of the Eternal has begun, the world is also eternal. There is also that which is governed by the lowest things, such as the virtue of the whole, or even the physician that exists within it. For there is a certain utility in it... or a darkness. For health <unclear>...</unclear> indeed, what we call nature exists in us as living beings. And those things which exist through other bodies. It is appropriate that it is thus in power. However, those who look toward the fluid and whatever color it may be, participate in it, and insofar as it is given through heat, a part sleeps there, and the composition of this is far from the peak. These things, then, we reasonably know to be small, because the harmony of this consists either in its lack of passion or its removal. But the other things within us, such as **loves** <note>original: "erotes" (ἔρωτες). Not merely romantic love, but the cosmic force of attraction that draws the soul toward the divine.</note>, are blamed for such things or for the nature of the divine. Most of all, such things are strengthened by this, and by the attraction that might occur through the holy temple. For it is known through sensory things. For those things which seemed then to be distinguished by a lack of passion were composed in the same way. Already the preparation is fulfilled or composed. It possesses a power close to that of the cause. Or why do we speak of God as the divine cause, seen as a concern that proceeds into him? It seems right to name it thus. The description of the whole world is by nature; we name it, as if nature is the leader of the manifest causes. Through the one who created, we seek the things that are known, or we name the distinction of the ancients which is least contradictory. And so the **Eternal One** <note>original: "ho aionios" (ὁ αἰώνιος). The timeless principle of the universe.</note> speaks. Our joy...

<summary>Proclus discusses how the invisible "powers" and "harmonies" of the Demiurge manifest in physical bodies and the elements. He uses the analogy of medical science and health to explain how the natural world is ordered and maintained by a "demiurgic reason."</summary>
<keywords>Demiurge, Harmony, Elements, Nature, Eternal World, Divine Cause, Symmetry, Physical Bodies</keywords>
auditTranslation:
<meta>This page transitions from the general discussion of material elements to the specific metaphysical principles—Providence and Analogy—that Proclus believes the Demiurge (the Creator) used to bind the cosmos into a unified "icon" of the divine. It expands on the mathematical ratios discussed previously, applying them to the immortality of the soul and the structure of the world as a "living being."</meta>

# Commentary on Plato’s Timaeus

<page-num>130</page-num>

Those who hypothesize the cause of the **dissolution** <note>original: "lyseos" (λύσεως). In Platonism, this refers to the breaking apart of a composite being into its constituent elements.</note> for each of the beings give the power to those prior things, which the one who divides has set to be divided. Therefore, the subsequent thinkers say that from these we have the causes of those things that are coming into being, which is the object of our inquiry. Consequently, the world appears to have been generated from **ungrudging bounty** <note>original: "ex aphthonon" (ἐξ ἀφθόνων). This refers to Timaeus 29e, where Plato explains that the Creator, being good and lacking any envy, desired all things to be as like himself as possible.</note> and is revealed to those being educated, having been awakened from every side. Indeed, he named that which succeeds it, and having naturally generated the cosmos, it is not as a whole for each part of the discursive intellect. For this indicates that which is generated itself, as well as the being and the continuity of those things under **Providence** <note>original: "pronoia" (προνοίᾳ). The divine foresight or care that maintains the order of the universe.</note>, setting himself outside the very process of generation. 

He named, therefore, the two of them to fit all things together, and we complete this for each thing. In another way, it is not entirely easy in both cases for one who is thinking to grasp how it holds. Let this be one thing, and the other be another part of them, for the whole is not what it ought to be in this regard. But all things are greater, and everything seemed to be so. We have this itself for them, for its very existence is the being of the **substances** <note>original: "hypostaseis" (ὑποστάσεις). The underlying realities or essential natures of things.</note>; the form is with and within it, and we learn this through change. Our aim there is how it seems to complete the fitting things, and there is a continuity and a sense of what is proper through its own nature, and this is what we complete. 

Because of his easy and ungrudging **imparting** <note>original: "metadosin" (μετάδοσιν). The act of the higher principle sharing its essence or goodness with the lower.</note> to it, he says that this imparting exists, and through it, we complete the **immortals** <note>original: "athanatous" (ἀθανάτους). Likely referring to the "younger gods" or the immortal part of the human soul.</note>. Generation and the earth and the whole undergo natural changes, and everything is becoming. And naturally, no part has its being after generation, but rather as that which is becoming. And this same continuity seems to come from learning; for it exists for it, and in a way that is perishable in the two or more elements. By this, we mean the first element and that which is becoming, and one part belongs to numbers; for it is similar to the **Cause** <note>original: "aitia" (αἰτίᾳ). The primary principle (the Demiurge or the Good) that sets the universe in motion.</note> that is moved. 

One part belongs to itself. Therefore, that which is according to the **analogy** <note>original: "analogoun" (ἀναλογοῦν). Mathematical proportion used as a cosmic glue to bind disparate elements like fire and earth.</note> makes these things become a kind of likeness. For its being belongs to itself, and we call this "analogies." This, then, we call nature: the ordering of things toward one another. It is equal because it exists by **participation** <note>original: "methexei" (μεθέξει). The central Platonic concept where material things "share in" the reality of the immaterial Forms.</note>. Since there is an ease and a consistency, it is impossible to be without them. For everything is its being. Its being is the same for both of them. How does it act toward that which is there by its power? Because of the cause, that which is becoming is itself one thing, and another is another part of them. For this is the greater cause. Because of the things of the cosmos, this is the cause for it: that even this is a **wanderer** <note>original: "planetes" (πλανήτης). Often refers to the planets, but here perhaps to the "wandering" or unstable nature of material existence.</note> among that which is established. And so it reveals the nature of physical theory. There is no need to give way to the established order or to be drawn there; rather, it exists in a certain **ratio** <note>original: "logo" (λόγω). In this context, a mathematical ratio or a rational principle of organization.</note>, and is thus itself established otherwise. Because of the easy cause, Timaeus says that **harmony** <note>original: "harmonias" (ἁρμονίας). The fitting together of parts into a musical or mathematical whole.</note> belongs to the composition of the cosmos, and symmetry is upon it through this.

<column-break/>

<page-num>131</page-num>

The aim for the Maker is a **cosmic icon** <note>original: "eikon kosmike" (εἰκὼν κοσμική). The physical universe is viewed as a "statue" or "image" of the eternal, intelligible Living Being.</note>, as those things are to that analogy. This indeed produces **procession** <note>original: "proodon" (πρόοδον). The Neoplatonic movement where reality flows out from the One into multiplicity.</note> and remains. For it is clear from the name that it has one reference toward that which is becoming; hence Timaeus rightly says this regarding the whole of this subject. And then, after an interpolation, he named it two equalities which he uses: the **bond** <note>original: "desmos" (δεσμός). Plato calls proportion the "most beautiful bond" because it creates unity.</note> is equal, and the bond is most sovereignly created by analogy. He holds this as more demonstrative, and being upon the very thing sought, it was not entirely easy to see it dissolved by one who is not at all a specialist. For it acts as twelve to twelve. 

Nothing is dissolved by the dissolution... in the higher part of the genus, to be left behind at a sign, but rather wherever the whole is. According to which the universe is a **living being** <note>original: "zoon" (ζῷον). Plato describes the cosmos as a single, visible living being that contains all other living beings within it.</note>, two parts of the cosmos, the whole; whence in the making of it, he says, there is still the Same and the Other of them. Because the living being is eternal from all things, and they will be so even in perishable forms, and in the two or more where such a thing exists, as is likely. Not since it is not possible for these things to be held after he made them, but again toward this, these things are a certain reality. And indeed, from this, it comes to be, from which those who learn are shown what is likely; and it might be possible, in another way, in their analogy and in its likelihood. And we see many things by learning otherwise, because of seeking among the "easinesses" <note>Note: Proclus uses "easiness" (eukolia) to describe the effortless way the divine acts.</note> that one thing is not, and how it is, and it is the beginning of number. But always for him there is a continuity and a sense of his own affairs from learning, but always continuity and likelihood. And so it reveals the nature of physical theory. 

For the parts are limited even with him, and in order as toward a similar thing that is to be. In terms of numbers and oneself, we are able, because it is not otherwise, to first say that **geometry** <note>original: "geometrian" (γεωμετρίαν). The study of continuous magnitudes, essential for understanding the structure of space.</note> is necessary for the response, though not in the *Timaeus*. Regarding numbers, then, it is so. See how these things are also an icon. Since he himself wishes to show that **Being** <note>original: "to on" (τὸ ὄν). True, unchanging reality as opposed to the "becoming" of the physical world.</note> is properly beyond these, and to provide them as the two principles of the cosmos, we call these analogies the "likely." This, therefore, is indicated in that which is becoming, for there the learning of the part is to be similar through one's own nature. 

Therefore, he gives him help from divine, canonical, and political positions, since he is about to become that which Timaeus set him to be; and he did not say this was a wanderer, at least in the cause of what was seen. And in the whole and in such things. This is also because with him there is hope where there is difficulty. To those who compose the things of the cosmos and the whole as this, and as an icon, this is in a certain ratio; this is the cause of the difficulties being the whole itself. It is a ratio; and if it is the most **paradigmatic** <note>original: "paradeigmatikotaton" (παραδειγματικώτατον). Relating to the eternal Archetypes or Forms that the physical world copies.</note> number, it is so by participation. It is clear that the same thing becomes the analogical, not according to each part, for one must not nowhere move that which is similar to this from its established place!

<summary>This page discusses the metaphysical "bond" of analogy (proportion) that the Demiurge uses to unify the cosmos. Proclus explains that the world is an "icon" or image of eternal reality, held together by mathematical ratios that ensure its continuity and prevent its dissolution.</summary>
<keywords>Demiurge, Providence, Analogy, Cosmic Icon, Proportion, Continuity, Participation, Timaeus, Geometry, Arithmetic</keywords>

# Meditations
## On Grammar, Motion, and the Afflictions of the Mind

**Column 1**

There is a deception even regarding the name **apolic** <note>original: *apollikēn*; the term is obscure, possibly referring to a name that is "removed" or "distant" from its object</note>. What belongs to one, it says, but much is that which is equal to being. Among equals. A name was given to things that exist. The form is derived from these. This is what we say. A pretext <unclear>s'</unclear> of blame, for these are not those things by which they measure, from which we name things in some way. But those things of private victories. To seek a name in this way. In which also to remain. This was better said of common things. But the external, is it possible? The "splendid" used <term>catachrestically</term> <note>original: *katachrēstikōs*, the use of a word in a sense different from its proper one, like calling a "silver" cup "golden"</note> of common things. For the one who shares frequently tends to follow it.

And immediately after this: speak concerning **structure**; as many things as he sees regarding structure in a single way. And there is a humble thing of his, the steps. It is itself, and one will find it. It is equal. What kind of thing is the <term>pronoun</term> <note>original: *antōnymia*</note>, and its feminine form, "this woman." And "that man" and "that woman" for example. For it is not first for him. It is used <term>infinitively</term> <note>original: *aparemphatikōs*</note>. ...and you will have the double mercury of the sages <note>a classic term for the Philosopher's Stone or its primary material</note>, which lacks nothing except to be cooked and reduced into projection powder. As for the white liquor that comes out of the oil of gold, it is an animated mercurial spirit that has the aurific principle. It serves to multiply and to ferment the double mercury from before when it is reduced to powder.

Proceed thus: take one ounce of the double mercury reduced to powder, put it into an egg-shaped vessel with half an ounce of the white liquor, seal it, and cook it at a regulated fire until reduced to powder. Take this powder and mix it with half its weight of the white liquor, cook as before, and reiterate this work as much as you judge appropriate. This is called "inceration" <note>the process of softening or making a substance wax-like</note>; it multiplies the powder in quality and quantity, and one can push it almost to infinity.

It must be noted that with this white liquor, one can make very lucrative ores with gold and mercury, and that promptly. One can make them with the aforementioned powder, and it is good to understand in passing that it is from this single trunk and this root that all the particularities and all the transmutatory branches start.

Take the projection powder from before and mix it with ten times its weight of common mercury, cook the whole together in a matrass for 40 days, then add ten times the weight of this common mercury and cook everything as before. Take the cooked mass and divide it into two, melt one part, and you will find good gold that stands every test, and with the other part, join its weight of common mercury and cook for a month, and thus you will be able to draw half every month to melt.

...and this is done the same way every 40 days with the spirit, when one has dissolved enough gold or silver in it and one has then reduced the whole into powder. All the sulfurs of minerals, marcasites <note>a variety of iron sulfide</note>, hematites, dilated <note>likely referring to substances expanded by chemical treatment</note>, and animated by this white mercurial spirit, have the same effect, and the sulfurs thus prepared are called "living gold." One works them thus: take a mercurial liquor, from whatever liquor it is drawn, provided that one has followed our precepts, sell/make fusible with this liquor the alkali salt drawn from the same material; this will form a homogeneous liquor that is called "double mercury."

One takes this mercury and soaks in it, little by little, the sulfur drawn from the same material, and this until it is reduced into a homogeneous liquor. Then this liquor is called "living sulfur," or "animated," or "living sun," because it is the pure part of the mixture from which it is drawn.

This living sulfur, by repeated cooking, becomes by itself, without addition, projection powder, and this is what is called "the work of the poor." But to shorten the time, one gilds gold with the mercurial liquor, draws its sulfur, and dilates both, then reduces them into a homogeneous liquor. To make a "regenerated gold," one takes one part of this regenerated gold and as much living sulfur from before, one puts the whole into a hermetically luted matrass, and one lights it at a regulated lamp fire until everything is reduced...

one who is in dread, there was not one among them whose heart was not suddenly gripped by fear, and not without cause. For it was the <term>Truchement</term> <gloss>interpreter</gloss>, who from the moment they left the pavilion had followed Charide's tracks. He had expected to find her hidden nearby in some small neighboring woods, but recognizing her path step by step, he could not stop himself from following her continuously, driven like a mad dog. Having arrived at the river Araxes and knowing they had crossed, his fury drove him cruelly. He wished to cross the water, taking for reinforcement only these two dogs, which he took from some shepherds he found nearby. Scythian dogs are naturally cruel and strong, not fearing to attack bulls, lions, tigers, and other such wild beasts. They are of a large build, and their barks are terrible. It is said that Alexander, King of Macedonia, having received two of them as a gift from the King of Albania, who had them brought from Scythia, wanted to test their strength. He had a lion presented to them, which was immediately strangled by one of them. Then he had a

elephant presented to them, which fared no better. When the female dogs are in heat, those who keep them lead them to the forests to be bred by some tiger. This is the source of the cruelty and strength found in these beasts. The fear that Charide felt for herself and for those in her company gave wings to their feet. Finding no other safety, they all threw themselves into a cavern located at the bottom of a valley at the foot of the Amodacian mountains, from which flow the river Tyrias and the river Araxes. They were not very far into this cavern when the <term>Truchement</term> <gloss>interpreter</gloss> arrived at its entrance. Seeing by their footprints that they had entered there, he made a soldier, whom he had brought with him, get down from his chariot to discover if they were inside. This man, hearing some noise in his opinion, entered further in. However, he could see nothing at all. Charide and the others had moved aside, seeing this soldier pass beyond them. He did not perceive them in any way, as his vision, clear in the daylight, was dulled by the sudden darkness. This Scythian cried out as loudly as he could in his language: "Come here, miserable fugitives and thieves! Come quickly to my master!"

<margin>In your seed all nations [shall be blessed]: because you obeyed my voice. Genesis 22.</margin>
<margin>Obedience is better than sacrifices. 1 Samuel 15.</margin>
<margin>Embrace discipline, lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the way of the just. Psalm 2.</margin>
<margin>Prudence shall keep you, to deliver you from the evil way. Proverbs 2.</margin>

"All bound by hands and feet,
And at the open door a prisoner;
And I am called by my right name
Obedience, and so reclaimed.
My cords and also my bonds,
These are various commandments
Which bind the own will
So that it can do nothing according to its liking."
### <term>Discipline</term>
"And I," said she with the file,
"Am called Discipline,
Who everywhere here keeps the order
So that one does not bite into evil.
The file which is in my mouth
Is the rebuke of evil;
I polish and scour everything
Where there is rust and filth.
There is nothing that I do not file away,
Entirely down to the root.
And so that I do everything perfectly
And do not fail in anything,
With this shield of Prudence,
Which is very necessary for this,
I am armed, as you see well;
Thus my bearing is more beautiful.
For certainly if I did not have it,
I would not be sufficient
To correct or to file,
Or to remove the rust of another."

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts several figures seated at a long table in a refectory. They are being served by figures that represent the "dead" or ancestors who have provided for the monastery through their legacies.</note>

"What will be/and the condition
Of these tables/and those eating,
And of these dead whom I see serving,
For which I am greatly astonished."

<column-break/>

<margin>You shall be refreshed before the Lord your God. Deuteronomy 12.</margin>

### <term>Abstinence</term>
"Certainly," she said, "I tell you
That I am the Refectorer
Of all here, and the stewardess,
Who gives to drink and to eat
To everyone as there is need
To sustain the human body
And maintain it in health.
I am named Abstinence,
And armed with the <term>gorgerette</term> <gloss>neck-armor</gloss>
Which is called Sobriety,
By which the taste is guarded;
Also the throat from swallowing
Any morsel that could be harmful.
And do not be astonished
By the dead who feed the living
And serve them devotedly;
Know that these are good people
Who passed away long ago,
Who have given so much of their goods
To the living/that they are sustained
Very sufficiently and fed.
He would certainly be too foolish
Who would not know that service
He had from the dead/who would eat
Their own/and would live from their goods."

<margin>Abstinence truly is to abstain from sins. Distinction 5.</margin>
<margin>Nature is content with few and minimal things. Boethius, book 2 of the Consolation of Philosophy.</margin>
<margin>It is a virtue to have abstained from pleasing goods. Ovid.</margin>

<margin>Rebuke is just when: first it is done in oneself, and afterward it is excited in another. Case 3, question 7.</margin>

### The Pilgrim
<note>A decorative initial V is printed here.</note>
"I saw another pass soon
Toward the refectory going,
Who had a neck-armor
Which closed her throat well.
After her soon I went
And therein I looked.
Several dead people all shrouded,
Giving food to those seated,
And they served them very sweetly,
On their knees and devotedly.
And I saw that the Refectorer
Was she who had the neck-piece,
For she visited all the eaters
And filled their needs.
I wished to know what it was;
To this one I went straight away,
The Refectorer I saw,
Whom I had already followed.
'Tell me,' I said, 'what is your name?'"

<summary>The Pilgrim meets Obedience and Discipline, who explain their roles in the spiritual life. He then sees Abstinence in the refectory, where the "dead" (benefactors) serve the living monks.</summary>

<margin>You shall be refreshed before the Lord your God. Deuteronomy 12.</margin>
"And because one takes service from them
Just as if they were present,
In praying for them/one must
Thank and regrate them.
For this they put themselves on their knees
<margin>If you shall immolate a sacrifice for thanksgiving to the Lord, and it shall be pleasing: you shall eat it on that same day <note>original Latin note abbreviated</note>.</margin>
As if to pray for us,
They said/from our goods you live,
You should be grateful to us."

### The Pilgrim
From there soon I returned,
And then I saw a staircase
By which two ladies were climbing
And going up to the dormitory;
And it seemed to me one was naked,
<margin>Seneca: And healthy is the knowledge to pray for the deceased. 2 Maccabees 12.</margin>
<margin>Bear the burden of poverty willingly. Cato says.</margin>
Except only that she was clothed
Only in a <term>gambezon</term> <gloss>a padded defensive tunic</gloss>.
The other carried a large staff,
And so she was armed in the hands,
Gloved in good gauntlets;
And she was neatly clothed
In a very white <term>rochet</term> <gloss>a vestment resembling a surplice</gloss> that she had.
Then I went to look
At what they would do/and to ask
What offices they had,
Also what they served.
And soon enough I saw a part of it,
For she with the staff went
From bed to bed through the dormitory,
<margin>The blessed father [Francis] loved poverty in himself and in his own, so that he always called poverty his lady.</margin>
And did all her turn;
Everywhere she spread white sheets
And made them all clean.
And her companion in the <term>gambezon</term>
Sang such a song:
"I must sing/I must do it,
I carry nothing with me,
I will not be [heavy]/for I am naked."
To this one I spoke first:
"I pray you," I said to her, "and require
That you tell me/what is your name,
And what is your condition."

### <term>Pourete Voluntaire</term> <gloss>Voluntary Poverty</gloss>
<margin>Nature is content with few and minimal things. Boethius, book 2 of Consolation of Philosophy.</margin>
<note>A decorative initial P is printed here.</note>
"I am," she said, "Voluntary
Poverty, who of my own will
Have left all whatever I had
In the world/and that I could have there.
I have stripped myself of everything,
By which I would be entirely naked
If I did not have this <term>gambezon</term>

<note>A woodcut illustration shows two women in a dormitory. One, representing Chastity, is shown in a white robe smoothing the sheets on a bed. The other, Voluntary Poverty, stands nearby holding a staff and wearing a simple tunic.</note>

Called, which has the name Patience;
It is he who makes me sing
And very willingly endure
That I am as you see me, naked;
For by this/I well know that received
In heaven above I shall be the better for it,
And the goods that are there I shall have."

### The Pilgrim
"Why have you," I said, "added
To you, who call yourself Voluntary
Poverty?" Then she said, "Listen:
### Poverty
Whatever one does is worth little or nothing
If it is not done with the will.
And well you shall see Poverty,
The one who is not at all voluntary,
There you will take a good example."

### The Pilgrim
She led me into a corner
Which was not too far from there.
There an old woman was sitting
Who seemed to be out of her mind,
And who had her mouth quite
A bit higher than her nose,
And she grumbled and muttered
And ground her teeth together.

### Voluntary Poverty
"Look here," she said, "at Poverty,
The one who is not so by her choice;
If you wish, you shall ask her."

<margin>Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Matthew 5.</margin>
<margin>Our poverty was sufficient for us. Tobit 5.</margin>
<margin>Keep faith with a friend in his poverty. Ecclesiasticus 22.</margin>
<margin>It is a virtue to have abstained from pleasing goods. Ovid.</margin>
<margin>God has made me grow in the land of my poverty. Genesis 41.</margin>

<summary>The Pilgrim meets Voluntary Poverty, who wears the "gambeson" of Patience and sings of her freedom from worldly goods. She contrasts herself with Involuntary Poverty, an unhappy and bitter figure.</summary>
<keywords>Poverty, Patience, monastic life, dormitory, spiritual discipline, gratitude, Francis of Assisi</keywords>

puis la eglise se voida par la mort de dit Thomas par que il appertient a luy a presenter et Johan
luy disturbe a tort. Johan dit que ne poet de dire la voidance ne le presentement de Thomas mes dit que
devant le presentement de dit Thomas un tiel fuit seisi de la moite de la eglise et de la moite de un
manoir de B. a que l'avoweson est appendant et presenta un son clerc Johan de C. que a son
presentement fuit receu et admis et institut de l'evesque en temps de pees en temps le Roy Edward
besael le Roy que ore est et puis de mesme le manoir et de l'avoweson enfeoffa un tiel de qui la

fuit receu et admis et institut de l'evesque en temps le Roy que ore est et puis Thomas de S.
fuit cree en evesque de Hereford par que la eglise se voida par que le Roy seisi les temporalites de l'evesque

pria aide de luy et de l'evesque de Hereford et le Roy par ses lettres appertient a luy a presenter

Une femme porta breve de dower vers un tiel et demanda la tierce partie de un mies et de
un carue de terre en B. de la dotation un tiel son baron. Le tenant dit que le baron la femme
ne fuit unques seisi de tiel estat que dower la poet aver et de ceo il se mist en pays et la
femme auxi. Et trove fuit par verdit de pays que le baron la femme fuit seisi de dit mies
et de la terre en son demesne comme de fee et de droit et enfeoffa le tenant et reprist estat a luy
et a sa femme et a les heirs de lour deux corps engendres et puis le baron morust sanz issue
entre eux par que la femme tient la moite de dit mies et de la terre par la forme de la taille
et le tenant l'autre moite par le feoffement le baron et issint le baron ne fuit unques seisi
de tiel estat que dower la poet aver.

Thomas de Hathewey, regarding the fact that he does not show the presentation in his own person: he was not on the same day one and the same person, for the presentation was made to one who was parson of the same church of Westcombe, to him and his successors; this John, who is now vicar, cannot be said to be a successor to the parson, by which it seems that this is a thing outside, or that which is outside their point. Wherefore he says that the Bishop of Norwich, neither in the writ of right nor in the [matter] of the parson John de Grendon and him, cannot be [held] by right of his church of Westcombe, for the vicarage is one, and the plaint is in the plaint <term>sicut vobis facit</term> <gloss>as it does to you</gloss> concerning that which you suppose to do; wherefore, concerning that which is a plaint, you ought not to proceed by another. John, although he is vicar, in a plea of trespass, the plaintiff shall not have [damages] by maintaining his plaint, but rather where the defendant pleads in the right of his vicarage, as the defendant does here, in such a case the plaintiff shall have aid of his parson. The plaintiff must, at the present time, [state] his plea in his plaint to the court that he had to do; the same proof is the cause of that, for he wishes to have the writings to him, by which the writings must be put to the court. [He] pleads in the writ of trespass to an issue of plea, for [himself] of right of the parson; for because the plaintiff is vicar, this is an issue to which he cannot be a party.
