<header>Topic M</header>
<margin>The Easy-going</margin>
<margin>The ranks of perfection in prophecy consist of revealing Truths. Sainthood is dominant in the emergence of [the Prophet].</margin>
The spirits of the <term>Paraclete</term> <gloss>Faraqlit</gloss>. It is attributed to the <term>Paraclete</term>, spelled with a 'f', then an 'a', then a 'r' with a <term>kasra</term>, then a silent 'q', then a 'l' with a <term>kasra</term>, then a 'y', then a 't', and an 'a'. It is a Hebrew word <note>likely Syriac/Greek in origin</note> meaning "the Divider between Truth and Falsehood." 
It refers to the manifestation of Sainthood <note>original: "wilaya"</note>, which is the inner aspect of Prophecy. As the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, foretold — and the explanation of the name's meaning will follow — when he said: "I am going to my Father and your Father," meaning "my Lord and your Lord." We previously mentioned that the ancients used to call the Principles "Fathers," but not in the sense understood by the Christians. This is indicated by his saying "and your Father." 
"He will send you the <term>Paraclete</term> who will distinguish between you by the Truth." It is said that his intention was our Master, the Seal of Prophets, peace and blessings be upon him. His emergence was upon Prophecy. Therefore, you see the forms of his legal symbols are extremely delicate. The signs of his comprehensive speech and superior symbols of Truth are extremely clear. This is as he indicated by his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "I have come to you with the easy-going, tolerant, white way." 
"Ease" and "tolerance" refer to the delicacy and subtlety. "White" refers to the appearance of Truths from beneath the fine veils. Since his emergence was the most intimate of the ranks of Prophecy in terms of delicacy, subtlety, and the dominance of Sainthood, Prophecy was sealed with his holy emergence. Nothing remained after him except pure Sainthood. 
My father, the Messiah, said: "The <term>Paraclete</term> whom my Father sends in my name will teach you all things." This means the interpretation of every form of the symbols I have brought to you in word and deed. His saying "in my name" means he is called "the Messiah" <note>The Anointed</note> because he anoints with light. 
"He shall judge" — meaning he shall overflow with the shining Light, which is the elixir of knowledge and power, as previously mentioned. This was indicated in the Quran where it is said: "Then surely upon Us is its explanation." The word "then" implies a delay. He means it is known from the saying "Then surely upon Us is its explanation" that the complete revealing of the truths of what was foretold by the symbols of the revealed laws
auditTranslation:
unto the Seal <note>of Prophets</note>, and stripping them entirely of the clothing of forms, is delayed from his time. For it only appears in the emergence of the one who is the <term>Paraclete</term> and the manifestation of his specific Sainthood. 
Even if he revealed it, it is because the Seal's Prophecy is its very essence in the most perfect way possible for the emergence of Prophecy. It was folded <margin>concluded</margin> and revealed <margin>exalted is its name</margin> in its naming. No forms remained upon it. The Truth has subtle, delicate rays that manifest in the permanence of the beauty of those Truths. 
Therefore, the <term>Paraclete</term> said: "All the prophets and the revealers of the truths of their prophets [remain]." However, some of those manifestations of Prophecy remained suspended and entrusted to his revelation <insert>unto there</insert> in the manifestations of his specific Sainthood, in consideration of what is appropriate for the preparation of the time. 
There is no doubt that the lights of the <term>Malakut</term> <gloss>the celestial realm</gloss> descend without end to those who perceive them. There is no prevention in them. The ray of Holiness spreads over prepared, detached souls. The path of Truth opens for whoever knocks on its door. This means the door of God is open. The Giver of Knowledge, who is "on the clear, highest horizon," is "not stingy with the Unseen." 
In this, meanings appear at a rank that is most hidden to one of intelligence. As the "Preserved Luminous Ones" <note>original: "al-hafaza dhat al-bariq"</note> reported. "Preserved" <note>original: "mahfuz"</note> in language comes from a root meaning "to snatch away." What is meant here is a subtle Unseen hidden from the world of the senses. 
"Extinguished lights" <note>original: "makhamid al-anwar"</note> are not fixed. They are followed by a flashing light upon the soul during the "Night of the <term>Nu'uja</term>." In language, this is the violent wind that uproots houses. What is meant here is the struggle that leads to the rejection of bodily faculties. 
This is not completed except by the blowing of the winds of "Divine Attractions" <note>original: "jadhabat"</note> from the High Source. As it was said: "Blessed is he who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy." The "easy" approaches in an hour from its possessor — meaning the possessor of the "Preservation" — descending and approaching the light within it, while the form of that witnessing ascends from it.

And if it is large, its edges do not meet because it is circular, spaced apart, and of varying shape, and a lot of meat has been lost from it, so its treatment is suturing and preventing the accumulation of moisture in it by using astringent diluents, and using the plasters that we will mention. If it is deep, then scarring may also stick it together [through] frequent pulling toward the covering. Sometimes the covering gathers... that is where pulling it with a bandage to secure it does not help, as we will show, especially where the firm pulling does not fall on the base of the depth, so materials flow into it because of its weakness. The placement is necessary, and its circumstances are mentioned in the chapter on ulcers. If pulling is needed from its place, place cotton or what serves its function on its face to dry it, especially where the pulling does not fall on the base, [as this is] sufficient for it. And its pouring... its pouring, it is not possible for the bad material to pour off it, or it contains bone or a fracture... and a very bad moisture has arisen from it, and it is then in the category of ulcers rather than abscesses. The scholar said: When the wound needs a bandage that brings the lips together if adhesion and healing are desired. But if it needs meat to grow in it, it does not need that, but it needs, at one time, a bandage that strikes the place, and at another time, a bandage for [the area] behind it, so it does not hold the medicine on it. He said: It is necessary that the position of the wound be a place from which the [superfluity] pours out always by its nature, either by placing the abdomen there, or by shaping it in that shape. For I have seen a large wound, its depth was where I write it, and placing it in the thigh, there it was [the] <term>‘afw</term> <gloss>the healing process</gloss>
and the <term>‘afwah</term> <gloss>the healing process</gloss>
auditTranslation: and the <term>‘awḍah</term> <gloss>the remedy</gloss> [is] below it, or it is not [positioned] at the bottom. Likewise, the hand, the palm, and others are hung; the <term>‘awḍah</term> always hangs downward. This is his statement, and he says: The wound sometimes occurs where it forces you to complete amputation. As for the organ, if the wound in it is a cutting [that results in loss], it needs things that grow meat. It is not enough to only dry and prevent [swelling], but rather the drying and preventing [agent] may, from one perspective, irritate the material from which it grows. The depth and the loss in the bone may be such that it is not possible to grow completely, so a depth remains, as is the case that may happen where it grows more than is necessary, so it becomes excessive flesh. The patient who is intended to grow flesh in a wound must be moderate. Without this, the good [can turn into] excess. The growth [agent] may be such that it is possible for the meat to grow. As for the skin, it is because if it has been cut off entirely, rather, solid flesh grows in its place; hair and veins do not grow upon it. It only produces branches and grows like the meat. Among the wounds are wounds of danger: wounds that occur in the nerves and the arm, and we will mention it in the chapter on nerves. Often, hateful, bad symptoms follow it; the worst that follows a wound of the arm's extremity is discoloration, the cessation of the pulse afterward, [the arm] becoming thin, and a tendency toward fading, and the loss of strength. Spasm may follow it. Likewise, that which occurs in front of the knee at the kneecap, for bad symptoms follow it, and it is a leader [that is] rarely parted from. If a spasm occurs from such arm wounds and the treatment does not heal [it], then the treatment is the amputation of the arm.

**الصغد**

ومن بخارا الى بلد الصغد لمن اخذ نحو القبلة سبع مراحل وبلد الصغد واسع وله مدن جليلة منيعة حصينة منها تبوسية وكشانية وكش ونسف * وهي ذخشبة افتتح هذه الكور اعنى كور الصغد قتيبة بن مسلم الباهلي ايام الوليد بن عبد الملك 

**سمرقند**

ومن كش الى مدينة الصغد العظمى اربع مراحل سمرقند من اجل البلدان واعظمها قدرا واشدها امتنعا واكثرها رجالا واشدها بطلا واصبرها محاربا وهي في تخوم الترك انغلقت سمرقند بعد ان افتتحت عدة مرار لمنعتها وشجاعة رجالها وشدة ابطالها افتتحها قتيبة بن مسلم الباهلي في ايام الوليد بن عبد الملك وصالح دهاقينها وملوكها وكان عليها سور عظيم فتهدم فبناه الرشيد امير المؤمنين ولها نهر عظيم يأتي من بلاد الترك كالفرات يقال له باسف ويجرى في ارض سمرقند ثم الى بلاد الصغد ثم الى اسروشنة ويعم بلاد سمرقند واشتاخنج واسروشنة وشاش، ومن سمرقند الى اسروشنة مملكة افشين خمس مراحل مشرقا ومملكة اسروشنة واسعة

<term>Khorasan</term> and reformed it until it was stable. <term>Raja' ibn Abi al-Dahhak</term>, who was the husband of <term>al-Fadl ibn Sahl</term>'s sister, governed all of <term>Khorasan</term>. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> arrived in <term>Baghdad</term> in the middle of <term>Safar</term> in the year two hundred and four. <term>Khorasan</term> had completely deteriorated under <term>Raja' ibn Abi al-Dahhak</term>, so <term>al-Ma'mun</term> appointed <term>Ghassan ibn Abbad</term> over <term>Khorasan</term>. He reformed it and it became stable under his hand. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> supported him, and he stayed for the remainder of the year two hundred and four and several months of the year two hundred and five. Then <term>Tahir ibn al-Husayn ibn Mus'ab al-Bushanji</term> maneuvered until <term>al-Ma'mun</term> appointed him over <term>Khorasan</term> and granted him a covenant for it. He set out for it in the year two hundred and five. He received news of <term>al-Ma'mun</term>'s ill-will toward him, so he showed signs of rebellion without openly declaring it. When <term>al-Ma'mun</term> heard of this, it is said that he was dealt with through a poisoned drink. <term>Tahir</term> died in the year two hundred and seven. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> appointed in his place his son, <term>Talhah ibn Tahir ibn al-Husayn</term>, who remained the emir of <term>Khorasan</term> for seven years with stable authority. Then <term>Talhah ibn Tahir</term> died in the year two hundred and fifteen. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> had previously appointed <term>Abd Allah ibn Tahir</term> over the provinces of <term>al-Jabal</term> and <term>Azerbaijan</term>. He set out but remained ill in <term>Dinavar</term>. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> then appointed him over <term>Khorasan</term> in place of his brother <term>Talhah ibn Tahir</term>, sending him his covenant and commission with <term>Ishaq ibn Ibrahim</term> and <term>Yahya ibn Aktham</term>, the Chief Judge. <term>Abd Allah ibn Tahir</term> departed for <term>Khorasan</term> and settled in <term>Nishapur</term>. No governor of <term>Khorasan</term> before him had settled there; he made it his home. <term>Abd Allah ibn Tahir</term> remained over <term>Khorasan</term> and its dependencies with stable authority and strong power, and all the lands were stable for fourteen years. He died in <term>Nishapur</term> in the year two hundred and thirty at the age of forty-eight. <term>al-Wathiq</term> then appointed his son <term>Tahir ibn Abd Allah ibn Tahir</term> over <term>Khorasan</term>. He remained in <term>Khorasan</term> throughout the caliphates of <term>al-Wathiq</term>, <term>al-Mutawakkil</term>, <term>al-Muntasir</term>, and part of the caliphate of <term>al-Musta'in</term>. He ruled for eighteen years with stable affairs. He died in <term>Nishapur</term> in <term>Rajab</term> of the year two hundred and forty-eight at the age of forty-four. <term>al-Musta'in</term> then appointed his son <term>Muhammad ibn Tahir ibn Tahir</term> over <term>Khorasan</term>.

<summary>This page details the succession of Tahirid governors in Khorasan under various Abbasid caliphs, highlighting their role in stabilizing the region and the shift of the capital to Nishapur.</summary>

...wronged <term>Isma</term> at <term>al-Raqqa</term> and then consolidated his power. He dispatched <term>Ali ibn Isa ibn Mahan</term>, whom he had released, to <term>Khorasan</term>. When <term>al-Ma'mun</term> learned of this, he dispatched <term>Tahir ibn al-Husayn ibn Mus'ab al-Bushanji</term> from <term>Merv</term> with four thousand troops. He met <term>Ali ibn Isa</term> at <term>al-Raqqa</term> and killed him. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> then also dispatched <term>Harthama ibn A'yan</term> to <term>Iraq</term>. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> remained residing in <term>Merv</term> until <term>Muhammad</term> <note>the Caliph al-Amin</note> was killed at the end of <term>Muharram</term> in the year one hundred ninety-eight, and the oath of allegiance for the Caliphate was given to him. Then <term>al-Ma'mun</term> stayed in <term>Khorasan</term> during the years one hundred ninety-nine and two hundred, while he was sending men to <term>Iraq</term>. He sent <term>Humayd ibn Abd al-Hamid ibn Rub'i al-Ta'i al-Tusi</term>, then <term>Ali ibn Hisham ibn Khusraw al-Marwazi</term>. Then he sent <term>Dhu al-Alameyn</term> <gloss>Possessor of the Two Banners</gloss> <term>Ali ibn Abi Sa'id ibn Khallad al-Fadl ibn Sahl</term> over the land tax of <term>Iraq</term>, and then sent <term>al-Hasan ibn Sahl</term> over all affairs. <term>Harthama</term> returned from <term>Iraq</term> in anger and went to <term>al-Ma'mun</term>, who imprisoned him; he died in prison in <term>Merv</term> three days later in the year two hundred. Then <term>al-Ma'mun</term> gave the oath of allegiance to <term>al-Rida Ali ibn Musa ibn Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib</term> (peace be upon them) in <term>Merv</term> as the heir apparent in the year two hundred and two. He departed from <term>Merv</term> in that year, traveling at a leisurely pace, and arrived at <term>Sarakhs</term>, where he stayed. His vizier <term>al-Fadl ibn Sahl</term> was killed in the bathhouse at <term>Sarakhs</term>, and <term>al-Ma'mun</term> executed a group because of it. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> then traveled to <term>Tus</term>, and when he arrived there, he stayed during the year two hundred and three. <term>al-Rida</term> (peace be upon him) died in <term>Tus</term>. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> had written to all the kings of

<vocab>བདེ་གཤེགས་ (Sugata), བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ (Bodhisattva), སངས་རྒྱས་ (Buddha), དགེ་བའི་དགེ་བ་ (Virtuous merit)</vocab>

The meaning of the great cloud of glorious excellence. For the sake of the two accumulations <note>merit and wisdom</note>, I bow to the supreme three jewels <note>Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha</note>. 

The state of becoming the <term>mandala</term> <gloss>sacred circle</gloss> that appears in the sky of wisdom. The meaning of the great sun of glorious excellence. Of the excellent history that has no equal, the flower of great bliss blossoms. One should enter the path adorned with the speech that constantly thinks, "This is excellent." Furthermore, because of this harmony, it is made into a support. Likewise, I bow. The virtue is made the lord of the tree that possesses the crown ornament of the great bliss of the <term>dakinis</term> <gloss>sky-goers</gloss>. One has power over that light of wisdom. It is desired. One should make it the subject of the crown ornament of incomparable great bliss. Likewise, in the <term>tantras</term>, it is the mind. It has arisen as the thought of that light of wisdom. One should know that one should contemplate the root of virtue that is not conceptually elaborated by other thoughts. In that way, the power of great bliss. One should enter it.

<summary>This page serves as an invocation and concludes with a guide to entering the path of great bliss, emphasizing the accumulation of merit and wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Lama, Wisdom, Merit, Great Bliss, Mandala, Dakini, Path</keywords>
auditTranslation:
<margin>May the teachings be illuminated.</margin>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta> Through this virtue that I have cultivated in this way, may I attain the state of all-knowing <note>omniscient Buddhahood</note> through this engagement with the wisdom of the Victorious One. Furthermore, the eleven and seventeen <term>sutras</term> <gloss>discourses of the Buddha</gloss> of the Great Vehicle are to be grasped by the method of the wisdom of the teachings established by the Thus-Gone One <note>a title for the Buddha</note> in order to purify the obscurations of all beings. 

As for the overcoming power of how one knows, it is considered that there is no contradiction with others who are obscured by conceptual elaboration and the like. It is the Thus-Gone One's wisdom of victory, the emptiness that obscures the faults of sentient beings' defilements, just as gold is covered by impurities. Just as the power of my own authority, the authority of the authority of the authority does not clarify others who are gathered for the sake of amending garments, so too is the wisdom of liberation from the teachings of the Thus-Gone One, which is the wisdom of conceptual elaboration and correction, the same as the clarity of that wisdom which belongs to the minds of my own <term>sutras</term> <gloss>discourses</gloss> and <term>tantras</term> <gloss>esoteric scriptures</gloss>.

<summary>This page concludes an invocation focused on the attainment of omniscient wisdom through the purification of defilements, likening the process to refining gold and aligning the practitioner with the wisdom of the Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>Omniscience, Sutras, Tantras, Emptiness, Purification, Wisdom of the Thus-Gone One</keywords>

...during the time of the eight secret [teachings]. During the time of the great joys, such as the implicit meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom and other [ten Dharma teachings], and the time of the goddess of the <term>Gandharvas</term> <gloss>celestial musicians</gloss> who are singers of patience. From the city of the golden glory, returning to meet, there was the occasion of the offering and the fruit of the deities. According to the accumulation of the fortress, the two great Gandharva spirits who dwell in the teachings [provided] the basis. 

[He] manifested in the sky, looking out, which showed the joy of the sangha at the victory celebration. He wished to show the omniscient mind of the teacher. Having obtained the thousand wisdoms and the methods of the emanation of the Dharma assembly, the speech was clearly shown, followed by the auspiciousness of the clearing of the wheel of Dharma. He wished to show the omniscient mind of the teacher. Through the love of the six glorious goddesses, etc., he made offerings to the Guide, the one who holds the thought. When departing, he held the glory of the body. He quickly cultivated the six signs of the teachings. At the end of the emptiness of the assembly of the holders of the teachings, he [attained] the glory of the body that makes the connection for the offering and accomplishment. That very thing, at that time, during the time of thought of the clear truth, he enjoyed the feast of the Dharma of the face.

...and so on, he gave permission and remained. Then, he explained the prayer made by the gatekeeper of the emptiness towards the upper direction. The teachings that remained between the abandonment and the keeping of the remnants were made clear. The emptiness that is clear and fills the entirety of the upper direction manifested as an emanation. He entered into the power of the destruction of the three gatherings and remained, having performed the great emptiness. 

Then, on the twelfth day, a good day of the Fire-Horse year, he relied on the armor of constructing the auspicious reliquary stupa. Having completed the work according to the beautiful writing, he met with the elder scholar to establish the seat and remained. Regarding the Lord himself, the clarity of the visualization was the white <term>Tara</term> <gloss>deity of compassion and longevity</gloss>. Because of the purpose of granting the empowerment of the Thus-Gone Ones, the work was not left incomplete. At the very summit of the victory of the upper government of the royal state, he held the mind of the Dharma King of Compassion, having attained the power of speech. He remained for a long time, turning the wheel of Dharma without interruption. The state equivalent to the <term>Tushita</term> <gloss>Heaven of Joy</gloss> Dharma gate, where the supreme teacher Maitreya resides, was shown clearly as the place to which he went and resided. Then, the place of the assembly of the golden-colored deities of the Lama of this place, the Lord of Dharma, was [established].

The red pavilion enters the forest as the white rain rises. The wind comes to the rush pond before the auspicious autumn. When the frost arrives, the tiny evening does not open.

### Waking Early at Cheongho

The water is bright, and I know the energy of the Way is before the mountain. I see the spirit clearly and could paint the new clearing. The color is deep blue as the sun rises in the east.

### Evening View at Cheongho

A new coolness is born after the rain. I wake from sleep and go up before the tower. The fields are moist, and the cicadas sing in the trees. The river is flat, and seagulls pass through the sky.

### Blocked by Rain at the Small Leisure House

The dark forest mist is like water. In the house by the stream, the wine is like spring. This was formerly a place for seeking flowers. Now I am a person blocked by the rain.

<summary>Observations of the landscape at Cheongho through various times of day and weather, emphasizing the peacefulness after rain.</summary>

The teaching of poetry in the Eastern Country <note>original: "Dongguk," referring to Korea</note> is different from the Middle Province <note>original: "Jungju," referring to China</note>. In the Middle Province, current trends are followed, and the style flows daily toward detailed craftsmanship and delicate ornamentation. In the Eastern Country, we still value the ancient methods. Although there may be times when the tones do not harmonize perfectly or the choice of words feels forced, the natural spirit is so overflowing that it does not harm its excellence. 

In the Gyeongja year <note>likely 1840</note>, I met with the brothers Li Chunkye and Nianzhai to discuss this and composed a book. Now, Buyuan <note>the author's nickname, Ch'oe Hyang-wŏn</note> has brought and shown me this collection. Its sentiment is transcendent and vast. It is what one might call a spirit that emerges with ancient singularity and extraordinary charm. From time to time, it reveals a crisp and refreshing posture that is enough to startle one's eyes. Knowing what he possesses in his heart, one cannot help but feel there is no one else like him in this generation. Is Buyuan's rise not different from ordinary men? If the state of Lu had no gentlemen, where could he have acquired such qualities? Truly, the Eastern Country has many worthies! 

Holding this volume and adjusting it, I cannot bear to let it go. It is truly as the saying goes: by the time one finishes reading new poems, the blue mountains have already turned to dusk. Yet, like the colors of floating clouds and trees, or the sound of the setting sun on the Jialing River, his charm is boundless. The old masters like Master Yu in the past wrote of "the frost of the fifth watch entering one's clothes" or "autumn rising in the Yu garden." Lines such as "few guests arrive at the high tower" or "many butterflies speak" are so fine they would make even Du Fu <note>original: "Du Lan"</note> or the poets of the High Tang feel humble.

auditTranslation:
The mountain of the cape is a wild cherry tree. Why?
The mountain of the cape is a wild cherry tree. Why?
The person who hears it calls it mountain climbing. Ah, a man.
Towards the direction that is good, they say.
The memories that arise, how they move the heart.
Ah, climbing the mountain, the cherry blossoms fall.

<column-break/>

The mountain of the cape is marked by ritual.
Attached without pause, the request is made.
The noise of the world is scattered.
It is as if I could run.
The mountain journey of today is narrow.
In the manner of the layering of plum blossoms.
What is called the exterior encounter is an encounter with a stranger.

consecrato a Baccho per le scientie inferiori che sono tutte l'altre parti di philosophia excepto la prima philosophia & metaphysica: & theologia: perche alle cose mondane quelle sono a bastantia per tutte quelle: & helicone ponga per la theologia: laquale ha sola cognitione delle cose celesti. **ARINGO** rimaso: Aringo in toscano fignifica pulpito & luogo elevato. Onde noi diciamo ringhiera: Adunque per similitudine chiama el gioco ho aringho. Me uopo e uopo .i. bisogno ame chome in latino diciamo. Mihiest opus. **ENTRA** nel pectonella mente & spira in me tal canto quale usasti quando uince sti Marsia: E scripto nelle favole che Minerva sonando latibia che e o zufolo: o piffero sopra l'acqua della pallude trito ne si uide gonfiare le gote. ilche gli parue cosa si brutta che gitto latibia: ne piu uolle sonarla: Marsia fatyro latrouo: & perseverando nel sonarla diuerto docto musico: ma tato insolente & temerario che si preponeua ad appolline dio dellar te musica & prouocollo a cantare. Sedeuono iudici Minerua & Mida re dilidia: Vinxe Appolline secõdo el uero iudicio di Minerua. Ma mida chome indocto fauori a marsia. Ilperche appolline fece amida orecchi da sino: & marsia scortico. **DEL LA** uagina: della pelle laquale equasi guaina del corpo. **O DIVINA** uirtu. o diuino furore dappolline: & per trasito dimo stra che benche dica apolline intenda ladiuina gratia illuminante cooperante & consumante & finalmẽte epso spirito san cto. **LOMBRA** fegnata nel mio capo: la imagine impressa nella mia memoria: laquale e nell'ultimo detre uentricoli del capo: & dixe ombra adimostrare che non hauea expressa la propria imagine del cielo nella memoria: ma era adombrata. **VEDRAMI** apie: non fara indarno collocata in me latua gratia Imperoche lusero in modo che io meritero dessere corona/ to dilauro chome optimo poeta: & accioche non paia arrogante in attribuirsi tante laude dice che non lui o suo ingegno si fara degno dital corona: maladiuina gratia & lamateria della quale tracta **SIRA** de uolte padre sene coglie: Quasi dica e tanta la pigritia & lanegligentia degli huomini che radi si danno o alla poetica o alla disciplina militare: i forma che di/ uenghino degni di coronarsi di lauro: & quanto piu rari sono tanto piu debbi fauorire chi cerca coronarsi: & posse es/ fare per ogni huomo triumphante. **COLPA** & uergogna dellhumane uogle e colpa dellhumane uogle: perche leuogle & gliappetiti nostri facti ribelli alla ragione seguitano la sensualita: & sono infinite in cercare cose corporee: & per lacura di quelle niente che excellente fa appetiscono: e adũque colpa & uergogna perche arrecha grande ignomina alla uita humana. **CHE** partori letitia ela fententia che la fronde pennea. i. ellauro elquale e nato di daphne figliola dipenneo do uerebbe partorire letitia alla deita delphica. i. ad apolline el quale e decto delphico: perche rende gli oracoli ne' tẽpio suoi el quale e in delphi cipta: o di phocide non lontana da parnaso ogni uolta che alcuno fene coronassi. **POCA** fauilla grã fuoco feconda. Dimostra che modestamente parlando dise che merita che appollo lo fauorisca. Imperoche benche lui non facci cose excellenti: nientedimeno quegli che uerranno dietro a lui mossi dall'uso di tempo in tempo acresce ranno la poetica faculta: chome ueggiamo che duna piccola fauilla spesso facciende gran fiamma. **CON** miglior uoci cõ piu elegante stilo: cõ piu arte poetica: perche cyrrha rispõda. i. perche sia exaudito da Appollie al quale e dedicata cyrrha. Onde iouenale dixe: Cyrrhe i picula uatis. Cyrrha e citta i phocide uicina a crissa: & non lontana da parnaso.

**D**opo lainuocatione comincia la fua narratione & descriue la fua afcéfione al prio cielo che e della luna. Preterea descriue che comicio afalire da matina quãdo il fole furgeua aq̃llo hemifperio doue lui era & facea matina. Et era el fole nel principio del lariete nel qual fegno questo pianeto ha la fua exaltatione Ilpche produce piu degni effecti. Et era nel circulo equinoctiale de ue chome appare nella fpera materiale fi cõgiungono q̃tro circoli. q̃llo dellorizzonte: quello dal zodiaco. Item el coluro & lo equinoctiale. Et in questa coniunctione fi fanno tre croci cioe tre intersectioni. Finge adunque che el fole fuffe in ariete chome habbiamo decto: pche chome el fole mondano in quello opera piu eccellentemente nelle cofe inferiori: cofi el fole celefte che e epfo iddio excellentiffima gratia infonde allanima humana quãdo la tira a cõtemplare fua diuinita. Sono molti che equatro circoli allegoricamẽte pongono perle quattro uirtu morali: & letre croci perle tre theologice Et ordina el texto. La lucerna del mondo .i. el fole el q̃le illumina el mondo furge & nafce ai mortali da diuerfe foci. Imperoche quando furge col lariete apparifce nel uero oriete. Surge adunque da diuerfi parti delloriente: Ma conmiglor corfo .i. conpiu felice influentia furge dal legno & dio uernale oue fono e circuli & lecroci giadecte: Et cõ migliore stella: & chiama el fegno dariete stella ponẽdo una stel la per tutte laltre che fanno quel fegno & dice migliore perche chome habbiamo decto lariete e laexaltatiõe delfole: oue/ ro intefe uenere laquale nel principio della feconda cantica pofe nepefci uicina al fole. Et lamondana cera: dice adũque che elfole quando furge collariete: & ha uenere congiunta feco: puo meglio con la fua influentia difporre la terra & glãi/ mali a produr fructo: Adunquetempera .i. dispone & fugella. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Dante's Paradiso, Canto I. The commentator is explaining the classical and theological references in Dante’s invocation to Apollo, specifically focusing on the myth of Marsyas and the geographical/astrological setting of the poem’s opening.</meta>

<header>CANTO ONE</header>

...consecrated to Bacchus for the lower sciences, which are all the other parts of philosophy except for "First Philosophy" <note>Aristotle's term for Metaphysics</note> and Metaphysics, and Theology. For worldly things, those sciences are sufficient; and let him set Helicon for Theology, which alone has knowledge of celestial things. **ROSTRUM** <note>original: *aringo*</note> remaining: *Aringo* in Tuscan signifies a pulpit or an elevated place. From this we get the word *ringhiera* <note>a balcony or railing for public speaking</note>. Therefore, by likeness, he calls the game a "rostrum." **I NEED** <note>original: *me uopo*</note>: that is, a need for me, just as in Latin we say *Mihi est opus* <note>"It is a need for me"</note>. **ENTER** into the breast, into the mind, and breathe into me such a song as you used when you defeated Marsyas. It is written in the fables that Minerva, playing the *tibia*—which is a flute or pipe—over the water of the Triton marsh, saw her cheeks swell. This seemed such an ugly thing to her that she threw the flute away and would play it no more. Marsyas the satyr found it, and by persevering in playing it, he became a learned musician. But he was so insolent and reckless that he set himself above Apollo, the god of the musical art, and challenged him to sing. Minerva and Midas, King of Lydia, sat as judges. Apollo won according to the true judgment of Minerva. But Midas, being unlearned, favored Marsyas. Because of this, Apollo gave Midas the ears of an ass and flayed Marsyas. **FROM THE** sheath: from the skin, which is like the scabbard of the body. **O DIVINE** virtue: O divine fury of Apollo. By transition, he shows that although he says "Apollo," he means the divine grace—illuminating, cooperating, and consuming—and finally the Holy Spirit itself. **THE SHADOW** marked in my head: the image impressed upon my memory, which is in the last of the three ventricles of the head. He said "shadow" to show that he did not have the exact image of heaven expressed in his memory, but it was overshadowed. **YOU SHALL SEE ME** at the foot: your grace will not be placed in me in vain. For I shall use it in a way that I will deserve to be crowned with laurel as an excellent poet. And so that he does not seem arrogant in attributing such praise to himself, he says that neither he nor his talent will make him worthy of such a crown, but divine grace and the subject matter of which he treats. **RARELY** O Father, are they gathered: as if to say, the laziness and negligence of men is such that they rarely give themselves to poetry or to military discipline in a way that makes them worthy of being crowned with laurel. And the rarer they are, the more you ought to favor one who seeks to be crowned; and it can be done for every triumphant man. **FAULT** and shame of human wills: it is the fault of human wills because our wills and appetites, having rebelled against reason, follow sensuality. They are infinite in seeking bodily things, and because of their care for those, they desire nothing excellent. It is therefore a fault and a shame because it brings great ignominy to human life. **WHICH** brought forth joy: this is the sentence that the Penean leaf—that is, the laurel, which was born from Daphne, daughter of Peneus—ought to bring forth joy to the Delphic deity—that is, to Apollo, who is called "Delphic" because he gives oracles in his temple in the city of Delphi in Phocis, not far from Parnassus—every time anyone is crowned with it. **A SMALL** spark breeds a great fire. He demonstrates by speaking modestly of himself that he deserves Apollo’s favor. For although he himself might not do excellent things, nonetheless those who come after him, moved by the practice from time to time, will increase the poetic faculty; just as we see that from a small spark a great flame often arises. **WITH BETTER** voices, with more elegant style, with more poetic art: so that Cyrrha may respond—that is, so that he might be heard by Apollo, to whom Cyrrha is dedicated. Thus Juvenal said: *Cyrrhe i picula uatis* <note>original Latin: *Cyrrhaei spicula vatis*—"the darts of the Cyrrhean prophet"</note>. Cyrrha is a city in Phocis near Crissa and not far from Parnassus.

<columns>2</columns>
> The lamp of the world rises for mortals
> from various outlets; but from that one
> which joins four circles with three crosses,
> with a better course and with a better star
> it comes forth joined, and the worldly wax
> it tempers and seals more in its own way.
> It had made morning there and evening here,
> almost such an outlet; and all was white
> that hemisphere, and the other part black,
> when Beatrice toward the left side
> I saw turned, and gazing into the sun:
> an eagle never so fixed himself upon it.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'D' containing a landscape scene with a building on a hill and mountains in the background.</image-desc>
**A**fter the invocation, he begins his narration and describes his ascent to the first heaven, which is that of the Moon. Furthermore, he describes that he began to ascend in the morning, when the sun was rising in that hemisphere where he was, making it morning. And the sun was at the beginning of Aries, in which sign this planet has its exaltation; therefore it produces more worthy effects. And it was at the equinoctial circle where, as appears in the material sphere, four circles join: that of the horizon, that of the zodiac, also the colure and the equinoctial. And in this conjunction, three crosses are made—that is, three intersections. He feigns, then, that the sun was in Aries, as we have said, because just as the worldly sun works most excellently in lower things there, so the celestial sun, which is God himself, infuses the most excellent grace into the human soul when He draws it to contemplate His divinity. There are many who allegorically set the four circles for the four moral virtues, and the three crosses for the three theological virtues. And the text proceeds: "The lamp of the world"—that is, the sun which illuminates the world—"rises and is born for mortals from various outlets." For when it rises with Aries, it appears in the true East. But then from day to day it rises toward the North until Cancer. And from there, likewise descending degree by degree into Libra,

<column-break/>
<margin>245</margin>
it is in the same place as it was in Aries. And then, departing from there, it goes descending through the southern signs until Capricorn; and from that, through Aquarius and Pisces, it rises again to the equator. Thus, although the sun always rises from the East, nonetheless it is not always from the same part of the East. Because of this, astrologers divide the East into three parts: the equinoctial, the northern, and the southern. It rises, therefore, from various parts of the East. "But with a better course"—that is, with a more happy influence—it rises from the vernal sign where the circles and the crosses already mentioned are. "And with a better star": and he calls the sign of Aries a "star," using one star for all the others that make up that sign; and he says "better" because, as we have said, Aries is the exaltation of the sun. Or, he meant Venus, which at the beginning of the second *cantica* <note>Purgatorio</note> he placed in Pisces, near the sun. "And the worldly wax": he says, then, that the sun, when it rises with Aries and has Venus joined with it, can better with its influence dispose the earth and the animals to produce fruit. Therefore it "tempers"—that is, disposes—and "seals." The "worldly wax"—that is, it disposes and impresses its virtue just as wax becomes apt to receive a figure impressed by a seal when it is well-disposed. And it is true, because in that season, heat and moisture rise in a tempered way, from which tempering the best generation is born. **HAD MADE**: "there," in that hemisphere where I was then, it was "morning." And "here," in our hemisphere, it was "evening." And allegorically, "evening" means death, because there are vices and ignorance; and "there" is "morning" because there are those who are purged of vices and illuminated by divine grace. **TOWARD THE LEFT SIDE**: from which, in that hemisphere, the sun casts its rays for one who is turned toward the East. That Beatrice could look at the sun signifies that only Theology can look upon the Divinity, which is the true sun. **AN EAGLE** never so fixed himself: for the eagle is said to have such eyes that, beyond the faculty of any animal, he fixes his eyes upon the sun and is not dazzled. Because of this, Beatrice is similar to it, because alone of all doctrines, Christian Theology can endure the rays of the divine sun; and look.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of Canto I of the Paradiso. The previous page discussed the invocation to Apollo and the myth of Marsyas, establishing the transition from earthly knowledge to the divine heights Dante is about to explore.</meta>

# PARADISE

...rejoice in the Lord <note>original: "re in dño [Domino]"</note> with the first light and to know Him without being dazzled: [he is like] the figure of the eagle because he discerns the divinity above all others.

And just as a second ray
is wont to issue from the first and mount upward again,
like a pilgrim who wishes to return,
So from her action, infused through the eyes
into my imagination, my own was made;
and I fixed my eyes on the sun beyond our wont.
Much is permitted there which here is not
to our powers, thanks to the place
made as the proper home for the human race.
I did not endure it long, yet not so little
that I did not see it sparkling round about,
like molten iron coming out of the fire.
And suddenly it seemed to me that day to day
had been added, as if He who has the power
had adorned the heaven with another sun.

...suspended wonder: And to look into the sun: this is nothing else than that, illuminated by divine grace, one can look into the sun, that is, into the speculation of the divinity. Nevertheless, he did not endure it long: because if the eyes, that is, the sharpness of the intellect, had endured the light for a longer time, he would have been able to discern the entire solar body, that is, he would have had true knowledge of the divine essence. But he did not have so powerful an eye. Nevertheless, for the little that he endured, he saw the sparks and flashes that were born from the solar body, in the same way that they are born from a glowing iron. The allegorical sense is that the purified soul can contemplate God: but not in a way that it knows His essence: but it has knowledge of the sparks that come from the sun, that is, of the effects that proceed from God; seeing that we know the cause through the effects, and not the effects through the cause. And that the sun had so much greater light that it seemed doubled signifies that theological contemplation illuminates the intellect much more than philosophy does, because it is not without the infusion of the Spirit, as you will see a little further down.

Beatrice was standing with her eyes fixed
entirely upon the eternal wheels, and I on her
fixed my eyes, removed from those above.
In her aspect I became such within
as Glaucus became upon tasting the herb
that made him a peer in the sea among the other gods.
To <term>transhumanize</term> <note>original: "trashumanar" - to pass beyond the limits of human nature</note> could not be signified
by words; therefore let the example suffice
for him to whom grace reserves the experience.

Whether I was only that part of me which You created
last, O Love who governs the heavens,
You know, who with Your light raised me up.
When the wheel that You make eternal
by being desired, made me intent upon You
with the harmony that You attune and distinguish,
So much of the heaven then seemed to me kindled
by the sun's flame, that no rain or river
ever made a lake so widespread.
The novelty of the sound and the great light
kindled in me a desire for their cause,
never felt before with such sharpness.

<column-break/>

This same reason causes the Evangelist John to be represented in the figure of an eagle <note>The eagle is the traditional symbol of St. John the Evangelist because his Gospel "soars" to the heights of Christ's divinity.</note>.

Just as a ray of the sun, reflecting itself, returns upward from whence it had come, like a man who returns home from a pilgrimage; so the fixed act of Beatrice in looking fixedly at the sun entered into my "imagination" <note>original: *imagine* – in medieval psychology, the faculty that receives sensory impressions</note>, and disposed me to look similarly at the sun. Because when the rays of the divine sun strike back into theological doctrine—which alone can sustain their gaze—it illuminates us: it strengthens and corroborates our eyes so that we too can look at the sun. Therefore rightly writes Augustine: "The good of God is known through theology which perfects the intellect and directs the affection" <note>original Latin: *Bonum dei cognoscitur per theologiam que perficit intellectum: & dirigit affectum*</note>. And so that we do not wonder that he could look fixedly at the sun beyond our custom, he adds: that the power of that place is such that we can do many things there that we cannot do here. Because that place is made specifically for the human species; and Earthly Paradise was created by God so that man might inhabit it for a longer time in a state of innocence; and then, when it pleased Him, he would be assumed to his beatitude. Therefore, since through the purgatorial virtues we have returned to the state of innocence, it is no wonder if in that place—that is, in such a state—it is permitted for us to look into the sun, which is not permitted here—that is, in the state of sin. **I DID NOT** endure it long. The meaning of the poet is that once the sun rose, he began to rise toward heaven, that is, to contemplate; for "contemplation is the free and clear gaze of the mind into the speculation of wisdom with suspended wonder."

The Poet wishes to express something else by demonstrating that Beatrice held her eyes fixed on heaven, and he held his on the eyes of Beatrice; which means nothing other than that sacred theology contemplates nothing but divine things, and whoever wishes to understand them must place their entire mind in theology and in its doctors. And it follows that in looking at her so fixedly, he became such "within"—that is, in the soul—as **GLAUCUS** became, who by eating the herb became a god. Thus it shows that his soul was deified. And certainly, through the contemplation of the divinity, we become divine and gods, as Boethius <note>original: *Boetio*</note> demonstrates at length. Glaucus, the son of Anthedon, was a fisherman. And placing the fish he had caught on the meadow so that the nets might dry, it happened that some of them, tasting a certain herb, regained their strength and jumped back into the water. Glaucus was stunned by the event and tasted the same herb himself; and seized by a sudden madness, he threw himself into the sea, and there from a man he became a sea god. **TRANSHUMANIZE**: that is, to transcend from human nature to divine.

The poet shows that he was rapt by the Holy Spirit, and by the sweetness of the song that he heard, and by the very great light that shone. Thus, his sight and taste were filled with ineffable joy. Wherefore, turning to the Holy Spirit, he speaks like a man now returned to the world: "O Holy Spirit who are Love, who governs the heavens: only when I was in such meditation was I that soul <note>Dante refers to himself as the "newly created" soul, the part of man created directly by God</note> which You created of me newly when You transformed me, You know it. Because You raised me with Your light," that is, You made me elevated to such contemplation with the light that You infused into my mind. And it shows here that there was in him that which the sacred letters affirm: that without the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, one does not come to such high speculations. **WHEN THE WHEEL**: because not only the heavens but all things created by God turn around with the desire they have to see Him. Therefore, "when the wheel"—that is, the revolution of the heavens which You, Holy Spirit, make eternal because every creature desires to enjoy God as much as its nature allows—"made me intent upon You," that is, made me...

<summary>This page covers Dante’s initial ascent from the Earthly Paradise, using the metaphor of the sun to represent divine truth and the myth of Glaucus to explain "transhumanization." The commentary emphasizes that through theology and the Holy Spirit, the human soul is "deified" and strengthened to behold things beyond earthly capacity.</summary>
<keywords>Paradiso, Beatrice, Glaucus, transhumanization, theology, Holy Spirit, divine grace, deification, Augustine, Boethius</keywords>

obtained in the horoscope <term>Horoscope: here referring specifically to the Ascendant, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term>, and it seems to claim two [dignities] for itself, since it exists in its own term <term>Term: a specific subdivision of a zodiac sign ruled by a particular planet, granting it "essential dignity" or strength</term>: whence without any controversy, Jupiter held dominion over the entire sky at that time. Furthermore, we saw that Saturn was in its own triplicity <term>Triplicity: a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element; a planet in its own triplicity is considered comfortable and strong</term>, which attributes three dignities to it. Both are also oriental <term>Oriental: rising in the east before the Sun, a position considered robust for superior planets</term>, and free from combustion <term>Combustion: the "burning up" of a planet's power when it is too close to the Sun; being free from this is a sign of strength</term>, which is a good thing for the three superior planets. Both are Direct <term>Direct: moving forward in the zodiac rather than "retrograde" or appearing to move backward</term> and, due to their direction in the epicycle <term>Epicycle: in the pre-Copernican model of the universe, a small circle on which a planet moves, while the center of that circle moves around a larger orbit</term>, they are stronger. Both are found to be increasing in motion because they are direct; both possess a masculine degree; finally, both are diurnal <term>Diurnal: belonging to the day; some planets are considered more beneficial when the Sun is above the horizon</term>. From this it is clear that these planets, joined together, overflow with both essential and accidental dignities. However, Jupiter seems to be exalted in honor and dignity many degrees above Saturn (for the reasons previously alleged). It is evident (I say) that both these planets are fortunate and well-disposed. We find, therefore, according to the opinion of the most learned astrologers, that Saturn, when well-disposed, makes *men venerable in their condition, profound thinkers and students of difficult arts, serious, with a certain austerity, whose works are heavy and full of labor, and makes them silent and solitary.* Jupiter, truly fortunate, produces *just, honest, good, and beneficent, religious, and reverent men, who are gracious, prudent with sweet speech, and lovers of their own.* And from its mastery, it denotes Prophets, Bishops, *and princes of religion,* Judges,

### Pancration. Cap. CII

<margin>P</margin> Pancration, sunt qui & hac scyllam malint appellare, radice bulbi magni, colore rufo, purpurascenteue, gustu amaro, qui os accendat, folijs lilij uerum longioribus. Plinius pancration, aliqui pusillam scyllam uocant, folijs albis in longioribus, crassioribusq;, radice bulbi magni, colore rufo. Sunt qui Gallis propriè loquentibus sciponiam existiment appellari, sed imperitum uulgus hoc nomē iam cepis communicauit. Galenus radicem tum gustu tum uiribus scyllæ similem fecit, ita ut nonnulli, cum eius non datur occasio, pancration in uicem sufficiant. Omnes siquidem scyllę repræsentat effectus, sed longe censetur inualidior. Paulus & specie & uiribus cōparauit scyllæ. Pancration aliqui pusillam scyllam appellare malunt. Aluum soluit succo cum farina erui sumpto, ulcera purgat. Hydropicis splenicisq; cum melle datur. Alij decoquunt eam donec aqua dulcis fiat, eaq; effusa radicē terentes digerunt in pastillos sole siccatos, & postea utitur ad capitis ulcera, & cætera quæ repurgāda sunt: item ad tussim, quantum tribus digitis apprehenderit in uino dantes, & ad lateris dolores. Peripleumonicis in eclegmate præbetur, propter ischiada in uino bibendum, & propter tormina mensesq; ciendos. Et in summa, potest ad quæ scylla. Paratur ministraturq; modo eodem, morbos omnino quos illa pellens, quanquam lenitas huius maior quàm scyllæ. Radicis succus cum erui farina cogitur in pastillos, qui cum aqua mulsa splenicis & hydropicis utiles sunt.

...when taken from vinegar and honey. When placed under the tongue fresh, it keeps hydropics from feeling thirst. It also disperses swollen glands with its leaves in four days when dissolved. It heals dandruff and flowing ulcers when smeared on after being boiled in oil; likewise cracks in the feet. It is boiled in honey for the sake of food, most especially to promote digestion: thus it also purges the internal parts. It is applied to the pain of the loins from honey. Pythagoras records that when hung in the doorway, it drives away the entry of evil medicines. It is boiled in many ways in a pot, which is cast into a kiln or oven, either smeared with bread or clay, or in pieces in pans. Likewise, it is dried raw, then cut and boiled in vinegar: then it is applied to the bites of serpents, and it is roasted and cleaned, and the middle of it is boiled again in water. The use of it so boiled is for dropsy and for moving urine, drunk in three obols with honey and vinegar. It is given to those with spleen ailments and stomach troubles, if they do not feel an ulcer. The scilla elicits in animals a desire for mating, for if a mare does not suffer the stallion, a ground scilla is smeared on her private parts, which thing kindles lust.

### Pancration. Chapter CII

<margin>P</margin> Pancration, there are those who prefer to call this *scilla* as well, with a large bulb root, red or purplish in color, and a bitter taste which inflames the mouth, with leaves like a lily but longer. Pliny calls it *pancration*, some call it "little scilla," with white leaves, longer and thicker, and a large bulb root of a red color. There are those who, with the French speaking properly, think it is called *sciponia*, but the ignorant common people have now communicated this name to onions. Galen made the root similar to the scilla both in taste and in powers, so that some, when the opportunity for it is not given, substitute *pancration* in its place. For it represents all the effects of the scilla, but it is considered to be far weaker. Paulus compared it to the scilla in both appearance and powers. Some prefer to call *pancration* "little scilla." It loosens the bowels when taken in juice with einkorn flour, and it cleanses ulcers. It is given with honey to hydropics and those with spleen ailments. Others boil it until the water becomes sweet, and after pouring that off, they grind the root into pastilles dried in the sun, and afterwards use them for ulcers of the head and other things that need to be cleaned out: likewise for a cough, giving an amount that one can grasp with three fingers in wine, and for pains of the side. It is offered to those with peripneumonia in an electuary; it is to be drunk in wine for sciatica and for colic and to move the menses. And in short, it can do what the scilla can. It is prepared and administered in the same way, [curing] entirely the same diseases that the other drives away, although its mildness is greater than that of the scilla. The juice of the root is worked with einkorn flour into pastilles, which with honey-water are useful for those with spleen and dropsy ailments.

### Capparis. Chapter CIII

<margin>C</margin> The caper grows spontaneously in fallow fields in very many provinces. But in places where there is a scarcity of it, if it is planted, it will desire a dry place. And this should be surrounded beforehand by a small trench, which should be filled with stones, and the area hollowed out in the digging, and the banks built up all around with a wall, so that it may be like a certain breastplate, so that the shrubs of this seed which wander through the fields cannot burst through; and unless they are coerced by a surrounding fortification or a circular ditch, and restrained by a built-up trench, they force the soil to become sterile. For they pour out a harmful poison and belch out a juice that is inconvenient to the crops growing there, unless they are frequently uprooted. The caper is content with cultivation that is either light or non-existent: for they wish to wither from diligence. In lean soil, it pursues herbs spontaneously, most familiar to fabulous places: since this thing thrives even in desert fields without the work of a farmer. Both are sown at the Equinox, flower in summer, and wither at the setting of the Pleiades. The shrub is of firmer wood, thorny and low; it crawls in a circle, with a short stem, branches thorny like a rose, with hooked and barbed spines, and a rounded and rough leaf, with berries like an olive, round, as they burst open, a rose-colored, white, and fragrant flower shines forth. After this has fallen off, having been shaken, a long pod swells, full of granular seeds, with a black, manifold, woody root. A reddish and least friable bark clothes it. It remains green until the setting of the Pleiades. Aristotle and Theophrastus denied that the caper dwells in cultivated lands, although, as we have already said, it is carried in many places. The seed, the flower, and the berry are principal to kitchens, and common foods, with the stem also frequently plucked along with them. Foreign kinds were once avoided. For the Arabian was pestilential, as Pliny says and Galen confirms; the African was an enemy to the gums; the Apulian caused vomiting; the Italian was more innocent.

...the Italian. Now, mild ones, from wherever they are brought, are not rejected as food. Paulus commended its use with vinegar and oil, because it both invites appetite and loosens the spleen, and drives out phlegm through the bowels. In pharmacies, it has retained its name; the common people, happy to abbreviate names, by wearing down two letters, bring forth *capres* as if *cappares*. Some of the Latins call it *inturim*, for the shrub is seen to be of a thorny kind, scattering itself in a circle on the ground. It has thorns like a bramble, curved into a hook, leaves like a quince, fruit like an olive, upon the bursting of which a white flower breaks out; when this falls, an oblong pod coalesces, which, finally unfolding itself, represents small grains that are red, such as are seen in the pomegranate, with large, branch-like roots. Small stems, leaves, flowers, seeds, and pods preserved in salt are brought to us in this appearance and shape which we have described. France now nourishes the shrub. In Cyprus, the caper grows in great abundance. It offers little nourishment to those eating, because it excels in the thinness of its parts, being born for medicine rather than for food. The fruit is preserved sprinkled with salt, otherwise it quickly senses corruption. Fresh [fruit] not having experienced salt nourishes more than that which has been aged in it, yet it moves the bowels more. Washed and soaked for a short time until it lays down the whole nature of the salt, it nourishes very little indeed, but invites a languishing appetite. It disperses the loathing of foods, casts down phlegm that had gathered in the belly, and clears out the obstructing blockages of the spleen and liver. But to perform these uses, it ought to be preferred to other dishes in honeyed vinegar or oil and vinegar. They eat the tender buds while they are green with vinegar and salt, and store them away for uses. They say that those who eat them daily are not endangered by the resolution of the nerves, nor by pains of the spleen. The root removes white vitiligo if they are ground and rubbed in the sun. It is beneficial to those with spleen ailments when drunk in wine, two drachms of the bark of the root, with the use of baths removed. And they say that in thirty-five days, the entire spleen is emitted through urine and the bowels. It is drunk for pains in the loins and for paralysis. The seed ground and boiled in vinegar, or the chewed root, soothes pains of the teeth. A decoction in oil is infused for pain in the ears. The leaves and fresh root with honey heal ulcers which they call phagedenas. In this way, the root also disperses swollen glands and parotids. Boiled in vinegar, it removes ulcerations of the mouth; it also cures ailments of the liver and kills worms of the ears. They give it in vinegar and honey for dandruff. It is agreed among authors that they are useless for the stomach. The stem and fruit are preserved for the sake of food. It disturbs the bowels, harms the stomach, and creates thirst. However, it is more useful for the stomach when boiled than raw. The seed itself, taken in two drachms in wine for forty days, consumes the spleen. It draws out urine and drives out bloody scrapings. It is beneficial for pains of the hips and resolution of the nerves; likewise for ruptures and convulsions. It moves the menses and elicits phlegm of the head. The seed boiled in vinegar soothes pains of the teeth if the mouth is rinsed. The dried bark of the root has the same effects. It purges all ulcers that are old, dirty, and that have become calloused. For those with spleen ailments, it is smeared on with barley flour. The root, seized bitingly with the tooth, relieves that evil. It removes white vitiligo when ground with vinegar. The ground root and leaves disperse swollen glands and hardness. The juice is infused against worms of the ears. The foreign caper which is brought from Marmarica in Libya excites great inflations. The Apulian causes vomiting; [as does] the very harsh African, and that which is conveyed from the Red Sea, for it raises pustules in the mouth and is an enemy to the gums, for it eats them away down to the bone, which is why it is condemned in foods.

### Lepidium. Chapter CV

The appearance of *lepidium* is not represented by Dioscorides. *Lepidium* was once foreign; now it is sown in many places by Fauonius; then, when it has grown into a shrub, it is cut close to the ground and harvested like cut leeks, but more rarely. It should not be cut after the Kalends of November, since it dies from being violated by the colds, especially if the severity of winter worsens, for it is most impatient of the cold: yet in two years, it extends its life up to ten years. It grows, as Pliny records, to a cubit's height, with laurel-like leaves, but soft. Its use is not without milk. Paulus Aegineta, in the third volume, in the mention of sciatica, says: "Lepidium which grows among us is shrub-like, with laurel leaves, [but] far larger; they are more efficacious in summer." If the time of year denies these, it will be appropriate to use the bark of the root in place of the leaves. It has provided wonderful experience for those with sciatica and long illnesses. This herb is cultivated among us, not unknown to the pharmacies, though under the borrowed name of another plant. For herbalists now call it not *lepidium* but *raphanus*, perhaps [because of the] root.

Quis enim vere doctus ignorat plurimas esse rerum naturalium vires occultas, quas si cognitas perspectasque haberet & ad usum accommodare nosset, haud dubie mira posset efficere. Multa sunt, ait Perer. c. 3. *Natura miracula incomperta rationis*, & ut Plin. loquitur in *Naturae maiestate penitus absita, quae si hominum quispiam, illis rebus naturalibus occulte utens, faceret, Magus vulgo diceretur, & non nisi auxilia daemonum eius modi facere putaretur, cum tamen opera illa essent naturalia & naturaliter a causis naturalibus orta, mediante applicatione sive Magia naturali, aut Physica aut Mathematica.

**V.** *Naturalis Magia Physica* est ars quae circa occultas rerum naturalium virtutes, rerum mirabilium effectrices, occupatur: nam commiscet vires activas passivis, e quibus artificiose, loco, tempore, modoque conveniente sibi mutuo applicatis effectus naturales quidem & veri, sed quia earum causae multos latent, novi & mirabiles consequuntur. Hac ratione, inquit Azor, fructus arborum ante tempus aliquando nascuntur; procreantur hyeme rosae, uvae, &c. *Mathematica* vero Magia est ars quae sola Mathematicarum artium notitia, sine aliis rerum naturalium actionibus, mira quadam & insolita perficit. Hac ratione, quidam fecerunt olim aeneos boues mugientes, angues sibilantes, passeres cantillantes, statuas lapideas in mensa vel tabula saltantes, &c. quemadmodum alii exacta numerorum cognitione praediti vulgo incognita & abstrusa manifestarunt, quae additis detractisque numeris saepiusque subductis ratiocinando collegerunt.

**IV.** Furthermore, there are not wanting those who say it is partly practical and partly speculative, while they subdivide it into Operative and Divinatory, of which the latter concerns itself with guessing at hidden and future things, concerning which we speak in the present. That such a natural and operative Magic exists, no learned man calls into doubt. For who, being truly learned, is ignorant that there are very many hidden powers of natural things, which, if one had them known and perceived and knew how to adapt them to use, he could undoubtedly perform wonders. There are many, says Pererius in chapter 3, *miracles of Nature hidden from reason*, and as Pliny speaks in his *Natural History*, *deeply hidden in the majesty of Nature, which if any man were to do, secretly using those natural things, he would be called a Magus by the vulgar, and would be thought to do such things only by the aid of demons, when yet those works would be natural and naturally arisen from natural causes, through the means of application or Natural Magic, either Physical or Mathematical.*

**V.** *Natural Physical Magic* is an art which is occupied with the occult virtues of natural things, the producers of wonderful effects: for it mixes active powers with passive ones, from which, when artificially applied to each other in a convenient place, time, and manner, natural and true effects ensue, but because their causes lie hidden to many, they appear new and wonderful. For this reason, says Azor, the fruits of trees are sometimes born before their time; roses, grapes, etc., are produced in winter. *Mathematical* Magic, however, is an art which performs some wonderful and unusual things solely by the knowledge of Mathematical arts, without other actions of natural things. By this reason, some once made bronze oxen bellowing, snakes hissing, sparrows chirping, stone statues dancing on a table or board, etc., just as others, endowed with an exact knowledge of numbers, revealed to the vulgar things unknown and abstruse, which they gathered by reasoning, with numbers added, subtracted, and often deduced.

**VI.** Although Natural Magic in itself is not evil, being a most noble part of Physical, Medical, and Mathematical doctrine, as Pererius says in chapter 14, nevertheless, as Lessius shows in the aforementioned doubt, it is dangerous, because it vehemently entangles human minds in curious and useless things, and makes them more curious from curious ones, and gradually introduces them to superstitious Magic. For under the guise of an occult operation of Nature, the devil easily mixes himself in, and thus what is done by his works or prestidigitation is attributed to the occult virtue of a Natural cause. Whence we see, he says, that even the greatest Magicians want to be considered only as professors of Natural Magic, and try to cover all their doings with a certain image of the occult virtue of nature; for although they sometimes apply certain natural causes, these are either entirely worth nothing for the intended effect, or are insufficient, and—lo—there are certain signs which pertain to superstitious Magic to add: wherefore St. Augustine, in *The City of God*, book 8, chapter 19, rightly says, *All the miracles of Magicians are done by the doctrines and works of demons.*

**VII.** From which it can be inferred, First, that almost all books which teach natural magic are to be held suspect by a Christian philosopher, and are to be avoided by youth as dangerous. A good long list of these books and authors was composed by Martin Delrio, book 1, chapter 3. Secondly, that the study and public treatment of Magic can rightly be prohibited in a Republic if it is feared that, being produced among the common people, it might offer an opportunity to many (such is the inclination of the human mind toward evil) to abuse it for the ruin and destruction of others. And although physicians could also abuse Medicine, which for the same reason would also seem to be prohibited, yet the rationale of Medicine is one thing, that of Magic another; since Medicine and its use are in themselves necessary to mortals, and its abuse is more manifest than that it could be entirely hidden, and therefore it is easier to punish and correct: but the use of Magic is not in itself necessary to human Society, and its abuse is occult, for it lies hidden by what things and in what manner Magic operates. For which reason it can be greatly feared that, the more occult it is in its operation, the more, by the confidence of impunity, it becomes prone to doing harm, says Pererius, chapter 14.
auditTranslation:
**VIII.** Diabolical and superstitious Magic is a certain rationale or art of working wonders through signs by the aid of demons. For just as natural Magic uses natural causes, so superstitious Magic uses signs which are moral causes; for by these, according to a pact, the demon is enticed to do what the Magician seeks, and thus the signs themselves seem to perform something, as St. Augustine intimates in *The City of God*, book 12, chapter 6, where he also relates that these signs and the whole discipline were instituted first by demons, who nevertheless are not pleased by the signs viewed in themselves, but insofar as they are honored by them, or insofar as they depend on their institution. But who among men was the first author, and the first instrument, through which the devil infused this plague into the world? Gregory of Tours, in *History of the Franks*, book 1, chapter 6, says that Cush, the firstborn of Ham, the devil imbuing him, was the inventor of the whole Magical art, whom the Persians, seeing him coming, named Zoroaster (as if to say "living star"), and because he was struck by lightning, held him as a God. St. Clement, in *Recognitions*, book 2, thinks also that Magic flourished before the flood and after the flood was handed down by Ham to his son Mizraim, from whom the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Persians, who were most addicted to these arts.

**IX.** Furthermore, as it is certain to Christian Philosophers that demons exist, so it is certain that Demoniacal Magic exists, which relies neither on the industry or artifice of men, nor on merely natural causes, but on a certain immaterial and separate virtue or action, that is, one proceeding from immaterial and separate substances, and is most especially demonstrated by experience; for to give responses about most hidden things, to attain knowledge suddenly without any labor of learning, to subtract bodies from the eyes of beholders, etc., can be reduced to no cause other than some intellectual and separate nature, but this is not God, nor any good genius (who do not mix themselves in vain things), and therefore it is only the Cacodemon <note>i.e., evil spirit</note>, as Delrio rightly proves, book 2, question 2, from which you may learn that, besides the natural one explained above, there is no White and licit Magic, which flows to us immediately from God Alone, or mediately from the same through good angels, but all other is Black and illicit, as being handed down by malignant spirits and resting upon their explicit or implicit pact.

**X.** Since, therefore, there is no White Magic, or theurgy, as they call it, it is clear that all other (preternatural) magic is to be condemned and avoided, that is, Magic universally.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between pleasure and pain, specifically addressing why intellectual pleasures do not have painful opposites, before moving into a detailed taxonomy of Fear.</meta>

# ON THE NATURE OF MAN.

...but rather mastering them. Pain is opposed to moderate pleasure as an evil is opposed to a good. However, pain is opposed to excessive pleasure as an evil is to an evil; but such excesses occur only in bodily pleasures. For theoretical pleasures <note>original: θεωρητικαὶ (theorētikoi). This refers to intellectual or contemplative pleasures, such as those found in study or philosophy.</note>, being supreme and having attained perfection, do not admit of excess. Nor is pain opposed to them, nor does it even exist in relation to them; for these pleasures do not arise as a remedy <note>original: θεραπεία (therapeia). The author argues that bodily pleasures often satisfy a physical lack or pain (like eating satisfies hunger), whereas intellectual pleasure is not a "cure" for a prior pain but is good in itself.</note> for a preceding pain.

### ON FEAR. CHAPTER 20.

Fear is divided into six types: hesitation, reverence, shame, terror, anxiety, and amazement. 

**Hesitation** <term>oknos: ὄκνος</term> is a fear of a future action. 

**Terror** <term>kataplēxis: κατάπληξις</term> is a fear arising from a grand mental image. 

**Amazement** <term>ekplēxis: ἔκπληξις</term> is a fear arising from an unusual or unfamiliar mental image. 

**Anxiety** <term>agōnia: ἀγωνία</term> is a fear of failure—that is, of falling short of success; for when we fear we may fail in a task, we feel anxiety. 

**Reverence** <term>aidōs: αἰδώς</term> is a fear involving the expectation of blame; this is a most beautiful passion. 

**Shame** <term>aischynē: αἰσχύνη</term> is fear over a disgraceful deed already committed. If there is no hope [of repairing the deed], it leads to anxiety. In this way reverence differs from shame: the person who feels shame is overwhelmed and "sinks down" because of what they have already done, while the person who feels reverence fears falling into some future dishonor. The ancients, however, often called reverence "shame" and shame "reverence," using the terms interchangeably. 

Fear occurs through a chilling of the body, as all the heat rushes together into the heart toward the governing faculty <note>original: τὸ ἀρχικόν (to archikon). In ancient psychology, this refers to the ruling part of the soul, which Nemesius identifies as fleeing to the heart during a fright.</note>; just as the common people, when they are afraid, flee for refuge to their rulers.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the taxonomy of fear. It transitions into the physical manifestations of grief and introduces the physiology and categorization of anger.</meta>

<header>NEMESIUS</header>

The organ of grief <note>original: λύπη (lypē). While "pain" is a general translation, in this context of emotions, "grief" or "distress" is more appropriate.</note> is the mouth of the stomach. For this is the part that feels the "biting" sensation during times of grief. As 
> **Galen** says in the sixth book of his *Demonstrations*: 
> In those who are grieving, a considerable amount of yellow bile flows down into the stomach; this is what causes the biting sensation for them, and they do not stop grieving and feeling "bitten" until they have vomited the bile. 
For this biting occurs just below the middle of the chest at the cartilage called the **xiphoid** <note>The xiphoid process is the small cartilaginous extension at the lower part of the sternum.</note>. However, the heart lies much higher up. Relative to the diaphragm, the stomach is located lower down, while the heart is higher. Yet, the ancients commonly called both the heart and the mouth of the stomach by the name *kardia* <term>kardia: καρδία</term> <note>In ancient medicine, "kardia" referred to both the heart and the upper opening of the stomach. This is why we still use the term "cardiac" in relation to the stomach's upper sphincter.</note>. This is seen in **Hippocrates** and also **Thucydides**, who, when describing the Great Plague, says: 
> "And whenever it settled in the *kardia* [the stomach], it upset it, and discharges of bile—all those named by doctors—followed." 
For that which is "upset" or overturned is the mouth of the stomach, which is forced to vomit, and not the internal organ we call the heart.

### ON ANGER. CHAPTER 21.

**Anger** <term>thymos: θυμός</term> is a boiling of the blood around the heart, caused by the evaporation or the agitation of the bile. For this reason, it is also called *cholē* <note>original: χολὴ (bile/gall)</note> and *cholos* <note>original: χόλος (bitter anger or bile)</note>. Sometimes anger is also defined as a desire for retaliation. When we are wronged, or believe we are being wronged, we become angry; in such cases, the passion becomes a mixture of desire and anger. 

There are three types of anger: **wrath** <term>orgē: ὀργὴ</term>, which is also called *cholē* or *cholos*; **rage** <term>mēnis: μῆνις</term>; and **resentment** <term>kotos: κότος</term>. For while anger at its beginning...

[Caesarius] also narrates of a certain man who, being harassed by one of these **incubi** and solicited to lust, was nonetheless totally liberated from it by the sacrament of **confession**. He finally reports an example of another **nun** troubled in this way by a **Demon**, who neither through prayer, nor confession, nor through any other spiritual exercise, would ever stop entering her bed; after she was taught by a certain man to say **Benedicite** <note>original: "Benedicite"; a Latin word meaning "Bless [the Lord]," commonly used as a greeting or grace in religious houses.</note>. And doing so <gloss>doing so</gloss> many times, the Demon suddenly abandoned her.

As for the **change of place**, the same author says that after a young virgin had been raped by one of these **incubi**, she became frantic with great grief; by the advice of her father, passing over a river and moving far from the original place, she was abandoned by that cursed spirit. But her father, for having sent her from there to that other place, was so struck by the **Demon** that within the space of three days he died.

Regarding **excommunication**, then—which is sometimes the same thing as **Exorcisms** regarding these spirits—it is manifest from what is read in the life of **Saint Bernard** <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a famous Cistercian abbot known for his influence and miracles.</note> about a woman who, in the regions of **Aquitaine** <note>original: "Equitania"; a historical region in southwestern France.</note> for the space of six years, was harassed by one of these <gloss>these</gloss> **incubi** with an incredible abuse of lust. XV. 'T begin en de oorfprong der Ophiten is ons onbekend. Zo veel nogthans kan men wel bykans verzekeren, dat ze ouder zyn, dan de geboorte onzes Heilands. PHILASTER van Brescia geeft hen, uitdrukkelyk, onder de Partyen, welke, vóór onzes Zaligmakers komst in het vleesch, de zuivere waarheid hebben bedorven, niet slegts eene plaats, maar zelfs de eerste plaats, beschryvend tef-rede vind, haar jonger te maken, en onder de Chriften-Secten te stellen. Nu is 't wel zo, dat dit getuigenis alleen zo ftérk en zo gewigtig niet is, dat het de zaak geheel konde afdoen. PHILASTER is een man, die noch bekwaamheid, noch naarftigheid genoeg bezat, om alle fouten te verhoeden, en uit dien hoofde slegts in een zeer middelmatig aanzien is.
