Zy waren, gelyk wy vervolgens zullen toonen, verdeeld in twee Partyen. De ééne erkende onzen Jezus voor dien Perzoon, waar mede zig de Christus of Messias, dien zy verwachtten, ter verlossinge der van den Waereld-god gekluifterde zielen, hadt vereenigd. De andere was zo weinig genegen, in Jezus te gelooven, dat zy hem, veelééer, even als de overige Jooden deden, vervloekte, en op een anderen Messias hoopte. Wat kan men anders denken, wanneer men van deze verdeeldheid hoord, dan dat ze reeds in de Waereld moeten geweest zyn, toen Jezus, onze Heiland, zig als Gods Zoon en den beloofden Messias openbaarde? Van waar de bittere en heftige haat tegen Jezus, indien hunne Voorvaders niet tot de Jooden hadden behoord, die den Zaligmaker aan het Kruis hegtten? <margin>They are older than the Christian era. Their founder, <term>Euphrates</term>.</margin>
XV. The beginning and the origin of the <term>Ophites</term> is unknown to us. So much, however, one can almost assure, that they are older than the birth of our Savior. <term>Philaster of Brescia</term> explicitly gives them not just a place, but even the first place among the parties which corrupted the pure truth before our Savior's coming in the flesh. He is satisfied to make them younger and to place them among the Christian sects. Now it is indeed so, that this testimony alone is not so strong and so weighty that it could entirely settle the matter. <term>Philaster</term> is a man who possessed neither the ability nor the diligence enough to avoid all errors, and for that reason is held only in a very mediocre regard. But all kinds of similar reports come alongside his testimony and support it so that one can hardly reject it. The

<column-break/>

Hebrew name which the <term>Ophites</term> bore proves that their community was founded in a land where Hebrew was spoken. Anyone who does not doubt this cannot find it difficult to believe that they first appeared in a corner of the Promised Land before Jerusalem was destroyed and the Jewish people were scattered. They were, as we shall subsequently show, divided into two parties. The one recognized our Jesus as that person with whom the <term>Christ</term> or <term>Messiah</term> whom they expected had united Himself for the redemption of the souls shackled by the <term>World-god</term> <gloss>the Demiurge</gloss>. The other was so little inclined to believe in Jesus that they rather cursed him, just as the other Jews did, and hoped for another Messiah. What else can one think when one hears of this division than that they must already have been in the world when Jesus, our Savior, revealed Himself as God's Son and the promised Messiah? From where would the bitter and intense hatred against Jesus come if their ancestors had not belonged to the Jews who fastened the Savior to the Cross? The <term>Gnostic Wisdom</term> <gloss>Gnosticism</gloss> had already reigned in the Eastern lands for many years when Jesus came into the world: and the Jews had brought it, like many other fictions, from their captivity back to their fatherland. For which reason it is generally much more credible that all Gnostic communities that emerged from Judaism existed already before the Savior's
auditTranslation:
coming than that they first arose after His Ascension. Regarding the founder of the <term>Slangenbroederen</term> <gloss>Snake-brothers, the Ophites</gloss>, nothing more than the name has been left to us. This was <term>Euphrates</term>, and he was still honored in the third century by that part of the <term>Ophites</term> which hated Jesus as a great and excellent man. <margin>(a) Origen, Book 6 against Celsus, section 28, page 652. Volume 1.</margin> <note>original: "ORIGENES Lib. 6. contr. Cels:, § 28. pag: 652. Tom. I."</note> By descent he was, undoubtedly, a Jew. This can be gathered clearly enough from his faith, which, from beginning to end, is interwoven with Jewish names, sentiments, and words of the Old Testament. And, however deeply he debases the God of the Jews, he still allows this people more than a heathen would ever have granted. <term>Sophronius</term> makes mention, among the heads of the ancient heretics whom he curses, of a certain <term>Euphrates</term>, to whom he gives the surname of <term>Perser</term> or <term>Persian</term>. <margin>(b) Synodal Letter in Hardouin's Councils, Volume 3, page 1287.</margin> <note>original: "Epist. Synod. HARDUINI Concil. Tom. III. pag. 1287."</note> It seems to me that we are free to suspect that he means the father of the <term>Ophites</term>. And, if this is probable, then we also almost know his fatherland. He was a Persian Jew who held the false wisdom, which he had learned in a school of his country, in such high regard that he forsook the faith of his fathers. He was so successful in this that he found some among his brothers in Judea who would rather believe him than <term>Moses</term>

<column-break/>

with the Prophets. Truly, in the doctrine of the <term>Ophites</term>, many pieces look so Persian that one cannot long refuse to consider it the invention of a Persian.

* * * * * *

REMARK.

One cannot take it ill of scholars that they would gladly want to know more about the founder of the <term>Ophites</term> than the little which <term>Origen</term> tells us of him. It is very natural to wish to know those who played a more than common role among men. And it serves many matters, oftentimes, when one knows them rightly. Therefore, one has searched in the books of the ancients to see if a greater report of him were not to be found somewhere. Among those now who bore the name of <term>Euphrates</term> in the ancient world, two are primarily famous, who lived possibly at the same time, perhaps not long after one another, but both at that time when the <term>Ophites</term> arose among the Jews and Christians. The one is a Syrian philosopher, born of Tyre, whom <term>Pliny the Younger</term> praises as his friend and as an uncommonly clever and eloquent man. <margin>(a) Letters, Book 1, letter 9, page 18.</margin> <note>original: "Epistolar. Hic dicit quod logica tradit modum sciendi in acquisitione omnium aliarum scientiarum. quod modus sciendi est proponendus ante actualem acquisitionem scientiarum. quia absurdum est sic querere sciam et modum sciendi. # De vita

Here he says that logic provides the method of knowing for the acquisition of all other sciences. This method of knowing must be proposed before the actual acquisition of the sciences, because it is absurd to seek both the science and the method of knowing at the same time. Therefore, one who wishes to possess science should imitate the precepts of the logical art. Just as a banner is a sign of victory, so one instructed in logic possesses within himself a sign of power in gathering all other sciences possible for humans to have. This logic is of such a nature that it always makes the learned person wish to study; without it, if one wishes to approach other sciences—namely physics and metaphysics—he is like an inexperienced doctor who first visits a sick man wishing to cure him, and only afterwards looks at medical books. Returning, he finds the disease has worsened, and while leaving the sick person in an incurable state, he demands payment, denying him health and offering excuses for the failure to recover health, thus deluding the man. So it is in other sciences: those wishing to progress without logic do not arrive at the perfect health of the intellect, just as the doctor does not arrive at the recovery of health.

Here the author says that logical science is like a governor, not in the manner of a recipient, but as a servant in comparison to all other sciences. Aristotle began it, continued it, and finally completed it by perfecting it; he first very clearly handed down the knowledge of the ten categories, which are substance, quantity, quality, relation, action, passion, time (when), place (where), habit, and position.

# Aristotelis

Here he says that Porphyry handed down the knowledge of the five universals, which are genus, species, difference, property, and accident, the knowledge of which is useful for having knowledge of the categories, as is evident at the beginning of his book. Without the knowledge of these universals, nothing can be known in logic. However, these universals according to the doctrine of Plato are monsters, because they fall short of their perfections, since according to him they are subsistent in themselves, and thus they cannot give essence, name, and definition to singulars, which nevertheless according to the truth belongs to them in many things—namely, to singulars or inferiors.

# Golden Tallies
<note>original: 金節 (Jinjie). These were ceremonial staffs or tallies carried by imperial envoys to authenticate their identity and authority.</note>

<gloss>According to the "Duties of the Ministry of the Earth" in the *Rites of Zhou* <note>original: 周禮地官 (Zhou Li Diguan). An ancient text detailing the bureaucracy of the Zhou Dynasty</note>: For the envoys of various states, those from mountain states use the Tiger Tally; those from plains states use the Human Tally; and those from marshland states use the Dragon Tally. All of these are made of metal.</gloss> <gloss>Furthermore, the *Explanation of Names* <note>original: 釋名 (Shi Ming). A dictionary from the Han Dynasty</note> states: The Tally [Jie] serves as the standard for commands, rewards, and punishments. It also notes that the tassels of the Tally are layered one above the other, modeled after the joints [Jie] of a bamboo stalk.</gloss> During the Han Dynasty, the Tally was made with a bamboo pole eight feet long <note>approximately 1.8 meters or 6 feet in modern measurements</note>, with three layers of tassels made from yak tails. 

The *Institutional History of the Song* <note>original: 宋會要 (Song Huiyao)</note> records that it featured a black-lacquered pole topped with a circular plate. Around this plate hung eight layers of red silk tassels, and the entire assembly was enclosed in a yellow bag embroidered with dragon motifs. The system of the Yuan Dynasty was similar to a ceremonial banner with eight layers, sheathed in a yellow gauze bag decorated with clouds and dragons. The current system <note>The Ming Dynasty system</note> follows the same design as the Song.

# Bone-Clubs
<note>original: 骨朵 (Guduo). A type of ceremonial mace or flail with a weighted head, often used by the imperial guard.</note>

<summary>This page describes the 'Golden Tally' (Jinjie), a symbolic staff carried by imperial envoys, tracing its evolution from the animal-themed metal tallies of the Zhou Dynasty to the silk-tasseled versions of the Song and Ming.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of ceremonial regalia, moving from the Golden Tallies used by envoys to the "Bone-Bud" (Guduo), a bulbous ceremonial mace carried by elite imperial guards. It provides an etymological explanation for the weapon's unusual name and describes its physical evolution across the Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties.</meta>

Page Thirty-one
# Thirty-one: Official [...]

According to the *Notebooks* of Song Qi <note>Song Qi (998–1061) was a renowned historian of the Song Dynasty and co-compiler of the *New History of the Tang*</note>, the current dynasty employs "Bone-Bud Bearers" <note>original: 骨朵子直 (Guduozi Zhi). These were elite guards who carried ceremonial maces</note> among the guards who attend closely to the Emperor. I once served in the compilation of the *Daily Records* <note>original: 日曆 (Rili). The official court chronicles</note> and investigated the meaning of this term.

The people of the Guanzhong region <note>The central plains of Shaanxi province, the historic heartland of several dynasties</note> refer to a large, protruding belly as a *Guzhun* <note>original: 胍肫</note>. Colloquially, because the head of certain ceremonial staffs was quite large, they also came to be called *Guzhun*. This was later corrupted into the name "Bone-Bud" <note>original: 骨朵 (Guduo). The name suggests a budding flower or a rounded bone joint</note>. *Guzhun* is pronounced similarly to *Gutu*. 

The *Classic of Military Affairs* <note>original: 武經 (Wujing). Likely referring to the *Wujing Zongyao*, a comprehensive military compendium</note> states that the Bone-Bud exists in two varieties: the "Caltrop" <note>original: 蒺藜 (Jili). Named for its resemblance to the spiny water caltrop plant, often featuring spikes</note> and the "Garlic Head" <note>original: 蒜頭 (Suantou). A smoother, bulbous shape resembling a head of garlic</note>. These feature a large head fashioned from either iron or wood. 

The system of the Yuan Dynasty <note>1271–1368</note> utilized a red-lacquered rod head pierced through with a copper mallet that had been coated in gold. There was also an "Engraved-Pattern Bone-Bud" <note>original: 刻絲骨朵 (Kesi Guduo)</note>, which was shaped like a standard Bone-Bud but featured additional twisted-silk patterns. 

The current system <note>The Ming Dynasty, during which this text was likely compiled</note> utilizes a red-lacquered pole as the handle, decorated with gold at the base, with a Bone-Bud mace head pierced through the top.

<summary>This page explains the etymology and design of the "Bone-Bud" (Guduo), a ceremonial mace used by imperial guards, tracing its name to a regional term for a large belly.</summary>

mineral substances and mineral sperms come to the stomach, it goes to the worms.

## The Fifth Paragraph.

And it is to be noted with these that common sperm is fixed, and then, with its own dead body, it departs into a sensitive virtue and assumes a sensitive body (otherwise insensitive) from an insensitive body, as in the elements; because the generation of flies proceeds from air, of lizards from earth, of spiders from fire, snakes truly from water (fleas from minerals). The flies and lizards are all beetles that are not generated from dung; the flies grow from the element of air, for in the elements there is also menstrual sperm; the spider from the element of fire, that is, the principle of spiders is from the element of fire; from the element of water then, privatively, become the snakes.

## On the Cure of Worms.

Now about those things that pertain to the cure, and these are internal medicines, and what are external: it must be from one nature. Furthermore, it is necessary to also understand the internal genera, external medicines. It is also necessary to know most perfectly the process of poison. Finally, know that every medicine that kills worms is from poison. And those that cure external worms, the same also [cure] internal ones.

External worms, a compound from <term>colocinth</term> <gloss>bitter apple</gloss>, if they are touched, they die; let it be given to those suffering from worms: by the liquor from <term>centaury</term>, snake-eels die: by oil from the seed of <term>hypericon</term> <gloss>St. John’s Wort</gloss>, toads: geckos, lizards. <margin>XLIV. Motum non esse contrarium, sed quieti & determinationem in unam partem determinationi in partem oppositam.</margin>
Atque notandum est, unum motum alteri motui æquè veloci nullo modo esse contrarium: sed propriè tantùm duplicem hîc inveniri contrarietatem. Unam inter motum & quietem, vel etiam inter motus celeritatem & tarditatem, quatenus scilicet ista tarditas de quietis natura participat: Alteram inter determinationem motus versus aliquam partem, & occurfum corporis in illa parte quiescentis, vel aliter moti, atque pro ratione partis, in quam corpus alteri occurrens movetur, hæc contrarietas est major vel minor.

<margin>XLV. Quomodo possit determinari, quantum cujusque corporis motus mutetur propter aliorum corporum occursum; idque per regulas sequentes.</margin>
Ex quibus ut possimus determinare, quo pacto singula corpora motus suos augeant vel minuant, vel in alias partes convertant, ob aliorum corporum occursus, oportet tantùm calculo subducere, quantum in unoquoque fit virium, sive ad movendum, sive ad motui resistendum, ac pro certo statuere, illud semper, quod valentius est, fortiri suum effectum. Hocque facilè calculo subduci posset, si duo tantùm corpora sibi mutuò occurrerent, eaque essent perfectè dura, & à reliquis omnibus fic divisa, ut eorum motus à nullis aliis circumjacentibus impedirentur, nec juvarentur; ea enim regulas sequentes observarent.

<margin>XLVI. Prima.</margin>
Primò, si duo illa corpora, putà B & C, essent planè æqualia, & æquè velociter moverentur, B quidem à dextra versus sinistram, & C illi in directum à sinistra versus dextram, cùm sibi mutuò occurrerent reflecterentur, & postea pergerent moveri, B versus dextram, & C versus sinistram, nullâ parte suæ celeritatis amissâ.

<margin>XLI. Probatio prioris partis hujus regulæ.</margin>
Demonstratur autem prior pars hujus legis, ex eo quòd differentia fit inter motum in se spectatum, & ipsius determinationem versus certam partem; quâ fit, ut ista determinatio possit mutari, motu integro remanente. Cùm enim, ut antè dictum est, unaquæque res, non composita, sed simplex, qualis est motus, semper esse perseveret, quamdiu à nulla causa externa destruitur; & in occurfu duri corporis, apparet quidem causa quæ impediat, ne motus alterius corporis, cui occurrit, maneat determinatus versus eandem partem; non autem ulla, quæ motum ipsum tollat, vel minuat, quia motus motui non est contrarius; hinc sequitur illum idcirco minui non debere.

<margin>XLII. Probatio posterioris partis.</margin>
Demonstratur etiam pars altera, ex immutabilitate operationis Dei, mundum eâdem actione, quâ olim creavit, continuò jam conservantis. Cùm enim omnia corporibus sint plena, & nihilominus uniuscujusque corporis motus tendat in lineam rectam, perspicuum est Deum ab initio mundum creando, non modò diversas ejus partes diverlimodè movisse, sed simul etiam effecisse, ut unæ alias impellerent, motusque suos in illas transferrent: adeò ut jam ipsum conservando eâdem actione, ac cum iisdem legibus, cum quibus creavit, motum non iisdem materiæ partibus infixum, fed ex unis in alias, prout sibi mutuò occurrunt, transeuntem confervet. Sicque hæc ipsa creaturarum continua mutatio, immutabilitatis Dei est argumentum.

<margin>XLIII. In quo constat vis cujusque corporis ad agendum vel resistendum.</margin>
Hîc verò diligenter advertendum est, in quo consistat vis cujusque corporis ad agendum in aliud, vel ad actioni alterius resistendum: nempe in hoc uno, quòd unaquæque res tendat, quantum in se est, ad permanendum in eodem statu in quo est, juxta legem primo loco positam. Hinc enim id quod alteri conjunctum est, vim habet nonnullam, ad impediendum ne disjungatur; id quod disjunctum est, ad manendum disjunctum; id quod quiescit, ad perseverandum in sua quiete, atque ex consequenti ad resistendum iis omnibus quæ illam possunt mutare; id quod movetur ad perseverandum in suo motu, hoc est, in motu ejusdem celeritatis, & versus eandem partem.

<header>PART TWO.</header>

reduced to rest. And all the particular causes of the changes that happen to bodies are contained in this third law; at least those that are themselves corporeal; for we do not now inquire whether human or angelic minds have the power of moving bodies, and of what kind that power might be; but we reserve this for the treatment concerning man.

<margin>XLI. Proof of the first part of this rule.</margin>
The first part of this law is demonstrated from the fact that a difference exists between motion viewed in itself and its determination toward a certain part; whereby it happens that this determination can be changed while the motion remains intact. For since, as was said before, each thing—not composite, but simple, as is motion—always perseveres in being as long as it is destroyed by no external cause; and in the encounter of a hard body, there appears indeed a cause that prevents the motion of the other body, which it encounters, from remaining determined toward the same part; but there is no cause that takes away or diminishes the motion itself, because motion is not contrary to motion; hence it follows that it should not be diminished for that reason.

<margin>XLII. Proof of the second part.</margin>
The second part is also demonstrated from the immutability of the operation of God, who continuously conserves the world now by the same action by which he created it long ago. For since all things are full of bodies, and nevertheless the motion of each body tends in a straight line, it is clear that God, by creating the world from the beginning, not only moved its different parts in diverse ways, but also at the same time caused them to impel one another and to transfer their motions into one another: so that now, in conserving it by the same action and with the same laws by which he created it, he conserves the motion not fixed to the same parts of matter, but passing from one to another as they encounter one another. And thus this very continuous change of creatures is an argument for the immutability of God.

<margin>XLIII. In what the force of each body to act or resist consists.</margin>
Here, however, it must be carefully noted in what the force of each body to act on another or to resist the action of another consists: namely, in this one thing, that each thing tends, as far as it is in itself, to remain in the same state in which it is, according to the law placed in the first position. For hence that which is joined to another has some force to prevent it from being disjoined; that which is disjoined, to remain disjoined; that which is at rest, to persevere in its rest, and consequently to resist all those things which can change it; that which is moved, to persevere in its motion, that is, in motion of the same speed and toward the same part.

And that force must be estimated both from the magnitude of the body in which it resides, and from the surface area along which that body is separated from another; as well as from the speed of the motion, and the nature and contrariety of the mode by which diverse bodies mutually encounter one another.

<margin>XLIV. Motion is not contrary to motion, but to rest; and determination toward one part is contrary to determination toward the opposite part.</margin>
And it must be noted that one motion is in no way contrary to another motion of equal speed; but properly speaking, only two types of contrariety are found here. One is between motion and rest, or even between the speed and slowness of motion, insofar as this slowness participates in the nature of rest. The other is between the determination of motion toward a certain part and the encounter of a body resting in that part, or one otherwise moved; and according to the proportion of the part toward which the body encountering another is moved, this contrariety is greater or lesser.

<margin>XLV. How it may be determined, how much the motion of each body is changed due to the encounter of other bodies; and this by the following rules.</margin>
From these, so that we may determine how individual bodies increase or decrease their motions, or convert them into other parts due to the encounters of other bodies, it is necessary only to calculate how much force exists in each, either for moving or for resisting motion, and to establish for certain that the one which is more powerful always obtains its effect. ABOUT THE LETTERS: Sent to me by Caesar, about which he speaks at the beginning of the letter. The joy of the good, however, was stirred because there no longer seemed to be reason to doubt Cicero’s safety, with Caesar writing to him. OF THIS PLAN: For no one seeks safety from Caesar. For those who had gone to Asia to intercede with Caesar for their own safety did not want to proceed further, but are waiting there for the end of the Alexandrian war. Those, however, who are in Achaea are showing to Fusius, contrary to what they had done before, that they do not wish to intercede, and that they have changed that first plan of seeking safety from Caesar. I think, however, that it should be read "TAKE AWAY" <note>original: "AVFERVNT"</note>, not "BRING" <note>original: "AFFERVNT"</note>. I think so, however; I do not assert it.

-> 180. <-

DECIDED: <note>original: "CONSTITVTVM"</note> Deliberation, for they decided to entrust themselves to Caesar, but with the Alexandrian war interposed, and Caesar’s affairs brought into jeopardy, they reserved the matter for themselves, awaiting the outcome of the war. Therefore, the Alexandrian delay had the effect that their cause was, as it were, corrected, that their guilt was diminished, that their sin became lighter, provided they did nothing that would more gravely offend the Pompeians who are renewing the war in Africa. And just as the Alexandrian war helped their cause, so it ruined mine. For the less favorable Caesar’s fortune is, the more I am criticized, who was in a hurry to come to Italy, the cause of the Republic having been despaired of. BY THESE: By the Caesarians. 180:

WITHOUT DOUBT: Do not doubt, for the truth of these things offends me. 180:

ABOUT THESE LETTERS: Which were delivered to me by Caesar; you wish me to write, so that he, when he hears that Caesar is not angry with me, might take joy from this comfort of mine. But, he says, I am not doing this: first, because those letters do not delight me, since they are both written meagerly and have suspicions of not being from Caesar; then, because I understand from a friend’s letter that Quintus himself is not well-disposed toward me. THAT HE IS WRITING TO YOU: Quintus. 180:

IF YOU THINK IT IS RIGHT, AND THAT IT CAN BE UNDERTAKEN BY YOU: A double consideration; whether it is right that Terentia be advised about the will at all; and whether she ought to be advised by Atticus. For that, "If you think it can be undertaken by you," as I believe, this is what it means: if you seem to be so intimate with Terentia that you can deal with her about the will. CAMILLUS: For he, no less than Pomponius, was taking care of Cicero’s affairs and business, as the fourteenth book of the letters which are called "Familiares" shows on pages 236 and 238; and of these, which are written to Atticus, book V, page 72, and book VI, page 88. ABOUT THE WILL: Cicero desired that a will be made by Terentia, so that she, when she settled her own affairs, might satisfy those to whom she owed money. For it seemed less honorable to Cicero that Terentia, his wife, should be in debt.

<margin>Koers na 't Eyland Cocles.</margin>
Na dese verrigtinge / seylde men na 't Eyland Canon of Cocles, om aldaar de Scheepen te kalefateren / en sig van alle leef-togt te versorgen. Midlerwijl men hier mede besig was / sagen wij een Schip in Zee / koers na de Philippijnse Eylanden nemende; dit jaagde men na / en ingehaalt hebbende / roofden men de Koop-mans waaren daar uyt / en lieten het Schip vaaren.

<margin>Draak beraad sig om na 't Vaderland te vertrekken.</margin>
Als Draak nu sijne verrigting / dus verre gelukt sag / en herdenkende sijne gevaaren en ongemakken des togts / dat hij nu de geweldenaarpen en vermeetelheden / die sijn Koningin / van den Spaansen Koning geleeden had / genoegsaam gewroken had; so beraade hij sig / werwaarts hij sijn koers / wederom na Engeland wenden sou. Maar dewijl hij besorgt was / dat de Spanjaarden hem aller wegen souden soeken t' onderscheppen / en vermits de groote gevaaren / die hij bereyds door den storm / buyten de Straat Magellaan, aan de Zuyd-zijde / had uytgestaan / hem deden afschrikken / so nam hij eyndelijk sijn besluyt / om het na de Molukse Eylanden te wenden / houdende der Portugeesen koers / om het te Cabo de Bonesperance aan te setten. 

<margin>Wend het na de Molukse Eylanden.</margin>
Maar toen men te groote stilte had / wierden wij genoodsaakt / de Spaanse koers / Noordelijker op te stevenen / van waar wij nog ten minsten / 600 mijlen te seylen hadden. Hier over versleeten wij den tijd / van den sestienden April / tot den derden Juny. Den vijfden der selve / quamen wij ten Noorden op 42 Graaden / vonden 't daar so koud / dat het naauwlijks te lijden was / wierden derhalven genoodsaakt Land te soeken.

another ship along the way / provided with ship's equipment. Having seized this / one found in it 81 pounds of gold / along with a golden crucifix / set with a beautiful emerald / which, along with some of the ship's stores / was taken from it / as much as was needed.

<margin>Conquer a ship with good booty.</margin>
Thus we kept following the ship *Cacafuego* / which was overtaken at Cape Francisco / about 150 miles from Panama. Having seized this / we robbed it of many jewels and precious stones / along with 13 chests full of reals / 80 pounds of gold / and 13 tons of silver.

<margin>Overtake a richly loaded ship at C. Francisco. Great treasure robbed from it.</margin>
Likewise, the captain / named Don Francisco / was compelled to present his two gilded drinking cups / one to Drake / and the other / to his treasurer. When the commander Drake now wanted to leave this ship / the young man of the Spanish captain addressed him thus: Lord Captain / our ship formerly called *Cacafuego* or Fire-spitter / may now well be called *Cacaplata* or Silver-spitter / and yours henceforth be called *Cacafuego*. Which saying was pleasant for Drake and his men to hear.

Further, taking our course west by north / we discovered a ship / whose cargo consisted of linen / silk / and Chinese porcelain; from this we took what we liked. Its captain, being a Spanish nobleman / wore a gold falcon / decorated with a large emerald / on his chest: this he had to leave behind, along with his helmsman.

<margin>Sail to Guatulca.</margin>
Subsequently, we sailed to Guatulca / and found the judge there along with three officials / busy exercising justice / over some Moors <note>Likely referring to African slaves or people of North African descent.</note> / who had intended / to set this place on fire. We took these captive on board / and we forced the judge to write / that the inhabitants should vacate the village / until we had provided ourselves with fresh water.

<margin>Plunder a village.</margin>
As this was now done / we plundered the same / and found-

found in a house a small barrel of Reals <note>Spanish currency; pieces of eight.</note>; meanwhile, they also robbed a fleeing Spanish nobleman of a gold chain and some jewels.

<margin>Course to the Island Cocles.</margin>
After this operation, we sailed to the Island Canon or Cocles, to caulk the ships there and to provide ourselves with all necessities. While we were busy with this, we saw a ship at sea taking a course toward the Philippine Islands; we chased it, and having caught it, we robbed the merchant goods from it and let the ship go.

<margin>Drake considers departing for the Fatherland.</margin>
When Drake saw his operation had succeeded this far, and thinking back on his dangers and the inconveniences of the journey, and that he had sufficiently avenged the violence and insolence that his Queen had suffered from the Spanish King, he deliberated on which way he should turn his course back to England. But because he was worried that the Spaniards would try to intercept him everywhere, and because the great dangers he had already endured from the storm outside the Strait of Magellan on the south side deterred him, he finally took the decision to turn toward the Moluccan Islands, keeping the Portuguese course to set it via the Cape of Good Hope.

<margin>Turn toward the Moluccan Islands.</margin>
But when we had too much calm, we were forced to steer the Spanish course more northerly, from where we still had at least 600 miles to sail. We spent the time here from the sixteenth of April until the third of June. On the fifth of the same month, we arrived at 42 degrees north latitude, found it so cold there that it was barely endurable, and were therefore forced to seek land.

<margin>Arrive at 42 degrees, and endure great cold.</margin>
We then discovered low-lying land, but as it was entirely covered with snow, we did not land there. We sailed further to 38 degrees and found a beautiful harbor where we anchored.

## PROBLEM V.

### GIVEN TWO SIDES IN A PHONIC TRIANGLE, TO FIND THE THIRD by the extraction of the square root.

First, in the phonic triangle **A D B**, let the side **A B** (the direct path) be given as 25 paces, and let the line **A C** (the distance of the phonic center from the <term>cathetus phonicus: the vertical line or perpendicular used in acoustic geometry</term>) be 8 paces; you will find the third side **A D** in this way. Let the given sides be multiplied by themselves [squared], and from the sum of the two sides joined together, let the square root be extracted; and you will have the sought-after line **A D** by the 47th proposition <note>The OCR reads "4. lib. 1," but the text describes the Pythagorean theorem, which is Proposition 47 of Book 1 of Euclid's Elements.</note> of Book 1 of Euclid's *Elements*.

Secondly, let the sides **B D** and **A D** be known; you will find the third side **A B** if you subtract the square of line **D B** from the square of the whole **A D**. For the root of the remaining square will give the sought-after line **A B**. Thirdly, let two sides **A B** and **A D** be given; you will find the third, **B D**, in this way. Subtract the square of **A B** from the square of **A D**, and the root of the remaining square will give the sought-after line **B D**.

# SECTION III.
## THE CONSTRUCTION OF ACOUSTIC TUBES AND TRUMPETS.

->*******************<-

### *PREFACE.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'A'. The interior of the letter contains a landscape scene featuring a classical building with a dome or rounded roof, set among trees and rolling hills under a sky with light clouds.</image-desc>

We call those "acoustic instruments" by which we represent remote sounds to the ears—sounds otherwise hidden from the sense of hearing. Just as with optical instruments <note>original: "opticis instrumentis"</note> we bring remote objects that are entirely inaccessible to the sense of sight before the eyes as if they were nearby and close (about which we have treated extensively in the last book of the *Great Art of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Arte magna Lucis & Umbræ"</note>), so with acoustic instruments, sounds are narrowed and channeled <note>original: "coarctatos"</note> within organs manufactured with wondrous industry and skill according to nature’s own model.

This section contains, *First*, the construction of Halls, Private Rooms, and Porticos disposed with such ingenuity that within them, at a certain and determined point, Princes <note>referring to rulers or patrons</note> may be able to hear every utterance of words, no matter how whispered. *Second*, it covers the construction of acoustic instruments for the use of the hard of hearing <note>original: "surdastrorum"</note>, together with *Acoustic Cryptology* <note>The study of secret communication using sound</note>, or the hidden communication of mutual concepts through sounds, and other new and most secret inventions. But before we approach the matter, we have thought it necessary to set forth the properties and experiments of the Tubes and Trumpets themselves, which we shall use in the architecture of the work.

<summary>This page concludes the geometric rules for sound reflection and introduces Section III, which focuses on the practical invention of acoustic devices like speaking tubes and "secret" rooms for eavesdropping. The author compares these tools to the telescope, suggesting that sound can be "magnified" and directed just like light.</summary>

<meta>PROLÉGOMÈNES d'Ebn-Khaldoun.</meta>

# A chapter on how, when the nature of kingship is established through the exclusivity of glory and the attainment of luxury and tranquility, the dynasty approaches senescence.

Its clarification comes from several aspects. The first is that kingship necessitates exclusivity in glory, as we have mentioned. So long as glory is shared among the tribal group and their pursuit of it is unified, their ambitions in overcoming others and defending their territory are equal in their soaring power and strength, and their goal is collective dignity. They find death sweet in the building of their glory, and they prefer destruction over its corruption. But when one of them becomes the sole possessor of this glory, he breaks their staffs <note>a metaphor for curbing their power</note>, restrains their mounts, and appropriates wealth for himself to their exclusion. Consequently, they become lazy in seeking dignity <note>original: "الغزو" (raiding/striving) is suggested in the manuscript alternatives, which aligns with the context of losing their warrior spirit</note>, their resolve weakens, and they resign themselves to humiliation and enslavement. The second generation is then raised upon this, assuming that the support they receive is merely payment from the Sultan for their protection and compliance; nothing else occurs to their minds. It is rare for one to hire himself out for danger. This results in weakness in the state, a reduction in striking power, and the arrival of vulnerability and senescence due to the corruption of the <term>asabiyyah</term> <gloss>social cohesion</gloss> through the departure of courage from its people. The second aspect is that the nature of kingship necessitates luxury, as we have previously stated. Thus, their customs multiply, their expenses exceed their allowances, and their income does not meet their outlays. The poor among them perish, and the one living in luxury exhausts his allowance on his luxuries. Then this increases in their later generations until all allowances fall short of luxury and its customs, and need touches them. Their kings then demand that they restrict their expenditures to raiding and warfare, but they find no excuse for it. Consequently, the kings impose punishments upon them and extract what is in the hands of many of them, either to keep it for themselves or to favor their children and the clients of their state. They weaken because of that, and the ruler of the state weakens by their weakness. Furthermore, when luxury increases in the state and their allowances become insufficient for their needs and expenses, the ruler of the state, who is the Sultan, needs to increase their stipends so as to bridge their gaps and remove their ailments. Yet tax revenue has a known limit that does not increase or decrease. If it increases through newly invented taxes, its amount after the increase is still restricted. When tax revenue is distributed among the stipends, which have increased for each individual due to their luxury and high expenses, the number of the garrison decreases compared to what it was before the increase in stipends. Then luxury grows, and the amounts of stipends increase because of it, so the number of the garrison decreases, then a third and fourth time, until the army returns to the smallest possible numbers. Thus the garrison weakens, the strength of the state falls, and the neighboring states or the tribes and rebels under its control grow bold against it. God then permits the annihilation He has written for His creation. Moreover, luxury is corrupting to character due to the evil and foolishness it engenders in the soul and its customs, as will come in the chapter on civilization. The qualities of goodness that were a sign and proof of kingship depart from them, and they are characterized by the opposite—the qualities of evil. This becomes a sign of decline and extinction, as God has ordained in His creation. The state begins to experience the seeds of rot, its conditions falter, and it is afflicted with chronic diseases of senescence until it is finished off. The third aspect is that the nature of kingship necessitates tranquility, as we have mentioned. When they take tranquility and rest as a habit and custom, it becomes a nature and instinct for them, as is the case with all customs and becoming accustomed to them. Their succeeding generations are raised in the civilization of living and the cradle of luxury and tranquility. The nature of wildness changes, and they forget the customs of <term>badawah</term> <gloss>nomadic/desert life</gloss> through which kingship was achieved—such as intensity of spirit, the habit of predation, riding the desert, and navigating the wilderness. There is no difference between them and the commoners of the city except in culture and appearance. Their protection weakens, their courage departs, their striking power is harvested, and the burden of that returns upon the state in the garments of senescence it wears. They continue to be colored by the customs of luxury, civilization, stillness, tranquility, and soft manners in all their conditions, submerging themselves therein. In doing so, they distance themselves from nomadic life and roughness, shedding them little by little.

<meta>continues from previous page: ury suffers due to the gap between his lifestyle and his limited means</meta> in their later generations. Eventually, all the stipends are insufficient to cover the demands of luxury and its associated habits. Need touches them, and their kings demand that they restrict their expenditures to raids and wars. They find no way to escape this, so the kings impose punishments upon them and seize what is in their hands. They reserve these resources for themselves, or they bestow them upon their children and the clients of their state. Consequently, the people become too weak to maintain their own affairs, and the ruler of the state becomes weak as they weaken.

Furthermore, when luxury increases within the state and the stipends provided to the troops fall short of their needs and expenses, the ruler of the state, who is the Sultan, finds it necessary to increase their stipends to remedy their defects and remove their grievances. However, the amount of tax collection is fixed; it neither increases nor decreases. Even if it is increased through the introduction of new levies, the amount remains limited after that increase. When the total tax collection is distributed among the stipends, and an increase has occurred for every individual due to the escalation of their luxury and the abundance of their expenses, the number of the garrison necessarily decreases compared to what it was before the stipends were increased. Then, luxury grows, and the amounts of the stipends increase further for that reason, so the number of the garrison decreases a third and fourth time. This continues until the army returns to the smallest possible numbers. The garrison weakens as a result, the strength of the state falls, and neighboring states or the tribal groups <note>original: "العصايب" (asabiyyat/tribal factions)</note> and rebels under its control grow bold against it. God then permits the extinction that He has decreed for His creation.

Moreover, luxury is corrupting to character through what it produces.

<note>Footnote 1: Manuscript A and B read: العصبيات (tribal factions).</note>

<summary>Ibn Khaldun explains how the growth of luxury forces rulers to increase stipends, which inevitably reduces the size of the army and weakens the state's defenses, leading to eventual collapse.</summary>

## ON MARK

<margin>The Apostles used this word several times: it is derived from <term>praetore</term> <gloss>praetor</gloss>, which itself takes its name from <term>prae</term> <gloss>before</gloss> and <term>eundo</term> <gloss>going</gloss>. Among the Romans, the <term>praitōr</term> is called <term>stratēgos</term> <gloss>general</gloss>, as Suidas indicates, under whom are the military tribunes. The Praetorium is the tent of the praetor, and the house where he pronounces judgment. But the houses of kings, princes, and the highest magistrates are also called praetoria; as are the more magnificent buildings on country estates.</margin>

<term>Prasiai</term>.

Suidas interprets <term>prasion</term> as <term>lachanon</term> <gloss>vegetable/herb</gloss>. Likewise, <term>prasiai</term> are <gloss>the vegetable beds in a garden</gloss>. These are areas, or little plots, or mounds in gardens, in which vegetables and other garden plants are sown. By <term>catachresis</term> <gloss>misuse of a term</gloss>, unless I am mistaken, the grassy areas of meadows are meant here.

<term>prasiai prasiai</term> <gloss>in part</gloss>. Reference: 6.f. Erasmus: <gloss>They collapsed in garden-beds</gloss>, or <gloss>they reclined divided into greenery in groups of hundreds and fifties</gloss>. Valla reads, <gloss>In parts</gloss>, and corrects it to <gloss>in bundles</gloss>.

<term>Prattō</term> <gloss>I sell</gloss>.

<term>prathōsi</term> <gloss>to be sold</gloss>. Reference: 14.a.

<term>Presbys</term> <gloss>old man</gloss>.

It is also a title for those who excel not only in age, but also in wisdom, dignity, and power. Just as among the Greeks <term>presbys</term> is used for an <gloss>ambassador</gloss>; and <term>presbeion</term> is <gloss>dignity</gloss>, especially that of old age. Among the Romans they are called <term>senatores</term> <gloss>senators</gloss>, among the Hebrews <term>zekenim</term> <gloss>elders</gloss>.

<term>presbyteroi</term> <gloss>elders</gloss>. Reference: 11.d, 14.f. Formerly, bishops and elders, or presbyters, were the same. And Peter indeed calls himself a <gloss>fellow-elder</gloss>.

<term>presbyterōn</term> <gloss>the tradition of the elders</gloss>. Reference: 7.a, b. To the elders. Reference: 8.d, 14.e, 15.a.

<term>Prin</term> <gloss>before</gloss>.

षोडशाङ्गुलविस्तीर्णमुत्सेधे सर्पपाश्रयः ।
आयसं दृढमेतत्तत्तु विधयेत्सामजसन्निभम् ॥ ४४ ॥
दृढन्येतानि बधीयात्तस्तम्भशाखाद्वयान्तरे ।
त्रिवारमितनैव नरवक्षःसमुन्नतौ ॥ ४५ ॥
भित्वा तानि विनिर्गत्य निर्भिद्याग्रेण भूतळम् ।
यथावत्तिष्ठते बाणस्तथाविध्येत्क्रियायुतः ॥ ४६ ॥
अङ्गुष्ठभागपार्श्वे तु तर्जन्या सङ्गते शरे ।
चापमुष्टौ समे पुङ्खे समसन्धानमुच्यते ॥ ४७ ॥
समसन्धे रथे ज्यायामधःसन्धानकं भवेत् ।
तस्मादेवेर्ध्वतः सन्धादूर्ध्वसन्धानमिष्यते ॥ ४८ ॥
ऊर्ध्वदूरस्थिते लक्ष्ये नीचसन्धानसङ्गतिः ।
नीचलक्ष्ये तथा चोर्ध्वं समलक्ष्ये समं भवेत् ॥ ४९ ॥
षोडशाङ्गुलवृत्तं तु स्थूलं लक्ष्यमुदाहृतम् ।
अङ्गुलद्वितयं सूक्ष्मं पञ्चाङ्गुलशिरोरुहम् ॥ ५० ॥
शब्देनानुमितं लक्ष्यं परापरमुदाहृतम् ।
एवं पञ्चविधं लक्ष्यं दर्शयेत्तस्य वेधने ॥ ५१ ॥
तिर्यग्धावस्तथा गच्छन्भ्राम्यंश्चैव तथोत्पतन् ।
आकाशे भूतले तोये तेषां स्थानमुदाहृतम् ॥ ५२ ॥
उत्तमं द्विशतं प्रोक्तं शतं सार्धं तु मध्यमम् ।
विंशं शतं कनिष्ठं स्याद्दूरे धन्वन्तरे क्षितौ ॥ ५३ ॥
धर्षयेदुत्तमं दूरं चतुर्भिः सायकैः शनैः ।
समपत्रैः स्थूलसूक्ष्मैः निःपत्रैश्चैव नागरैः ॥ ५४ ॥
पाते त्वेकं करे त्वेकं गगने पञ्चसायकान् ।
दर्शयेल्लौघवत्वेवं विधयेल्लक्ष्यं महीपतिः ॥ ५५ ॥

कथितः सोमभूपेन जामदग्न्यमतानुगः ॥ ३२ ॥

षोडशदङ्गुलां भस्त्रां छागमांसेन पूरयेत् ।
एतन्मांसं दृढं विधेय्र्गजकायप्रमाणकम् ॥ ३३ ॥

गैजरा(जा)श्वखुराघातैः समन्तात्परिशोषित(तम्) ।
दृढमश्वखुरं नाम मध्ये मातङ्गमन(ज)कम् ॥ ३४ ॥

विषाणं सप्तवर्षस्य महिषस्य प्रगृह्य च ।
मूलामवर्जितं मध्ये द्विपकायसमं दृढम् ॥ ३५ ॥

सूत्रं पञ्चाङ्गुलोत्सेधं तिर्यग्भा(या)मकल्पितम् ।
निबिडं चर्मणा बद्धं विधेयत्करिसमं दृढम् ॥ ३६ ॥

कूर्मपृष्ठकपालं तु हस्तविस्तारवर्तुलम् ।
विधेयदस्थि दृढं नाम कुञ्जराङ्गप्रमाणकम् ॥ ३७ ॥

षोडशदङ्गुलं स्थौल्याद्वाल्कजङ्घ(जाङ्गल) पिण्डितम् ।
रज्जुभिर्वेष्टितं विधेयदिभगात्रसमं दृढम् ॥ ३८ ॥

अङ्गुलं दारुसारं तु षोडशाङ्गुलविस्तृतम् ।
इदं दारु दृढं विधेयन्तिदेहसमं नृपः ॥ ३९ ॥

भ्रमत्कुलालचक्रस्थं मृदः पिण्डं नवाङ्गुलम् ।
दृढं प्रवाह(विहि)तं विधेयत्समं नागेन चर्मणा ॥ ४० ॥

कार्पासनिर्मितं पुञ्जमुत्सेधेन षडङ्गुलम् ।
चर्मनद्धं दृढं विधेयत्सिन्धुराङ्गसमं नृपः ॥ ४१ ॥

करीषधान्यपांसूनां पृथक्पर्णं तु कर्कट(श)म् ।
अष्टाङ्गुलं दृढं विधेय्र्दारणाङ्गसमं नृपः ॥ ४२ ॥

द्वाङ्गुलं मांसवर्णां च षोडशाङ्गुलविस्तृताम् ।
शिलां विधेयदृढं सम्यक् स्तम्भेरसमां नृपः ॥ ४३ ॥

# Mānasollāsa | 166
### [Book 4]

Thus, the order of all sturdy targets for elephants, horses, and men has been told by King Someshvara, following the tradition of Jamadagni. <note>verse 135</note>

One should fill a sixteen-finger bag with goat meat. This meat should be made firm and equal to the measure of an elephant's body. <note>verse 136</note>

Dried thoroughly from the kicks of elephant and horse hooves, this firm target is called the <term>aśvakhura</term> <gloss>horse-hoof</gloss>, representing the middle of an elephant. <note>verse 137</note>

Taking the horn of a seven-year-old buffalo, fixed at the base, it is firm and equal to the body of an elephant. <note>verse 138</note>

A string five fingers high, arranged sideways, tightly bound with leather, should be made firm and equal to an elephant. <note>verse 139</note>

A tortoise-shell, round and a hand wide, should be made into a firm bone-target, equal to the measure of an elephant's limb. <note>verse 140</note>

Sixteen fingers thick, made of forest-products, wrapped with ropes, it should be made firm like the body of an elephant. <note>verse 141</note>

A wooden target, sixteen fingers wide, should be made firm and equal to the elephant's body, O King. <note>verse 142</note>

A nine-finger clay-ball on a spinning potter's wheel, made firm and bound with elephant hide, should be prepared. <note>verse 143</note>

A cotton cluster, six fingers high, bound with leather, should be made firm like an elephant's body, O King. <note>verse 144</note>

Dried cow-dung, grain, and dust, separately filled in leather, eight fingers high, should be made firm like the body of an elephant. <note>verse 145</note>

A stone, two fingers thick and sixteen fingers wide, the color of meat, should be made firm and equal to a pillar, O King. <note>verse 146</note>

# Mānasollāsa | 167
### [Book 4]

An iron target, sixteen fingers wide and of equal height, should be made to resemble an elephant, and one should practice upon it. <note>verse 44</note>

One should firmly tie these <note>targets</note> between two branches of a pillar, at the height of a man's chest, three times over. <note>verse 45</note>

Having pierced them and passed through, and then having penetrated the ground at the end, one should shoot in such a way that the arrow remains standing properly, while being skilled in the technique. <note>verse 46</note>

When the arrow is held by the thumb and the side of the index finger, and the bow is held in the fist, with the nock properly placed, it is called <term>samasandhāna</term> <gloss>even-joining</gloss>. <note>verse 47</note>

In <term>samasandhāna</term> <gloss>even-joining</gloss>, the release from the bowstring should be from below. Therefore, joining from above is known as <term>ūrdhvasandhāna</term> <gloss>upward-joining</gloss>. <note>verse 48</note>

When the target is far above, one should use the lower joining <note>technique</note>; for a low target, one uses the upper <note>joining</note>; for an even target, the even <note>joining</note> should be used. <note>verse 49</note>

A target sixteen fingers in circumference is called a thick target. A subtle one is two fingers <note>thick</note>, with a five-finger head. <note>verse 50</note>

A target inferred by sound is called supreme and secondary. Thus, five types of targets should be demonstrated in their piercing. <note>verse 51</note>

Moving sideways, moving forward, spinning, or leaping; their locations are said to be in the sky, on the ground, or in water. <note>verse 52</note>

Two hundred <note>fingers distance</note> is said to be excellent; one hundred and fifty is medium; one hundred and twenty is the lowest distance on the ground for an archer. <note>verse 53</note>

One should strike the excellent distance slowly with four arrows, which are even-feathered, thick or thin, or featherless and nimble. <note>verse 54</note>

The King should demonstrate the lightness of hand by shooting one arrow at a falling target, one at a hand-held one, and five at one in the sky, thus executing the target practice. <note>verse 55</note>

1 ‘Where stands yon sage, towards [facing] the sun’s orb, immovable as the trunk-of-a-tree, (his) body half-buried in an ant-hill, with (his) breast closely-encircled by a snake’s-skin, round the throat excessively pinched by a necklace (formed) of the tendril of a withered creeper, wearing a circular-mass-of-matted-hair enveloping (his) shoulders (and) filled with bird’s-nests.’ *Valmīkārdha*, &c., so read K. and the Mackenzie MS.; the other Deva-n., *valmīkāgra*. *Valmīka* (=*krimi-kṛita-mṛittikācaya*) is the mound of earth thrown up by the large ants of India. He is here said to be one of the Prajāpatis, or fathers of all created things, who were Brahmā's sons, created by him to supply the universe with inhabitants, and who, after fulfilling their mission, retired from the world to practise penance and prepare for death. The Vāyu-purāṇa certainly reckons Kaśyapa, with his father-in-law Daksha and other sages, among the Prajāpatis, but he does not belong to the seven original Prajāpatis of whom his father Marīci is one, nor to the ten enumerated by Manu (i. 35). Of the thirteen daughters of Daksha married to Kaśyapa, the eldest, and his favourite wife, was the Aditi introduced here, from whom were born the gods and particularly the twelve Ādityas, the several representatives of the sun in the twelve months of the year. From Diti, Danu, and others of the remaining twelve, came the Asuras or demons; and, from Vinatā, Aruṇa, 'the Dawn' (see p. 142, n. 3), and Garuḍa, 'the vehicle of Viṣṇu and king of birds.' Where stands yon sage, facing the sun’s orb, immovable as the trunk of a tree, his body half-buried in an ant-hill, his breast closely encircled by a snake’s skin, his throat excessively pinched by a necklace formed of the tendril of a withered creeper, wearing a circular mass of matted hair enveloping his shoulders and filled with birds' nests. <term>Valmīka</term> <gloss>the mound of earth thrown up by large ants</gloss> is the mound. <meta>This page continues the legal definition of heresy, following a discussion on fugitives from penance. It lists specific doctrinal errors and behaviors that classify an individual as a heretic according to Canon Law, referencing various decretals and legal commentaries.</meta>

# THE LANTERN
<header>LUCERNA</header>

...follows, or dogmatizes. <note>original: "sequitur, vel dogmatizat." Refers to the definition of a heretic as one who follows or invents false doctrines.</note> Question 24, point 3, in the chapter *Inter haeresim* and the chapter *Haereticus*.

**4** He is also called a heretic who understands Holy Scripture in a way other than the Holy Spirit requires. <note>Citing the chapter *Haeresis* in the same question; this implies that any interpretation of the Bible that contradicts the Church's official stance is considered heretical.</note>

**5** He is also a heretic who, concerning the sacraments of the Church or concerning confession, feels differently than what the Roman Church holds and observes. <note>Citing the chapter *Ad abolendam*, a foundational 1184 decree by Pope Lucius III against heretics.</note>

**6** He is also called a heretic who says or holds that simple fornication <note>Sexual intercourse between two unmarried people.</note> or any other carnal act outside of marriage is not a mortal sin, as is evident in the final *Clementine* decree <note>The *Clementinae* were a collection of canon laws published by Pope Clement V in the early 14th century.</note> concerning heretics, verse 7, and the commentary there on the word "is not."

**7** He is also a heretic who stubbornly says or holds that usury <note>The practice of lending money at interest, which was strictly forbidden by the medieval Church.</note> is not a mortal sin, as is evident in the single *Clementine* decree concerning usury, at the end.

**8** By analogy, he is called a heretic who not only holds that usury and carnal acts outside marriage are not sins, but also holds that other things prohibited by the Church, or by Holy Scripture, are not sins: because regarding similar cases, the judgment ought to be the same. <note>Citing the chapter *Inter caeteras* regarding rescripts, with the attached commentary.</note>

**9** It is also a condemned heresy to say that the [Mosaic] Law should be observed along with the Gospel, and circumcision along with baptism. <note>This refers to "Judaizing" heresies, where Christians attempted to maintain Jewish ritual laws. Citing the Code of Justinian and the chapter *Maiores* on baptism.</note> Joannes Andreae and Gemignano <note>Two influential legal commentators.</note> discuss this in the chapter *Contra Christianos* in the sixth book of the Decretals.

**10** One who does not receive communion every single year is a heretic. <note>Felinus Sandeus notes this in his commentary. This refers to the "Easter Duty," the minimum requirement for a Catholic to receive the Eucharist once a year during the Easter season.</note>

**11** He is also called a heretic who cuts himself off from the unity of the Church. <note>Defining schism (splitting from the Church hierarchy) as a form of heresy. Question 7, point 1, chapter *Denique*.</note>

**12** An apostate from the faith is a heretic, as you have above under the word "apostate" throughout.

**13** He is also a heretic who, around the altars of idols, utters wicked prayers, offers sacrifices, consults demons, or receives their responses; or who associates heretics with himself for the purpose of practicing divination; or who does the aforementioned things using the body or blood of Christ, or in divinations so that he may receive answers; or who re-baptizes a child, and similar things. <note>This entry links sorcery and sacrilege directly to heresy. Using the consecrated Host (the Body of Christ) for magic was viewed not just as a sin, but as a denial of the faith.</note> This is stated in the commentary on the word "they would know," in the chapter *Accusatus* in the sixth book.

**14** He is also a heretic who says, defends, or stubbornly holds that the rational or intellectual soul is not the form of the human body in and of itself and essentially. <note>This is a highly technical theological point from the Council of Vienne (1311-12). It defines the human being as a single substance of body and soul, opposing certain philosophical views that suggested the soul was merely "using" the body.</note>

**15** There are, furthermore, eight errors condemned as heretical belonging to certain people who devised them under a certain pretense of sanctity and perfection; these are listed and condemned in the third *Clementine* decree concerning heretics. <note>This refers to the "Heresy of the Free Spirit" or the Beghards and Beguines, who were accused of believing that a person could reach a state of perfection on earth where they could no longer sin.</note>

**16** He who says and holds that Christ and the Apostles held nothing in com- <note>The text cuts off here. This refers to the "Poverty of Christ" controversy, specifically the debate over whether Christ and the Apostles owned property individually or even in common.</note>

<meta>catchword: mon (completing "communi" or "common")</meta>

<summary>This page provides a numbered list of legal definitions for heresy, covering a wide range of offenses from theological errors regarding the soul and scripture to social sins like usury and fornication, and ritual crimes like sorcery and rebaptism.</summary>
<keywords>heresy definitions, usury, fornication, sacraments, sorcery, rational soul, canon law, Clementinae, apostasy, divination</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the legal and theological definitions of heresy, specifically addressing the poverty of Christ, the infusion of grace in infants, and the psychological requirements for an individual to be formally classified as a heretic.</meta>

# OF THE INQUISITORS.
<header>INQUISITORUM.</header>

...[common] even as to right and ownership, is a heretic, as is clear from the *Extravagant* <note>A collection of canon laws that circulated "outside" the main official codifications like the Decretals.</note> of John XXII, which begins: *Cum inter nonnullos* <note>original: "Since among several." This refers to a famous 1323 decree regarding the poverty of Christ.</note>.

<margin>17</margin> The opinion which holds that baptized infants are not infused with virtues and informing grace <note>term: <term>Informing grace</term> refers to the theological concept of "gratia informans," the grace that gives "form" or spiritual life to the soul.</note> as a habit—even if not at that time as to use—is rejected by the Church, indeed condemned, as is clear in the single *Clementine* decree <note>Part of the *Clementinae*, a collection of canon law.</note> regarding the Most Holy Trinity, at the end. Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> also rejects this opinion in the third part, question 69, article 6.

<margin>18</margin> Likewise, to stubbornly assert that Christ and his Apostles, in those things which Holy Scripture testifies they possessed, had no right of use over them, nor had the right to sell or give them away, or to acquire other things from them—since such an assertion concludes that their use and actions in the aforementioned matters were not just—is erroneous and heretical. This is clear through the said *Extravagant* of John XXII, which begins: *Cum inter nonnullos*. <note>This ruling specifically targeted the "Spiritual" Franciscans who argued that Christ and the Apostles owned absolutely nothing, neither individually nor in common.</note>

<margin>19</margin> There are, however, many other heresies or sects of heretics, which Isidore enumerates in the eighth book of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5; they are also placed in Question 24, point 3, in the chapter *Quidam autem haeretici* <note>original: "certain heretics however."</note>.

<margin>20</margin> Many other heresies are found as well, which are collected from the sayings of Blessed Thomas in various places, and are also listed in the table of the Reverend Father Master Peter of Bergamo <note>A 15th-century Dominican scholar who created the *Tabula Aurea*, a massive alphabetical index to the works of Thomas Aquinas.</note>, under the word "heresy." See them there: for whenever anything is said or held stubbornly that is against the determination of the Church regarding those things pertaining to the faith, that is always heretical. This is proven in Question 24, point 1, in the chapter *Haec est fides* [This is the faith], and the final commentary on the chapter *Cum Christus* [Since Christ] regarding heretics, at the end; and the commentary on the word *docuit* [he taught] in the single chapter regarding the Most Holy Trinity in the sixth book. For it belongs to the Church to determine doubts if any should occasionally arise concerning the faith, as is clear in the chapter *Quotiens* [Whenever], Question 24, point 1; regarding baptism, the chapter *Maiores* [The ancestors] at the beginning; regarding the Most Holy Trinity, chapter 2 at the end; and the single *Clementine* decree under the same title, in the section "We therefore." This is supported by Distinction 22, the chapter *Omnes* [All]. Blessed Thomas agrees in the *Second Part of the Second Part*, question 11, article 2, in the response to the third argument. For the Church, in those matters pertaining to the faith, cannot err, as is held and noted in Question 24, point 1, in the chapter *A recta ergo fide* [From the right faith therefore] and the chapter *Memor sum* [I am mindful]. And this is because the Lord prayed for her that her faith might not fail. In the 22nd chapter of Luke, the Lord said: "I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail." This is also placed in Distinction 21, section 1, in the verse *Ego pro te* [I for you].

<margin>21</margin> It must be noted, however, that for someone to be properly called a heretic, four things are required. The first is an error in the intellect, such that one holds a wrong opinion regarding the truth. Thus, if someone were to trample upon the body of Christ <note>The consecrated host or Eucharist.</note>, yet believing it to be the true body of Christ and knowing this act to be evil, but doing it to please the devil, that person would not be called a heretic; for they have no error in the intellect, nor do they hold a wrong opinion regarding the Sacrament of the Altar. <note>This distinguishes the crime of sacrilege or devil-worship from the crime of heresy; heresy requires a doctrinal disagreement, not just bad behavior.</note>
The second requirement is that such an error must concern those things which pertain to the faith, or be against the determination of the Church in those things pertaining to faith and good morals, which are necessary for the attainment of eternal life.

<meta>The catchword "Te" indicates the next page will begin with "Tertium," the third requirement for defining a heretic.</meta>

<summary>This page outlines specific theological errors regarding the poverty of Christ and infant baptism while defining the legal requirements for heresy, emphasizing that heresy requires an intellectual error against Church dogma rather than just sinful or sacrilegious behavior.</summary>
<keywords>heresy, John XXII, poverty of Christ, Thomas Aquinas, Peter of Bergamo, infant baptism, ecclesiastical infallibility, Sacrament of the Altar, canon law, Clementines</keywords>

This part of the early winter, which precedes the winter of the following year of 1597, begins on December 11 of this present year of 1596, early in the morning at 5:33. At this time, the Sun enters the solstitial sign of Capricorn <term>Steinbock</term>, where it causes the shortest day. At this time, the 29th degree of Virgo <term>Jungfr.</term> is in the ascendant. The <term>Medium Coeli</term> <gloss>midheaven</gloss> contains the 25th degree of Virgo, from which Saturn <term>Saturn.</term> has just fallen at the 22nd degree of the same. Mars and Mercury <term>Mercurius</term> occupy the first house: Mars is in the 11th and Mercury in the 16th degree of Sagittarius <term>Schütz</term>, currently in retrograde <term>Retrog.</term> The Sun and Moon <term>Mon</term> run in Capricorn; the Sun is at 0 degrees, 0 minutes, and the Moon is at 23 degrees, 37 minutes. The Sun has a trine <term>Triangel</term> to Jupiter <term>Jovi</term> at 1 degree of Taurus <term>Stier</term> in direct motion. These aspects provide significant content for Saturn in the part of the law.

However, what this and the aforementioned solar eclipse, which still holds a strong influence, indicates for the coming year (God willing) when we begin this part again, shall be described at length. We wish only to mention a little of the weather in conclusion.

But you child of wisdom, listen also to me, and take heed of my teaching and speech, that all the supposed proposals of the sophists are mostly nothing at all, and cannot be spoken from understanding and any certainty, because through inexperience they have laid no foundation, nor learned the right examination in demonstration. For thoughts are duty-free, they fly into the heaven and also into the lowest of the earth, and if experience and clear test do not agree with the thoughts, then the thoughts can miss by far, and stand quite naked in a supposed delusion, as when the speculator must say: I would not have thought that I would not have found my thinking thus correct in the work.

In the time of the emperor Theophilus, Scholasticius the door-keeper was chamberlain, and in the time of Michael, son of Theophilus, the patrician Damian was chamberlain and after him, in the same reign, Basil, the Christ-loving emperor, was chamberlain. In the time of Basil, the Christ-loving sovereign, there was no chamberlain during all his reign. In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Samonas was chamberlain, and after him, in the time of the same emperor, the patrician Constantine. In the time of Alexander the emperor, the patrician Barbatus was chamberlain; and in the time of Constantine, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Constantine, mentioned before in the time of the sovereign Leo, was chamberlain again; and in the time of the sovereign Romanus, the patrician Theophanes; and in the second reign of Constantine, the patrician Basil.

In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving and ever-memorable emperor, lived the late Ktenas, an aged cleric of great wealth, who was precentor of the New Church and was skilled in singing as was no other at that time. This same Ktenas besought the patrician Samonas, who was at that time chamberlain, to intercede for him with the emperor so that he might be made protospatharius and wear the shirt and go in procession to the Lausiacus and take his seat as protospatharius and receive a stipend of one pound, and in respect of this remuneration might give the emperor forty pounds. But the emperor could not bring himself to do this, saying that it was out of his power, and «to the great disgrace of my imperial majesty if a cleric becomes protospatharius». On hearing this from the patrician Samonas, this same Ktenas added to the forty pounds a pair of ear-rings valued at ten pounds, and a silver table with animals on it in gold relief, also valued at ten pounds. And the emperor, besought by the request of the patrician Samonas, the chamberlain, took the forty pounds of gold and the pair of ear-rings and the table with its gold on silver relief work, so that the total gift of the same Ktenas amounted to sixty pounds. Then the emperor made him protospatharius, and he received a stipend on that occasion of one pound. After being honoured with the rank of protospatharius this same Ktenas lived two years and then died; and he received a stipend of one pound for each of the two years.

## 50

It should be known that in the time of the emperor Theophilus, Scholasticius the door-keeper served as chamberlain. In the time of Michael, the son of Theophilus, the patrician Damian served as chamberlain, and after him, in the same reign, Basil, the Christ-loving emperor, served as chamberlain. In the time of Basil, the Christ-loving sovereign, there was no chamberlain throughout his entire reign. In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Samonas served as chamberlain, and after him, in the same emperor's reign, the patrician Constantine served. In the time of the emperor Alexander, the patrician Barbatus served as chamberlain; in the time of Constantine, the Christ-loving sovereign, the aforementioned Constantine, who served under the sovereign Leo, served again as chamberlain; in the time of the sovereign Romanus, the patrician Theophanes served; and in the second reign of Constantine, the patrician Basil served again.

<margin>235</margin> It should be known that in the time of Leo, the Christ-loving and ever-memorable emperor, there was that old man Ktenas, a very wealthy cleric, who was also a <term>domestikos</term> <gloss>official or leader</gloss> at the New Church, and was an expert in singing, such as there was no other at that time. This same Ktenas begged the patrician Samonas, who was chamberlain at that time, to intercede for him with the emperor so that he might become a <term>protospatharios</term> <gloss>first sword-bearer, a high court rank</gloss>, and wear the <term>epikoutzoulon</term> <gloss>a specific cloak or garment of rank</gloss>, and proceed to the Lausiacus <note>A ceremonial hall in the Great Palace of Constantinople</note> and sit as a <term>protospatharios</term> and receive a stipend of one pound, and for such a favor he would give the emperor forty pounds. The emperor, however, would not agree to do this, saying that it was impossible, and stating: "It is a great disgrace to my imperial majesty for a cleric to become a <term>protospatharios</term>." Upon hearing this from the patrician Samonas, the same Ktenas added to the forty pounds a pair of <term>scholarikia</term> <gloss>earrings or jewelry</gloss> valued at ten pounds, and a silver table with gold relief work, also valued at ten pounds. Being swayed by the request of the patrician Samonas, the chamberlain, the emperor accepted the forty pounds of gold, the pair of <term>scholarikia</term>, and the gold-relief silver table, so that the total gift of the said Ktenas amounted to sixty pounds. Then the emperor made him <term>protospatharios</term>, and he received a stipend of one pound at that time. The same Ktenas lived for two years after being honored as <term>protospatharios</term> and then died; he received a stipend of one pound for each of those two years.

<summary>This page records the succession of chamberlains from the reign of Theophilus through Constantine VII and details the purchase of the rank of protospatharios by the cleric Ktenas.</summary>
<keywords>chamberlain, court rank, Ktenas, Samonas, imperial administration, protospatharios, New Church</keywords>

In the time of the emperor Theophilus, Scholasticius the door-keeper was chamberlain, and in the time of Michael, son of Theophilus, the patrician Damian was chamberlain and after him, in the same reign, Basil, the Christ-loving emperor, was chamberlain. In the time of Basil, the Christ-loving sovereign, there was no chamberlain during all his reign. In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Samonas was chamberlain, and after him, in the time of the same emperor, the patrician Constantine. In the time of Alexander the emperor, the patrician Barbatus was chamberlain; and in the time of Constantine, the Christ-loving sovereign, the patrician Constantine, mentioned before in the time of the sovereign Leo, was chamberlain again; and in the time of the sovereign Romanus, the patrician Theophanes; and in the second reign of Constantine, the patrician Basil.

In the time of Leo, the Christ-loving and ever-memorable emperor, lived the late Ktenas, an aged cleric of great wealth, who was precentor of the New Church and was skilled in singing as was no other at that time. This same Ktenas besought the patrician Samonas, who was at that time chamberlain, to intercede for him with the emperor so that he might be made <term>protospatharius</term> <gloss>first sword-bearer</gloss> and wear the shirt <note>referring to the ceremonial garment associated with the rank</note> and go in procession to the Lausiacus and take his seat as <term>protospatharius</term> and receive a stipend of one pound, and in respect of this remuneration might give the emperor forty pounds. But the emperor could not bring himself to do this, saying that it was out of his power, and «to the great disgrace of my imperial majesty if a cleric becomes <term>protospatharius</term>». On hearing this from the patrician Samonas, this same Ktenas added to the forty pounds a pair of ear-rings valued at ten pounds, and a silver table with animals on it in gold relief, also valued at ten pounds. And the emperor, besought by the request of the patrician Samonas, the chamberlain, took the forty pounds of gold and the pair of ear-rings and the table with its gold on silver relief work, so that the total gift of the same Ktenas amounted to sixty pounds. Then the emperor made him <term>protospatharius</term>, and he received a stipend on that occasion of one pound. After being honoured with the rank of <term>protospatharius</term> this same Ktenas lived two years and then died; and he received a stipend of one pound for each of the two years.

<summary>This page lists the imperial chamberlains across several reigns and describes the incident where the cleric Ktenas paid a significant sum to secure the court rank of protospatharius.</summary>

མཐའ་ཡས་པའོ༎བཅོམ་ལྡོན་འདས་ཀྱི་སུ་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་ཤིན་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ༎གསོལ་པ།བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་བདག་ཀུན་ཏུ་
མཐའ་ཡས་པས་མྱི་དམྱིགས་པ་སྟོང་བྱ་ཉིད་ཀུན་ཏུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ལེགས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ་ཀྱེ།མཐའ་ལས་འདེས་པ་སྟོང་
པ་ཉིད་དང་ཐོག་མ་དང་ཐ་མ་མྱེད་པ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རེ༎གསོལ་པ།བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་ཀུན་ཏུ་མཐའི་ཡས་པའི་སླད་དུ་དངོས་པོ་མྱང་པ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀུན་ཏུ་
མཐའ་ཡས་པའོ༎བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིསོ་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ་
རབ་འབྱོར་ཤིན་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པོའི་ཕྱིར་རོ༎གསོལ་པ།བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདིས་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་བདག་



མཐའ་ལས་འདས་པ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དང་ཐོག་མ་དང་ཐ་མ་མྱེད་པ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རོ༎གསོལ་བྱ༎བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་ཀུན་ཏུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པའི་སླད་དུ་ཟན་པ་ཉེ་བར་
གཞག་པ་ཀུན་ཏུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པའོ༎བཅོམ་ལྡན་འོདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ།རབ་འབྱོར་ཤིན་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ༎གསོལ་པ།བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཅིའི་
སླད་དུ་བདག་ཀུན་ཏུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པས།དྲན་པཱ་ཉེ་བར་གཞག་པ་ཀུན་ཏུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་རྣོམ་པར་དག་པ་ལགས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ།མཐའ་ལས་
འདས་པ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དང་ཐོག་མ་དང་ཐ་མ་མྱེད་པ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རོ༎གསོལ་པྲ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་ཀུན་ཏུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པའི་སླད་དུ་ཡང་དག་པར་སྤོང་བ་ཀུན་
ཏུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པའོ༎བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལོ་པ།རབ་འབྱོར་ཤིན་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ༎གསོལ་པ།བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་བདག་ཀུན་ཏུ་
མཐའ་ཡས་པས་ཡང་དག་པར་སྤྲོང་བ་ཀུན་ཏུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་ལགས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འོངས་ཀྱིས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ།མཐའི་ལས་འདས་པ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དེང་
ཐོག་མ་དང་ཐ་མ་མྱེད་པ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་རོ༎གསོལ་པ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་ཀུན་ཏུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པའི་སླད་དུ་རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི་རྐང་པ་ཀུན་ཏུ་མཐའ་ཡས་པའོ༎



༄
