<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
because of the <term>emptiness of that which has passed beyond limits</term> <gloss>atyanta-śūnyatā</gloss> and the <term>emptiness of that which has no beginning or end</term> <gloss>anavarāgra-śūnyatā</gloss>.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, because the self is entirely infinite, the <term>emptiness of nature</term> <gloss>prakṛti-śūnyatā</gloss> is entirely infinite.

The Blessed One replied: Subhuti, it is because of utter purity.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, why is it that because the self is entirely infinite, the purity of the emptiness of nature is entirely infinite?

The Blessed One replied: It is because of the emptiness of that which has passed beyond limits and the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, because the self is entirely infinite, the <term>emptiness of all phenomena</term> <gloss>sarva-dharma-śūnyatā</gloss> is entirely infinite, and the purity of the emptiness of all phenomena is entirely infinite.

The Blessed One replied: Because the self is entirely infinite, it is because of the utter purity of the emptiness of all phenomena.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One?

The Blessed One replied: It is because of the emptiness of that which has passed beyond limits and the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, in the same way the Blessed One replied, and the Blessed One replied, because it is entirely infinite, the purity of the <term>emptiness of non-existence</term> <gloss>abhāva-śūnyatā</gloss> is entirely infinite.

The Blessed One replied: It is because of the emptiness of that which has passed beyond limits and the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, Blessed One, Blessed One.

The Blessed One replied: Blessed One, why is it that <note>the transcription appears repetitive or corrupted here</note> because it is entirely infinite?

The Blessed One replied: Subhuti, it is because of utter purity.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, why is it that there is the emptiness and the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end?

The Blessed One replied: Subhuti, because the self is entirely infinite, the <term>emptiness of its own marks</term> <gloss>svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā</gloss> is entirely infinite.

The Blessed One replied: Subhuti, it is because of utter purity.

Subhuti asked: The Blessed One replied, the Blessed One spoke, and the Blessed One asked, it is because of the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

Subhuti asked: The Blessed One replied, Blessed One, why is the <term>emptiness of essence</term> <gloss>svabhāva-śūnyatā</gloss> itself without beginning or end?

The Blessed One replied: It is because of the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end.

Subhuti asked: Blessed One, the self is without beginning or end, and the Blessed One replied, the Blessed One is without beginning or end.

The Blessed One replied: Blessed One, the Blessed One replied: Subhuti, it is because of utter purity.

Subhuti asked: It was spoken, it is entirely without beginning or end, it was spoken.

<summary>This page contains repetitive dialectical exchanges between Subhuti and the Buddha concerning the emptiness of nature, all phenomena, non-existence, and own-marks. The text emphasizes that these various forms of emptiness are infinite and pure because they transcend temporal beginnings and endings.</summary>
<keywords>emptiness of nature, emptiness of all phenomena, emptiness of non-existence, emptiness of own-marks, purity, Subhuti, infinity</keywords>

༄༅། །བུ་དེས་སྔོན་གྱི་ཚུལ་དྲན་ཏེ་ཤིན་ཏུ་མྱུར་བར་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་དྲིན་བཟོའི་མཆོད་པ་འབུལ་བར་འོངས་སོ། །དེ་ལ་ཆོས་གསུངས་པས་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་
བུ་ཐོབ་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །དེའི་ཚེ་འོད་ཀྱི་སྣང་བ་ཆེན་པོ་བྱུང་བ་མ་ཧེའི་རྫི་བོ་དེ་དག་གིས་མཐོང་ནས་ཐེ་ཙོམ་སྐྱེས་ཏེ། མདངས་གསུམ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཐད་དུ་མཆིས་ཏེ་འོད་ཀྱི་སྣང་བར་བགྱིད་
པ་དེ་སུ་ཞིག་ལེགས་ཅེས་ཞུས་པ་དང་། མཧེད་ལྷར་ཇི་ལྟར་སྐྱེས་པ་སོགས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པས་མ་ཧེའི་རྫི་བོ་དེ་དག་ངོ་མཚར་དུ་གྱུར་ཏེ་དུད་འགྲོའི་སྐྱེས་གནས་སུ་སྐྱེས་པས་ཀྱང་འདི་ལྟར་འབྱུང་བ་བདག་
ཅག་གིས་ཅི་སྟེ་ཁྱད་པར་མི་ཐོབ་སྙམ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དགེ་འདུན་དང་བཅས་པ་ཞལ་ཟས་བཟང་པོས་ཚིམས་པར་བྱས་ནས་རབ་ཏུ་བྱུང་སྟེ། བརྩོན་པ་ཆེན་པོས་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་
དུ་བྱས་སོ། །ཡང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཚལ་དུ་བཞུགས་པའི་སྐབས་ཅིག །རྒྱལ་པོ་གསལ་རྒྱལ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱ་བའི་སྦྱོང་བ་དང་། པན་ཙ་ལའི་རྒྱལ་པོས་ཀོ་ས་ལའི་
རྒྱལ་པོ་གསལ་རྒྱལ་ལ་དཔྲལ་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་སྐྱེས་སུ་བཀུར་སྟེ་ངང་པ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཚལ་དུ་ཕུལ་ལོ། །གང་གི་ཚེ་སངས་རྒྱས་དགེ་འདུན་དང་བཅས་བ་བཤོལ་གསོལ་ཞིང་བཞུགས་པའི་ཚེ་ངང་པ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་བཅོ་
ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཐད་དུ་འགྲོ་ལ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དང་ཉན་ཐོས་ཆེན་པོ་དག་གིས་ཀྱང་དེ་རྣམས་ལ་ཁྱོས་མ་བྱིན་ཏེ། དེ་དག་གིས་ཟོས་ནས་ཚིམ་ཞིང་དབང་པོ་རྟགས་ཏེ་འཁོད་དོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་
ཤས་ཆེ་བ་རྣམས་སྐྱོ་བར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །དེ་ནས་ཨུད་པ་ལས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཞབས་ལ་མགོ་བོས་ཕྱག་འཚལ་ཏེ། བདག་གི་ནས་རྣག་ཅན་གྱི་ལུས་འདི་ལས་ཚོགས་ཆུང་ངུས་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲོལ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཆོས་
བསྟན་དུ་གསོལ་ཞེས་གསོལ་བ་གཏབ་པ་དང་། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་གསུངས་པས། འཁོར་དེ་ལས་ཁ་ཅིག་གི་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ། ཁ་ཅིག་གིས་ཕྱིར་འོངས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་
ཐོབ་པར་གྱུར། ཁ་ཅིག་གིས་ཕྱིར་མི་འོངས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པར་གྱུར། ཁ་ཅིག་གི་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉིད་ཐོབ་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །ཨུད་པ་ལ་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་ལ་དད་པ་རྙེད་ནས་རབ་ཏུ་བྱུང་ཞིང་བརྩོན་
པ་ཆེན་པོས་སྒྲུབས་ཏེ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉིད་མངོན་དུ་བྱས་སོ། །གར་མཁན་དེ་དག་གིས་ཀྱང་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་བྱས་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །ཡང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀ་ཙང་ག་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ནགས་ཁྲོད་
ན་བཞུགས་པའི་དུས། ཡུལ་དེ་ན་རྒན་མོ་ཀ་ཙང་ག་ལ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཞིག་གནས་པ་དེས་བུམ་པ་ཐོགས་ཏེ་ཁྲོན་པའི་དྲུང་དུ་ཆུ་ཆུར་སོང་བ་དང་། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀིས་ཀུན་དགའ་བོ་ལ་ཁྱོད་སོང་ལ་རྒན་
མོ་དེ་ལ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སྐྱེམས་ཀྱིས་ཆུ་ཕུལ་ཅིག་ཅེས་གྱིས་ཤིག་ཅེས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ་དང་། ཀུན་དགའ་བོ་སོང་ནས་དེ་སྐད་བསྒོས་པ་དང་། འཕགས་པ་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་འཚལ་ཏེ་མཆིའོ་ཞེས་

ཀྱི་ཅང་མི་གསུང་བས་གནང་སྟེ། འཁོར་མང་པོ་དང་བཅས་མཉན་ཡོད་ཕྱོགས་སུ་ཆས་ཏེ་གཤེགས་སོ། །ཕོ་ཉ་བ་ཡང་ཤིང་རྟ་ལ་ཞོན་ནས་ཆས་སོ། །དེ་ནས་ཕོ་ཉ་བ་དེས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཞབས་ཐང་ལ་
གཤེགས་པ་མཐོང་སྟེ་ཤིང་རྟ་ལ་བབས་ནས་ཐལ་མོ་སྦྱར་བ་བཏུད་ནས་ཐུགས་རྩེ་བའི་སླད་དུ་བདག་གི་ཤིང་རྟ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བཞེས་སུ་གསོལ་ཞེས་སྨྲས་པ་དང་། རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་རྐང་པའི་ཤིང་རྟ་དང་། །
ཡང་དག་རྩོལ་ལ་ང་གནས་ནས། །ཉོན་མོངས་ཚེར་མས་མ་སྣང་པར། །ས་སྟེངས་ཀུན་ཏུ་རྒྱུ་བར་བྱེད་ཅེས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ་དང་། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི་ཞབས་ཀྱི་གཤེགས་པ་ལས་ཀྱང་བདག་ལ་
ཕན་གདགས་པ་དང་ཐུགས་རྩེ་བའི་སླད་དུབ་ཅིབས་སུ་གསོལ་ཞེས་གསོལ་བ་གཏབ་པ་དང་། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདའས་ཕོ་ཉ་དེ་ལ་ཕན་གདགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱིས་ཤིང་རྟའི་སྟེང་དུ་བཞུགས་སོ། །དེ་ནས་བཅོམ་
ལྡན་འདས་ཤིང་རྟ་ལ་བཅིབས་བཞིན་དེའི་མཚན་མོ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཚལ་དུ་ཕེབས་སོ། །རྒྱལ་པོ་དང་བློན་པོ་དང་ཕོ་བྲང་འཁོར་གྱི་མི་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བསུ་བ་བྱས་ཤིང་ཆོས་མཉན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེའི་མཚན་མོ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་
ཚལ་དུ་འཁོད་དོ། །ཕོ་ཉ་དེ་ནི་ཚེ་ཐུང་སྟེ་ཆོས་ཐོས་པའི་འོག་ཏུ་དེའི་མཚན་མོ་ཤི་ནས་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གསུམ་པའི་ལྷར་སྐྱེས་སོ། །དེ་ནས་ཕོ་ཉ་བ་ལྷར་སྐྱེས་པ་དེས་གང་ནས་ཤི་འཕོས་གང་དུ་སྐྱེས་ལས་
གང་གི་སྐྱེས་སྙམ་དུ་བསམ་པས། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་སེམས་དགའ་བར་གྱུར་པས་མི་ལས་ཤི་འཕོས་ནས་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གསུམ་པའིལྷར་སྐྱེས་པ་ཤེས་ནས། བདག་ཞག་ལོན་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་
བོ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཐག་རིང་པོ་ཞིག་ནས་མཐོང་སྟེ། སྐད་ཆེན་པོས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་འདིར་ནི་མ་ཧེ་མ་རུངས་པ་མཆིས་ཀྱིས་ཤུལ་འདིར་མི་གཤེགས་སུ་གསོལ་ཞེས་སྨྲས་པ་དང་། ཀྱཻ་ངས་དུས་ཤེས་
ཀྱི་ཁྱེད་སྙིང་མ་ཆུང་ཞིག་ཅེས་གསུངས་ནས་གཤེགས་སོ། །དེ་ནས་མ་ཧེ་དེས་རིང་པོ་ཞིག་ནས་མཐོང་བ་དང་། རྔ་མ་ལྡང་དུ་གཟེར་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ག་ལ་བ་དེར་བརྒྱུགས་སོ། །དེ་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་
འདས་ཀྱི་མདུན་ལོགས་སུ་སེང་གེ་རལ་པ་ཅན་ལྔ་སྤྲུལ། གློ་གཡས་གཡོན་དུ་མེ་ཆེན་པོ་ལྔ་སྤྲུལ་ཏོ། །སྟེང་དུ་ནི་ལྕགས་ཀྱི་ཕ་བོང་ཆེན་པོ་ཞིག་སྤྲུལ་ཏོ། །དེ་ནས་མ་ཧེ་དེས་ཕྱོགས་ཀུན་ཏུ་འཇིགས་པ་ཆེན་
པོ་མཐོང་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་ཞབས་དྲུང་དུ་སོང་སྟེ་ཞབས་ལ་ལྕེས་བལྡགས་ནས་ཞུམ་པའི་བཞིན་གྱི་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་བལྟས་སོ། །དེ་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡནའདས་ཀྱི་དེ་ལ་བཞིན་བཟང་འདི་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་
ཐམས་ཅད་མི་རྟག་པའོ། །ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདག་མེད་པའོ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ནི་ཞི་བའོ། །ཞེས་ཆོས་ཚིགས་གསུམ་བསྟན་ནས་ཚེ་རབས་དྲན་པར་མཛད་པས་དེས་དུས་སོ། །དེ་ནས་ཡང་ཁྱོད་ནི་དུད་
འགྲོར་སྐྱེས་པ་ལ། །ད་ནི་ང་ཡི་ཅི་བྱར་ཡོད། །མི་ཁོམ་པར་ནི་སྐྱེས་ཟིན་གྱིས། །དོན་མེད་དུས་པས་ཅི་ལ་ཕན། །འདིར་ནི་རྒྱལ་བ་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཅན། །ང་ལ་དད་པའི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ལ། །དུད་འགྲོའི་

...that son of the gods remembered his former state and came very quickly to offer worship to the Blessed One to repay his kindness. Because the Dharma was taught to him, he obtained the fruit of Stream-entry. At that time, the buffalo herders saw the appearance of the great light and were filled with doubt. They went to the Blessed One and asked, "Who was it that made such a great light last night?" 

When the Buddha told the story of how the buffalo was reborn as a god, the buffalo herders were filled with wonder and thought, "If even one born in an animal state can achieve such a result, why should we not obtain something special?" They satisfied the Blessed One and the Sangha with excellent food, then took ordination and, through great diligence, manifested the state of an Arhat <note>original: "Dgra bcom pa"</note>.

Again, at one time when the Blessed One was staying in Jetavana, King Prasenajit was preparing to make offerings to the Blessed One. The King of Panchala sent five hundred geese as a gift to King Prasenajit of Kosala, who then offered those geese to the Jetavana grove. Whenever the Buddha and the Sangha were taking their meals, the geese would go to the Blessed One. The Blessed One and the great disciples would give them scraps of food; the geese would eat, be satisfied, and their faculties would become clear. 

The majority of those who heard the Blessed One's Dharma became weary <note>of samsara</note>. Then Utpala prostrated with her head at the Blessed One's feet and requested, "Please teach me the Dharma so that I may be completely liberated from this body of pus and blood through a small amount of merit." 

When the Blessed One taught the Dharma, some of the assembly obtained the fruit of Stream-entry <note>original: "Rgyun du zhugs pa"</note>. Some obtained the fruit of Once-returner <note>original: "Phyir 'ongs pa"</note>. Some obtained the fruit of Non-returner <note>original: "Phyir mi 'ongs pa"</note>. Some obtained the state of an Arhat. Utpala also found faith in the Buddha, was ordained, and through great diligence in practice, manifested the state of an Arhat. Those dancers also manifested the state of an Arhat.

Again, when the Blessed One was staying in the forest called Kachangala, an old woman named Kachangala lived in that country. She took a jar and went to a well for water. The Blessed One said to Ananda, "Go and ask that old woman to give some water to the Blessed One for his thirst." Ananda went and told her this, and she replied, "I will come myself to serve the Noble One."

plus difficiles à rendre les uns que les autres ; on est pour lors obligé de les ajuster en plaçant des lévres sur une plus grande ou plus petite corde du trou de la Flute, en donnant un vent plus ou moins fort, ce que fait l'homme dans les mêmes tons, où il est obligé de ménager son vent, & de tourner la Flute plus ou moins en dedans ou en dehors.

On conçoit facilement que toutes les lames placées sur le cilindre font plus ou moins longues, suivant le tems que doit avoir chaque note, & suivant la différente situation où doivent se trouver les doigts pour les former : ce que je ne détaillerai point ici, de crainte de passer les bornes d'un Mémoire concis, que je me suis proposé de donner.

Je ferai remarquer seulement que dans les enflemens de son, il a fallu, pendant le tems de la même note, substituer imperceptiblement un vent foible à un vent fort, & à un plus fort, un plus foible, & varier conjointement les mouvemens des lévres, c'est-à-dire, les mettre dans leur situation propre pour chaque vent.

Lorsqu'il a fallu faire le doux, c'est-à-dire, imiter un écho, on a été obligé de faire avancer les lévres sur le bord du trou de la Flute, & envoyer un vent suffisant pour former un tel ton ; mais dont le retour, par une issuë aussi petite, qu'est celle de son entrée dans la Flute, ne peut frapper qu'une petite quantité d'air extérieur : ce qui produit, comme je l'ai dit ci-dessus, ce qu'on appelle écho.

Les différens airs de lenteur & de mouvement ont été mesurés sur le cilindre, par le moyen d'un lévier, dont une extrémité armée d'une pointe pouvoit, lorsqu'on frappoit dessus, marquer ce même cilindre.

A l'autre bras du levier étoit un ressort, qui faisoit promptement relever la pointe.

On lâchoit le mouvement, qui faisoit tourner le cilindre avec une vîtesse déterminée pour tous les airs.

Dans le même tems une personne joüoit sur la Flute l'air qu'on vouloit mesurer ; un autre battoit la mesure sur le bout du lévier qui pointoit le cilindre, & la distance qui se trouvoit entre les points, étoit la vraie mesure des airs qu'on vouloit noter ; on subdivisoit ensuite les intervales en autant de parties que la mesure avoit de tems.

pour les former tous; c'est la différente ouverture des trous, par la levée des doigts, qui les caractérise : on est seulement obligé de placer sur le cilindre des lames sous les léviers, qui doivent lever les doigts pour former un tel ton.

Pour avoir les tons de la seconde octave, il faut changer l'embouchure de situation, c'est-à-dire, placer une lame dessous le lévier, qui contribue à faire avancer les lévres au-delà du diamétre du trou de la Flute, et imiter par-là l'action de l'homme vivant, qui en pareil cas tourne la Flute un peu en dedans.

Secondement il faut placer une lame sous le lévier, qui en faisant raprocher les deux lévres, diminue leur ouverture ; opération que fait pareillement l'homme, quand il serre les lévres pour donner une moindre issuë au vent.

Troisiémement, il faut placer une lame sous le lévier, qui fait ouvrir la soupape du reservoir, qui contient le vent provenant des soufflets chargés du poids de deux livres ; vent, qui se trouve poussé avec plus de force, et semblable à celui que l'homme vivant pousse par une plus forte compression des muscles pectoraux. De plus on place des lames sous les léviers nécessaires pour faire lever les doigts qu'il faut.

Il s'ensuivra de toutes ces différentes opérations, qu'un vent envoyé avec plus de force, et passant par une issuë plus petite, redoublera de vitesse, et produira par conséquent les vibrations doubles, et ce sera l'octave.

A mesure qu'on monte dans les tons supérieurs de cette seconde octave, il faut de plus en plus serrer les lévres, pour que le vent, dans un même tems, augmente de vitesse.

Dans les tons de la troisiéme octave, les mêmes léviers qui vont à la bouche, agissent comme dans ceux de la seconde, avec cette différence, que les lames sont un peu plus élevées : ce qui fait que les lévres vont tout-à-fait sur le bord du trou de la Flute, et que le trou qu'elles forment devient extrémement petit. On ajoute seulement une lame sous le lévier qui fait ouvrir la soupape, pour donner le vent qui vient des soufflets les plus chargés, sçavoir, du poids de quatre livres. Par conséquent, le vent poussé avec une plus forte compression, et trouvant une issuë encore plus petite, augmentera de vitesse en raison triple : on aura donc le triple octave.

them all to form them; it is the different opening of the holes, through the lifting of the fingers, that characterizes them: one is only obliged to place plates on the cylinder under the levers, which must lift the fingers to form such a tone.

To have the tones of the second octave, it is necessary to change the position of the embouchure, that is to say, to place a plate under the lever, which contributes to making the lips advance beyond the diameter of the hole of the Flute, and thereby imitate the action of the living man, who in such a case turns the Flute a little inward.

Secondly, one must place a plate under the lever, which, by making the two lips draw closer, diminishes their opening; an operation that the man likewise performs when he tightens his lips to give less outlet to the wind.

Thirdly, one must place a plate under the lever, which causes the valve of the reservoir to open, which contains the wind coming from the bellows loaded with the weight of two pounds; wind, which is found to be pushed with more force, and similar to that which the living man pushes through a stronger compression of the pectoral muscles. Furthermore, one places plates under the levers necessary to make the required fingers lift.

It will follow from all these different operations that a wind sent with more force, and passing through a smaller outlet, will redouble in speed, and will consequently produce double vibrations, and this will be the octave.

As one climbs into the higher tones of this second octave, it is necessary to tighten the lips more and more, so that the wind, at the same time, increases in speed.

In the tones of the third octave, the same levers that go to the mouth act as in those of the second, with this difference, that the plates are a little higher: which causes the lips to go entirely to the edge of the hole of the Flute, and the hole that they form becomes extremely small. One only adds a plate under the lever that causes the valve to open, to give the wind that comes from the most heavily loaded bellows, namely, of the weight of four pounds. Consequently, the wind pushed with a stronger compression, and finding an even smaller outlet, will increase in speed in triple proportion: one will therefore have the triple octave.

There are tones, in all these different octaves,
auditTranslation:
<header>( 16 )</header>

more difficult to render than others; one is then obliged to adjust them by placing lips on a larger or smaller string of the Flute hole, by giving a more or less strong wind, which the man does in the same tones, where he is obliged to manage his wind, and to turn the Flute more or less inward or outward.

One easily conceives that all the plates placed on the cylinder are more or less long, according to the time that each note must have, and according to the different situation where the fingers must be found to form them: which I will not detail here, for fear of passing the limits of a concise Memoir, which I have proposed to give.

I will only remark that in the swells of sound, it was necessary, during the time of the same note, to substitute imperceptibly a weak wind for a strong one, and to a stronger one, a weaker one, and to vary jointly the movements of the lips, that is to say, to put them in their proper situation for each wind.

When it was necessary to perform the soft <term>doux</term> <gloss>a musical term for piano or soft volume</gloss>, that is to say, to imitate an echo, one was obliged to make the lips advance to the edge of the hole of the Flute, and send a sufficient wind to form such a tone; but whose return, through an outlet as small as that of its entry into the Flute, can only strike a small quantity of exterior air: which produces, as I have said above, what one calls an echo.

The different airs of slowness and movement were measured on the cylinder, by the means of a lever, of which one extremity armed with a point could, when one struck upon it, mark this same cylinder.

At the other arm of the lever was a spring, which made the point rise again promptly.

One released the movement, which made the cylinder turn with a determined speed for all the airs.

In the same time a person played on the Flute the air that one wished to measure; another beat the measure on the end of the lever which pointed the cylinder, and the distance which was found between the points, was the true measure of the airs that one wished to note; one then subdivided the intervals into as many parts as the measure had beats.

○ The functions of the nose are twofold: 1. Distinguishing fragrance and foulness. 2. Clarifying the voice and expanding respiration. 3. Facilitating sleep and the discharge of mucus. 4. Nasal hairs prevent mucus from flowing freely and block dust and small insects from entering.

○ Chapter Twelve: The Tongue

○ The tongue is like a piece of flesh that is capable of movement. It is located inside the mouth, between the upper and lower jaws. It is the tool for regulating speech and perceiving taste. Its shape is blunt and round, narrow at the front and [broad] at the back.
auditTranslation:
The tongue tip is the narrow part at the front.
The root of the tongue is the broad part at the back. It is positioned alongside the throat.
In the center of the tongue, there is a longitudinal line. It appears when contracted and disappears when extended.
○ The front is flexible and loose; the back is firmly attached.
○ The back, facing the throat, is connected to the hyoid bone <note>original: 舌骨</note> by a membrane.
The hyoid bone is described in Volume Five. Its function is to allow the tongue to move and oscillate. The muscles attached to it, specifically the muscles connecting the chest to the hyoid bone, serve to lift the tongue and the hyoid bone and pull them backward.

The eight limbs of Yoga will be described. Through their practice, the five-fold error (<term>viparyaya</term>), which is the form of impurity, is destroyed. Upon its destruction, there is a manifestation of correct knowledge. As the practices are performed, the impurity gradually becomes thin. As it thins, the light of knowledge, corresponding to the sequence of destruction, increases. This increase attains its peak up to discriminative realization, meaning until the knowledge of the nature of the <term>guṇas</term> and the <term>puruṣa</term>. The practice of the limbs of Yoga is the cause of the separation from impurity, just as an axe is the cause of separation from what is to be cut. As for discriminative realization, it is the cause of attainment, just as merit (<term>dharma</term>) is for happiness; it is not a cause in any other way. How many such causes are there in the scriptures? It says there are only nine. That is to say:

> "Creation, existence, manifestation, change, cognition, attainment,
> separation, distinctness, and support—the cause is remembered as ninefold."

Among these, the mind is the cause of creation for knowledge; the purpose of the <term>puruṣa</term> is the cause of existence for the mind, just as food is for the body. The cause of manifestation...

<column-break/>

They destroy impurity through the direct and indirect paths of Yoga. "Five-fold error" is an indicator; merit and demerit are also forms of impurity, as they are the causes of birth, lifespan, and experience. The rest is easy. Because we see various types of causality, one might ask what kind of cause the practice of the limbs of Yoga is. It says: **"Practice of the limbs of Yoga,"** etc. It causes separation of the mind-stuff from impurity, so it is the "cause of separation from impurity." It provides an example: **"Just as an axe."** The axe separates the tree from its roots. By separating the mind-stuff from impurity, it leads to discriminative realization, just as merit leads to happiness. Thus, the practice of the limbs of Yoga is the "cause of attainment" of discriminative realization; it says it is not in any other way. Because of the hearing of this exclusion, one asks: **"How many are these?"** The answer: **"Only nine."** It shows them by a verse: **"That is to say—creation,"** etc.

Here, it provides examples: "Among these, the cause of creation," etc. The mind, by removing the unmanifested state and bringing the knowledge to its present state, is the cause of creation of knowledge. "Cause of existence for the mind is the purpose of the <term>puruṣa</term>." The mind, once arisen from egoism (<term>asmitā</term>), remains as long as it has not fulfilled the various purposes of the <term>puruṣa</term>. Once the two-fold purpose of the <term>puruṣa</term> is fulfilled, it departs from existence. Therefore, the unfulfilled purpose of the <term>puruṣa</term> is the cause of existence for the mind, which has arisen from its own cause. It provides an example: **"Just as for the body,"** etc.

Here, it gives a demonstration: **"Just as fire is for what is to be cooked,"** like rice, which is the cause of the change—the softening of the conjunction of parts of something previously hard. For something that already exists, the cause of cognition is the knowledge of smoke for the knowledge of fire. "Knowledge" is that which is known, and "fire" is the knowledge; it is the knowledge of fire. This is what is meant: for the existing fire that is to be known, it is the cause of the cognition. The acquisition of the work of causes that are independent and standard is attainment; the absence of it from somewhere is non-attainment. Just as the flow of water, which naturally moves downwards, is blocked by a dam, so here too, the natural capacity of the mind-stuff—which is of the nature of happiness and light—to generate discriminative realization is attainment. That does not happen because of the obstruction of merit or darkness (<term>tamas</term>). Through merit—or the practice of the limbs of Yoga—upon its removal, it attains that capacity to generate it because its nature is to have unobstructed movement. As it will say: "The cause is not the activator of the *prakṛtis* <gloss>primordial nature</gloss>, but the breaking of the cover, like a farmer."

Thus, the cause of attainment has been stated in relation to the work characterized as discriminative realization. However, it says it is also the cause of separation in relation to secondary works: **"Cause of separation."** It states the cause of distinctness: **"Cause of distinctness is like the goldsmith for gold,"** such as a bracelet, earring, or armlet, which are different or non-different from the gold. In terms of intent, when one wants to distinguish it from the bracelet, the gold is different from the earring; when one wants to see them as non-different, the bracelet and the gold are non-different. Thus, the bracelet-maker, the goldsmith, by making the earring different from the gold that is non-different, is the cause of distinctness. Although fire is also the cause of distinctness for what is cooked, one cannot say it is the cause of distinctness for the substance because the qualities of being *pulāka* <gloss>grain</gloss> and *taṇḍula* <gloss>rice</gloss> are fleeting, while the substance remains. ### LES EXPÉRIENCES MAGIQUES DU GROUPE INDÉPENDANT D'ÉTUDES ÉSOTÉRIQUES.

En 1889, nous avons fondé à Paris le *Groupe indépendant d'études ésotériques*, destiné à contrôler les expériences concernant les forces encore inconnues en action dans l'homme et dans la nature.

Les premiers mois furent consacrés à la propagande et les travaux purent être fructueusement poursuivis dès le début de l'année 1891. A ce moment le groupe était divisé en sections techniques dont l'une s'occupait de Magie pratique. Personnellement nous avions fait quelques expériences suivies de succès, ainsi que notre ami F. Ch. Barlet ; mais ces expériences avaient besoin d'un contrôle que la suite des études pouvait seule fournir. L'année 1891 fut consacrée aux études préliminaires, et au commencement de 1892 plusieurs essais, accompagnés d'entraînement végétarien et concernant la vision des élémentals, furent entrepris et couronnés de succès, principalement en ce qui touche les expériences de M. Delfosse. Au milieu de l'année, des faits rapportés dans les grimoires furent soumis à un contrôle expérimental et M. Michelet, un des commissaires, put même certifier le fait que le diamant pur empêchait le passage de l'action magnétique de l'aimant. Ce fait rapporté par Agrippa et inconnu des physiciens modernes est familier aux marchands de diamants, ainsi qu'il fut constaté. En même temps, une expérience d'évocation consciente fut tentée par M. M. H. et, malgré des oublis et des fautes nombreuses, cette expérience donna des résultats très curieux et très instructifs. Nous en rapporterons les principaux détails d'après les opérateurs eux-mêmes.

Au mois de mars 1892, en période de lune croissante, MM. H. et K., membres d'une commission d'enquête des phénomènes magiques, tentèrent l'expérience suivante qui fut conduite dans le secret le plus absolu :

### THE MAGICAL EXPERIMENTS OF THE INDEPENDENT GROUP FOR ESOTERIC STUDIES.

In 1889, we founded the *Independent Group for Esoteric Studies* <note>original: "Groupe indépendant d'études ésotériques"</note> in Paris, intended to control experiments concerning the forces still unknown in action within man and in nature.

The first months were devoted to propaganda, and the work could be fruitfully pursued from the beginning of the year 1891. At that moment, the group was divided into technical sections, one of which dealt with Practical Magic. Personally, we had conducted some experiments followed by success, as well as our friend F. Ch. Barlet; but these experiments needed a control that only the continuation of studies could provide. The year 1891 was devoted to preliminary studies, and at the beginning of 1892 several trials, accompanied by vegetarian training and concerning the vision of elementals, were undertaken and crowned with success, principally regarding the experiments of M. Delfosse. In the middle of the year, facts reported in the <term>grimoires</term> <gloss>books of magic spells</gloss> were submitted to experimental control and M. Michelet, one of the commissioners, could even certify the fact that pure diamond prevented the passage of the magnetic action of the magnet. This fact, reported by Agrippa and unknown to modern physicists, is familiar to diamond merchants, as it was noted. At the same time, an experiment of conscious evocation was attempted by M. M. H. and, despite numerous oversights and errors, this experiment yielded very curious and very instructive results. We will report the main details according to the operators themselves.

Subhuti, if the Bodhisattva, the great being, practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, through skillful means...

...practices the perfection, he practices up to the eighteen unshared Buddha-qualities, yet he does not apprehend the unshared Buddha-qualities or the one meditating on them. If he does not practice otherwise than those two dharmas, then at that time, the Bodhisattva, the great being, attains the path of enlightenment. Subhuti, if the Bodhisattva, the great being, practices the perfection of wisdom in this way, through skillful means, he manifests as complete and perfect buddhahood in unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. But if you cannot restrain that desire which you have persuaded yourself to reach toward truth by reason, many and long detours must be tolerated by you, so that reason does not lead you except by that which alone should be called reason, that is, true reason, and not only true, but so certain and alien to any semblance of falsehood, if it can indeed be found by man at all, so that no false or plausible disputations can lead you astray from it. Nothing is desired more prosperously. Let reason act and lead where it will, provided it leads correctly. God will do this, who must be invoked through such things alone, or certainly through these. But let us return to the matter I had instituted. For if it is known to you what a line is and what a figure is, tell me, I ask you, whether you think that figure can be made if the line is led to infinity from one side or the other? I affirm that this can be done in no way. What must be done so that I may make a figure? What else but that that line not be infinite and be led in a circle so that it reaches itself from the other side? I do not see how any space can be enclosed by one line unless it is done according to your description; it will not be a figure. If you wish to make a figure with straight lines, can it be done, or can it not be done from one line? By no means, nor from two. What about three? I see it can be done. Well then, you know and hold that a figure is to be made with three straight lines, and it cannot be done with fewer than three; if anything should oppose you, this reasoning will recall you to the truth. Clearly, if someone showed me this, there is nothing I would trust that I could know. Now, therefore, answer me how you will make a figure with three lines. When they join themselves at the ends. What, where they join themselves? Do you not see that angles are made? It is so. How many angles, therefore, does this figure consist of? The same number as the lines, M. Did you constitute the lines themselves as equal or unequal? D. Equal. M. What about the angles? They are patent. Or is one different from the other, either larger or smaller? Furthermore, I see that they themselves are also equal. Can it be made so that in a figure which is made with three equal straight lines, the angles are unequal or not?

Do you see how much equality you can find in them? D. I see it. D. I see it and hold it most firmly. M. Does nothing move you, even in these things, with such a great and hidden justice? D. In what way? M. That I think there is no justice except equality. And equity is indeed called by a certain derivation from equality, and what is equity in this virtue except that each be given his own?
